Thus far [the Zohar]. And this is what is intended in the verse "And God called," [referring to] the Mother who crowns [me'ateret] the firmament with the diadem [atarah] called "Heaven." And he brought a proof for this from the verse "And there was evening and there was morning, one day," explaining "evening" as Isaac and "morning" as Abraham. In their totality together, Tiferet comes into being and is clothed — which is called "one day," and this is "Heaven." And the totality of "Heaven" (shamayim) is "day," which is fire and water (esh u-mayim), evening and morning. And therefore he said "one day" (yom echad) — unified, for it unifies the two aspects. And we may say that from there [come] the twelve hours, in that it is seen [as] Vav in its full spelling, which equals "echad" (one). And the explanation: two faces unify [it]. A Vav from the right side is one face, a Vav from the left side is one face, and an Alef in the middle unifies the two faces together. And this is "echad" (one); and the two Vavs are the twelve hours: six [hours] of the rising of the morning until midday, which is Chesed; six from noon until night, which is the evening, Gevurah — this is "one day." There is no need to elaborate here. And it would have been possible to multiply proofs concerning the matter of Tiferet's arbitration between Gedulah and Gevurah; but since it is a simple and agreed-upon matter, we needed this only in order to understand this passage properly. And we have derived that Tiferet tips the balance between Gedulah and Gevurah, and they are two, one against one.

Tiferet further tips the balance between Gedulah and Hod, and between Gevurah and Netzach. The reason is that Gedulah and Netzach are the right side, Chesed; and Gevurah and Hod are Din, the left; and they require arbitration. And there is some proof for this from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Parashat Pinchas, folio 244a), whose words are: "And in the first composition: 'I have gathered my myrrh with my spice' [Song of Songs 5:1] — the right arm with the left thigh; 'my honeycomb with my honey' — Jacob with Rachel; 'my wine with my milk' — the left arm with the right thigh. Chesed with Hod — these are the right arm with the left thigh; Jacob with Rachel — the central pillar with Malkhut; Gevurah with Netzach — these are the left arm with the right thigh. And why are His attributes thus [crossed]? Rather, it is a secret that says thus. David said here, 'Let Your priests be clothed in righteousness, and let Your devoted ones sing for joy' [Psalms 132:9], and it is said there [that] 'and let Your Levites sing for joy' he ought to have said. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: it is not the way of the world to change My attributes; rather, after you have invited Me, it is for Me to do your desire [re'uta]. From here we learn that a householder who invites even a king — the king must do the host's desire; and therefore we have established: 'Whatever the master of the house tells you, do,' etc. And with all this, this secret is fitting," etc. Thus far his words.

What there is to be roused about in this passage is the prolixity of its language and the repetition of the matter, albeit not in different words. In his saying "the right arm with the left thigh, Chesed with Hod," etc. — have we not heard before now that the two arms are Gedulah (the right arm) and Gevurah (the left arm), and the two legs which are Netzach (the right leg) and Hod (the left leg)? And what need is there for this prolixity in explaining matters that are simple? Second, from the outset he should have used brief and clear language: "my myrrh with my spice" — Chesed with Hod; "my honeycomb with my honey" — the central pillar with Malkhut; "my wine with my milk" — Gevurah with Netzach; and been silent about "thighs and arms," so that he would not then need to explain them afterward. Third, the principal version of this passage is in Parashat Pinchas (folio 241a), for he said "and in the first composition" — the explanation in the Zohar being that it was the book prior to this one; and there in Parashat Pinchas he did not elaborate, neither in full nor in part, but only the beginning of the passage. And these are its words: "'I have gathered my myrrh with my spice' — the right arm with the left thigh; 'my honeycomb with my honey' — Jacob with Rachel; 'my wine with my milk' — the left arm with the right thigh." Thus far its words. And although he elaborated there on the matter of the arbitration, [with] the title "my myrrh" which is Chesed, and "my spice" Netzach, as expounded — nevertheless regarding the explanation of the words he did not elaborate further. And one must consider why he did not adopt this correspondence here. Fourth, in his saying "Jacob with Rachel," he did not say "the body (gufa) with the female (nukva)," in the manner and correspondence of the limbs that he attributed to the other sefirot. Fifth, after he set out to explain his words by saying "and these are," etc., it would have been fitting for him to say "the right arm with the left thigh — Chesed with Hod," for this is the correct order, and not to put the interpretation before the [scriptural] phrase by saying "Chesed with Hod — the right arm with the left thigh," etc., and so for all of them. Sixth, that which he found difficult — "and why are the attributes thus [crossed]?" — what is the difficulty? For sometimes Netzach draws sustenance from Gevurah, and likewise Hod from Chesed, even though most of their nourishment is Netzach from Chesed and Hod from Gevurah. For sometimes it happens, according to the blendings and the emanations, that Netzach draws from Gevurah and Hod from Chesed; and therefore each one includes all of them, so that they all agree to one action and one effluence. And therefore it is possible for two opposites to be equalized, even Gevurah with Chesed. And we shall explain that Rashbi, peace be upon him, found difficulty in the verse: for it would have been fitting to say "I have gathered my myrrh and my spice, I have eaten my honeycomb and my honey, I have drunk my wine and my milk" — why "with...with" (im, im)? For it is superfluous. To this he answered that there, above the passage before us (printed in Parashat Vayikra, folio 4b — see there), he said: "my myrrh with my spice" — Chesed with Netzach; "my honeycomb with my honey" — Gevurah with Hod; "my wine with my milk" — body and covenant (guf u-brit).

Now by this our question is partly resolved: that he said "with...with" in order to unite these attributes in the aforementioned manner. But because this answer is not sufficient — since the verse's intent is only to unite Chesed with Netzach, Gevurah with Hod, and Tiferet with Yesod — and nevertheless he could have been silent about "with...with," and it would be understood on its own that he means they are united, since this is their way, for three are united with three — therefore he said "and in the first composition" — explained in the Zohar in Parashat Pinchas — where another, more expansive interpretation is set forth, namely: "the right arm with the left thigh," the intent being that Chesed, despite its being the line of Chesed, is united with Hod, despite its being the line of Din. And likewise Gevurah, despite its being the line of Din, is united with Netzach, despite its being the line of Chesed. And now there is no difficulty as to why he said "with...with," for it was necessary because this is not their usual way. And since it is the reverse of their custom and nature, he therefore needed to say "with...with" in order to inform us of the reversal of this order. And the reason the Zohar spoke in the language of the titles of the limbs — "thighs and arms" — and not the attributes by their names, is that he found difficulty: since he interpreted the sefirot as reversed, contrary to their order, that is an impossible thing. For the manner of Netzach's nourishment is from the right, and likewise it is beneath Chesed, the line of Chesed; and the manner of Hod's nourishment is from the left, and likewise it is beneath Gevurah, the line of Din. And how is it possible that they should change their function? For this is impossible. And in order to explain this matter to us with a forceful figure of speech, he employed the language "thighs and arms," to tell you: that just as the thighs and the arms are joined together and connected with the body, and by means of the body it unites the right arm with the left thigh, and likewise the left arm with the right thigh — the central body being what unites and couples them together — so too is the matter above, by means of Tiferet, which branches out into the six extremities, and the extremities are its limbs; just as the limbs are branches to the body, so the extremities are limbs and branches to Tiferet. And therefore, by means of it, it is possible for these sefirot to be blended in this blending, and it is within possibility and not among the impossible. And nevertheless we have not yet been saved from the question "why are His attributes thus [crossed]?," as we shall explain.

Now the reason has been explained why he was compelled to say "thighs and arms" and not the attributes themselves by their names. But Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Ra'aya Mehemna intended to bring the language of the first composition by quoting its very wording, which is: "I have gathered my myrrh with my spice — the right arm with the left thigh; my honeycomb with my honey — Jacob with Rachel; my wine with my milk — the left arm with the right thigh." Thus far the [first] composition. And he elaborated in explaining the rest of the passage. The intent is to explain to us the fine precision of his language in saying "the right arm with the left thigh," etc. — that the matter is not by way of happenstance, but, with precise intent, that Chesed unites with Hod and not [that] Hod unites with Chesed. That is to say: that the dwelling of Chesed shall be in Hod, and the principal one shall be Chesed; and likewise Gevurah, that its dwelling and seat shall be in Netzach, and the principal one shall be Gevurah (a variant reads "Netzach"), and not the reverse. And likewise Tiferet within Malkhut below. For if we were to say that the principal one is above — the lower [sefirot subsumed] within the upper — the reason for "why are the attributes thus [crossed]?" would not be settled. For then it would emerge that the bride and her attendants ascend to the house of the groom and his attendants. And then it would not be fitting for the bride to change the customs of the groom at all, since she is lodging in his house. Rather, this is correct: Chesed within Hod, Gevurah within Netzach, Tiferet within Malkhut; and these are three upper [sefirot] within three lower. Thus the groom lodges with his attendants in the house of the bride with her attendants; and since he is in the bride's house, it is fitting that he conduct himself according to the bride's will, and it is in her power to change the custom according to her will, as is better in her eyes. And with this there is an answer to the question "why are the attributes thus [crossed]?," etc., as we shall explain, God willing. And this is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, intended in explaining to us the precision of his language, by placing the interpretation of the passage before the passage itself, saying "Chesed with Hod — the right arm with the left thigh," and not the reverse — to alert us to the precision of his language: that with deliberate intent he employed the idiom of "thighs and arms" and not the idiom of the attributes "Chesed and Hod," etc., to teach that this blending is by means of the body. And this he intended by placing the term "Chesed and Hod" before "arm and thigh," as if saying "scrutinize!" — for it would have been possible to be brief and say "Chesed and Hod," the idiom of the attributes, and not the idiom of the limbs; but rather to grant you understanding, that the secret of this blending — which seemingly appears reversed — is set aright by means of the body, which is the central Tiferet, as he explained. And on the contrary, "arm and thigh" is an explanation of "Chesed and Hod," and not [that] "Chesed and Hod" is an explanation of "arm and thigh." And by this we resolve [the fourth point]: that with Jacob and Rachel he did not need to change their names to the names of the bodily limbs, for their matter and their union involves no reversal but is as is customary in the world — Tiferet upon Malkhut — and therefore he did not change them.

And he further granted us understanding: that in the language of the first composition he said "the right arm with the left thigh," and likewise "the left arm with the right thigh," and did not say "with...with" but stated it concisely; whereas in this passage, in his explanation, he interpreted "Chesed with Hod," etc., and said "with...with." "And why are His attributes thus [crossed]?" — the explanation: granted, if we were to interpret that there is no reversal of the attributes except with regard to emanation and nourishment alone — that is, what had occurred to our mind in explaining "the right arm with the left thigh," that its intent is only regarding the effluence, that Chesed emanates into Hod and likewise that Gevurah emanates into Netzach — then it would not be difficult for us at all, for this is the way of the attributes, that these draw from those. But according to what he explained in this passage, "the right arm with the left thigh" means "with" in the full sense — that is, that Chesed unites below within Hod, and Gevurah below within Netzach — then it is difficult: why are the attributes thus [crossed]? For by way of literal union, this is not the way of the union of the sefirot, since Netzach binds with Chesed and Hod with Gevurah, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Thigh of Jacob, God willing, in chapters 3 [and] 4. And the matter is: with regard to emanation, even though Chesed emanates into Hod, nevertheless Hod performs its action, which is the action of Din — even if it does not act with the same force as at the time of its drawing from Gevurah — and there is no concern in this, since there is no reversal in the attributes. But in literal union there is concern, because the action of Din is nullified entirely. For when [Gevurah] wishes to act with the judgment of Gevurah, Netzach will subdue that judgment and not allow it to act, in the secret of the union. And therefore it is difficult: why are the attributes thus [crossed]? For this is a reversal of the attributes and a blocking of judgment, and this is not fitting. And this is the "it is not the way of the world" said to David. And He answered, "for the sake of David Your servant," etc.: He changed [the order] and drew down the power of Rachamim. For even the "song of joy" (rinah), which is from the side of Din, as is known, He wished to be from the side of Chesed; and this will be explained further in the Gate of Essence and Governance, God willing, in chapter 6. And likewise the matter with Tiferet: since it comes to the house of Malkhut, as it says, "I have come into My garden, My sister, [My] bride" [Song of Songs 5:1], it is therefore fitting for it to conduct itself according to her will, even to reversing the attributes, in order to draw down the power of Rachamim all the more. And this is what is said: Chesed within Hod, Gevurah within Netzach, and Jacob within Rachel — for they are three upper [sefirot] within three lower, by means of Jacob the groom who comes to the house of his bride Rachel, as we explained. But if the bride were ascending to the house of the groom, it would not be fitting to change [the order], for it is not the way of the world to change.
Now the explanation of the passage is complete, and we have derived good reason and knowledge that Tiferet also tips the balance between Gedulah and Hod, and between Gevurah and Netzach.

Since in the previous chapter we established, from the aforementioned passage, that Tiferet tips the balance between Gedulah and Hod and between Gevurah and Netzach — and the matter is somewhat strange to the listening ear — we have resolved to establish this topic further and to make the matters intelligible, to show that they are not far from reason nor strange, for the matter is very close to us. The matter is in what is well known: that Tiferet receives from Gedulah and Gevurah and emanates into Netzach and Hod. And there is no doubt that what Tiferet emanates into Hod must contain, within that effluence, a portion of effluence from Gedulah, which Tiferet received from it, as we explained; and likewise what Tiferet emanates into Netzach must contain, within that effluence, a portion from Gevurah. And there is no doubt that the effluence emanated from Tiferet to Netzach and Hod will not be, in its blend, exactly as [Tiferet] received it from Gedulah and Gevurah. Rather, it is blended by means of Tiferet into an intermediate blend, equalized to Gedulah and to Hod, and likewise equalized to Netzach and Gevurah; and thus it emerges that this arbitration is, in part, a constant thing. And sometimes it happens that Tiferet is compelled to have the principal part of its reception be from the judgment of Gevurah, in order to emanate into Netzach for the world's need of judgment — for retribution and the like. Or, because it received much from Gevurah, it emanates it into Netzach in order to sweeten the judgment. And likewise sometimes Tiferet receives much from the side of Chesed and emanates into Hod in order to sweeten Hod. And this blending, and the like, will be explained in the Gate of Channels (Tzinorot), chapter 2, God willing; and the matters are plain to the understanding and straight to those who find knowledge. We shall add further instruction in this matter and establish it from that on which all the Geonim agreed concerning the colors of the sefirot: that the color of Netzach is red inclining toward white, and the color of Hod is white inclining toward red.

Now regarding Netzach they explained that it is red inclining toward white: the explanation of the red is from its reception of the harsh judgment of Gevurah, by means of Tiferet, the arbiter, as explained; and because of this judgment it is red. But from the side of its abundant nourishment from Chesed — for there is its home — its inclination is toward white, to whiten the redness, to return it to white; and this is "inclining," for its intent is that most of it be white. And likewise the matter, in reverse, with Hod: for by its nourishment from Chesed, through Tiferet which equalizes and mediates between them, it is white. But because its principal nourishment is from the side of Gevurah — for there is its principal inclination and place — it must be inclining toward red, and it tips the Rachamim toward the side of Din.
Now it emerges, according to this, that Tiferet mediates by its color — which is of white and red — between Gedulah and Hod, and between Gevurah and Netzach.

And the matter of these colors will be explained in the Gate of Colors, God willing. And praise and thanksgiving to the One who bestows good upon the guilty, who has dealt bountifully with us. "The Lord is God, and He has given us light" [Psalms 118:27], to establish this matter with three faithful witnesses: by the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, by the reasoning of the Kabbalah, and by the words of the Geonim. The sum of the matter: the places requiring arbitration are five against five. Chokhmah against Binah, Gedulah against Gevurah — that is two against two; Gedulah against Hod, Gevurah against Netzach — that is two against two; together they are four against four. Further, Yesod tips the balance between Netzach and Hod, as will be explained in the Gate of Arbiters, chapter 4; thus they are five against five. However, the arbiters between the five and the five are only two: Yesod and Tiferet. How so? Yesod [tips the balance] between Netzach and Hod; and Tiferet [tips the balance] between Gedulah and Gevurah, between Gedulah and Hod, between Gevurah and Netzach, and between Chokhmah and Binah — in a concealed manifestation, in the secret of Da'at, as will be explained in the aforementioned Gate. And with this premise the mishnah that we are explaining will be understood — that it said "five against five" — for in truth they are five against five, and "the covenant of union is set in the middle," for the arbiters are in the middle and are set between the extremities. And "the word of the tongue" is Tiferet, and it is called "the word of the tongue" because, by means of Binah — which is the tongue — it ascends above to tip the balance between Chokhmah and Binah, in the secret of Da'at, as will be explained in the aforementioned Gate. And likewise by means of it [Binah] it mediates between Gedulah and Gevurah, as we explained in chapter 2; and "the word of the member" is Yesod, the second arbiter.

Now by this the matter is further settled, and what we asked is in substance resolved — that they are "five against five" and [with] the arbiter they are eleven — for we are now not [dealing] with the count of the sefirot but with the count of the arbitration, as explained; and there is no need to elaborate.

Now we have explained this mishnah according to the most well-known version in the books and among the commentators. Although it appears that Nachmanides (the Ramban), peace be upon him, had a different reading, nevertheless we shall be concerned only with the consensus of most of the books. And when the student looks at the variant readings, he will find this reading to be more precise; and furthermore, it has not yet been verified that that interpretation is the Ramban's, as appears from an examination of it.

After we have journeyed from the mountain of the Lord — the high and steep mountain that is the previous mishnah, in which we established the consensus of the Kabbalists that the sefirot are ten and no more — let us go to the "mountain of myrrh," the second mishnah relative to it, though it is the fourth from the head of the chapter. And these are its words: "Ten sefirot of belimah: ten and not nine; ten and not eleven. Understand with wisdom (havein be-chokhmah), and be wise with understanding (chakam be-vinah). Test them and probe from them, and know and reckon from them; and set the matter in its clarity, and restore the Former (Yotzer) to His place." Thus far its words.

We have resolved not to raise any difficulties on this mishnah at all, since its words are of themselves not [readily] ordered, and the text "demands to be expounded," and its surface meaning admits of no explanation, so that one must engage it in give-and-take. And we shall write what God places in our mouth concerning "ten and not nine" and its explanation. Namely, that his intent is to warn us against the error of saying that Keter is not among the sefirot — for we might think it is the Ein Sof — which is not so. For "one high above another watches" [Ecclesiastes 5:7]. And [it is] not as many have thought, that the Ein Sof is among the count of the sefirot and that it is Keter. And this opinion we shall refute in the Gate of Whether the Ein Sof is the Keter, God willing — and may the Compassionate One save us from this opinion. Rather, certainly they are ten apart from the Emanator; for otherwise the emanated sefirot would be nine, and this is not fitting. Rather, the emanated [sefirot] themselves are ten and not nine. He further explained that [the mishnah] comes to warn us not to err by separating Malkhut from the count — as there is one who supposed in his reasoning something close to this — and may the Compassionate One also save us from this opinion. Rather, it is with them in Atzilut; and even though it is not in their unity, because it was driven out, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Diminishment of the Moon, God willing. And close to this explanation, Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Parashat Teitzei, folio 277b), whose words are: "And there are others, masters of Scripture, masters of [the] attributes, who inherit souls from the side of the holy Malkhut, which includes ten sefirot — for whoever inherits it and merits it, merits the ten sefirot without separation. 'Ten and not nine,' for if they were to inherit Malkhut as a single one [in isolation], they would be nine, separated from it; and because there is no separation there, the author of the Sefer Yetzirah said 'ten and not nine.' And should you say that it ascends above [beyond] ten — the explicit name is spelled 'Yod-Heh, Vav-Heh,' behold, ten; the Yod that unites with it does not ascend above ten; and therefore 'ten and not eleven.'" Thus far his words.

The intent of this passage, which said "and there are others": for above, in [the context of] this matter, he said that among the men of [pious] deeds there is one who has a soul (neshamah) which is a "handmaid" (amah) from the side of Beriah — and this matter will be explained in the Gate of the Soul, God willing. And now he said that there are others, "masters of Scripture" (marei sifra de-orayta), who are those engaged in the divine Torah and its secrets. And because it might have been said that "masters of Scripture" refers to those engaged in the depths of the laws, homilies, aggadot, statutes, judgments, and ordinances according to the plain sense alone — to this he said that, although the reward of these is doubled and redoubled, and it is the choice portion, nevertheless they do not merit the level of this [particular] soul until they reach the secrets of the sefirot, which are the secret of the Godhead. And these are called "masters of [the] attributes" (marei middot); they are so called because all the engagement of the sages of Kabbalah is in the attributes and their matters. And he said that these inherit a soul from the side of Malkhut itself, not from the side of Metatron the servant, nor from the side of the "handmaid" (amah) mentioned there. And he said that one merits a soul that includes ten. And because he found difficulty — perhaps the other souls too include ten, or perhaps this soul does not include ten; and whence have we the power to distinguish between one soul and another, even though this one is more esteemed than that — to this he establishes that, with [regard to] Malkhut, he means: the soul that is from the side of Malkhut necessarily includes ten, for the reason that the sefirot do not separate but are bound and unified; and when we say "Malkhut," it is necessary that the other sefirot be attached to it. Which is not so with a soul from the side of Metatron or the handmaid, for they are of the world of separation, since they descend from [below] Atzilut. And this necessity applies only in Atzilut and not to them; and therefore [such a soul] would not include ten — only a soul from the side of Malkhut. And what we say — that the soul from the side of Metatron or the handmaid does not include ten — the intent is not that ten are not included in it, in the literal sense. For this is impossible: that there be an action drawn down from above that does not include all ten, for then separation would appear. And this is the reason for those with blemishes — such as those lacking hands and the like — who are deficient and indicate, by the defect of their action, that they damaged in a holy place and caused separation; and therefore their soul does not spread through the body in those limbs, and it is blemished and deficient; and all according to the place of their damage, so is their blemish. And a blemish [present] from the beginning of one's creation indicates its deficiency on account of [a previous] transmigration (gilgul), as we shall explain the matter of the limbs in the Gate of the Soul, chapter 7, God willing. And it is never possible in the world [for there to be] a soul or an action in which all ten sefirot are not included. And although it is declared "a soul from the side of Metatron, or from the side of the handmaid," the intent is not that they are not from above, God forbid — for all souls are drawn down from above. And the matter is as we shall explain in the aforementioned Gate, chapter 2, God willing; and it always includes ten, and they do not separate, as explained. And [the difference] between souls from Malkhut and the other souls is this: that the other souls include ten — not that ten literally appear in them, but rather that they are included in it [Malkhut], and it of itself includes ten. But the soul from the side of Malkhut is emanated from the ten sefirot that are in Malkhut, in that Malkhut has all ten sefirot appearing within it and unites with them.

And this matter will be further explained in the coming Gates, God willing. And this matter [applies] to the sefirot themselves: for there is a great difference between our saying "Malkhut includes ten" and our saying that it is in union with the other sefirot themselves, for they are not all one [and the same] thing. For the excellence of a sefirah when it [merely] includes [ten] is not like its excellence when it is united with the sefirot themselves — which is when ten sefirot literally appear within it — and this is clear. And this is what he intended in saying "includes ten sefirot." And he clarified that the intent in saying "includes" is not that it merely includes [ten], as is the usual nature of the sefirot, but rather that "whoever inherits it," etc., "merits ten sefirot without separation" — meaning that one truly merits the ten sefirot in their [actual] existence, in that ten sefirot literally appear within it, as explained.

And the matter of his saying "who inherits it and merits it": the explanation is that two things are needed in order to merit this esteemed soul. First, from the side of his preparation — from the side of his father at the time of begetting, at the time of [marital] union — as the Sages said, "one who sanctifies himself at the time of intercourse," etc.; and after his father is sanctified thereby, when that good intention of his ascends, he will merit a holy soul from a high place; and according to the measure of his sanctity, so will his drawing-down be elevated. And this is well known in the Zohar and the Talmud in many places, too numerous to count. And their saying "he merits worthy children" — the intent is that he draws down for his children a soul from a high place, such that they will be worthy; and this is called "inheritance from his father," and to this he referred in saying "who inherits it." Second, one needs in himself worthy deeds, pleasing before his Maker, so that that soul will not depart from him; and this will be explained further in the Gate of the Soul, chapter 3, God willing. And concerning this second [thing] he said "and merits it" — meaning that he is the one who, by his deeds, merits that holy soul. "He merits ten sefirot without separation" — meaning, as we explained, that when the soul is from Malkhut itself, then necessarily that soul will "include ten sefirot," meaning the ten sefirot themselves that are within it, because it unites with the ten sefirot and is not separated from them at all. And this is what he said, "he merits ten sefirot without separation" — that is, [they are] unified within Malkhut, not separated from it. And he established this from the words of the Sefer Yetzirah, which said "ten and not nine." And if it were possible to say that the soul could be separated — the soul which is necessarily a part of Malkhut, as it says, "and He breathed into his nostrils" (Genesis 2:7); whoever breathes, breathes from his own self — then [what happens] by way of the part would happen to the whole: for just as the soul drawn from it [Malkhut] would be separated from the other parts of the sefirot, so Malkhut would be separated, God forbid, from the other sefirot. And this is impossible, for then the sefirot would remain nine; therefore he said "ten and not nine," that they never diminish from ten. And therefore the soul must, besides including ten, have the sefirot themselves included within it, exactly as Malkhut [does], for whatever is in the part is in the whole. "And should you say that it ascends above," etc. — the explanation: he found difficulty in that one might say they [the sefirot] are ten apart from Malkhut, and according to this it would be possible to say that Malkhut is separated from the rest and yet they are ten. To this he answered, "the explicit name (shem mefarash)," etc. The explanation: the explicit name is the four-letter name, YHVH, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Four-Letter Name; and this name is in the attribute of Tiferet, and it is the male that unites with Malkhut, which is the female, and it unites with her. And this name indicates, in its full spelling, that it is a "private domain" (reshut ha-yachid), its height ten and its breadth four — which is YHVH, and this is its breadth; and its height is ten: Yod-Heh, Vav-Heh, behold ten, for it never ascends above ten. And if it were that they were ten apart from Malkhut, then when the Name unites with Malkhut they would be eleven — ten above and one that unites with the female; therefore the Sefer Yetzirah said "ten and not eleven."

Now the explanation of the passage is complete, and we have written, in passing, the explanation of the mishnah, "ten and not nine and not eleven." We may also explain "ten and not eleven" [as follows]: he intended to warn us not to bring into the count of the emanated [entities] the Throne, which designates Beriah, as we shall explain in the Gate of ABYA, God willing. And likewise he intended to warn us not to bring into the count of the emanated [entities] the angel, the Prince of the Countenance, Metatron — for although his name is like the name of his Master, he is only of [the world of] Yetzirah and not Atzilut, as we shall explain in the aforementioned Gate, God willing. And all these interpretations [arise] in explaining the mishnah, since it spoke in the language of affirmation and negation: "ten" is affirmation, and "not nine" is negation; likewise "ten and not eleven." And his intent is to affirm this number, which is ten, and to negate every kind of error that adds to the ten or diminishes from them.

They further explained for us another interpretation of this mishnah in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Parashat Tisa, folio 187b), whose words are: "A commandment to give the half-shekel in the sacred shekel. Said the Faithful Shepherd: What is the half-shekel? It is like the half of the hin; and this is the Vav, mediating between the two Hehs. 'A stone with which to weigh' — this is Yod; 'twenty gerah is the shekel' — this is the [spelled-out] Yod. 'The rich shall not give more' — this is the central pillar; it shall not exceed ten. For so it is said in the Sefer Yetzirah: 'Ten sefirot of belimah; ten and not eleven.' 'And the poor shall not give less' — this is the Tzaddik; it shall not be less than ten, as it says, 'ten and not nine'; and the half-shekel — it is ten." Thus far his words.

There are points to scrutinize in this passage. First, his saying "What is the half-shekel? It is like the half," etc. — the explanation being that "half the hin" is Tiferet, which mediates between the two Hehs. However, with regard to "the half-shekel," it is not apt to interpret thus — "mediating between" — for we do not know between what [it would mediate]. Second, his saying "a stone with which to weigh — this is Yod," etc.: here, according to the implication, the [spelled-out] Yod is twenty. And how did he say that one must not subtract from nor add to the ten — behold, the [spelled-out] Yod, whose half is ten, and behold it has added ten to ten, which is twenty? And according to his explanation, one must not add to the ten in any sefirah — for [it is] not specifically Tiferet or the Tzaddik, but he took these [as examples] because they are "rich" and "poor," and all the more so the others. Third, his saying "a stone with which to weigh — this is Yod" — how does one weigh with this stone, given that it is twenty gerah, while the weight needs to be in ten, which is only the half-shekel? And if we say that his intent is to speak of the manner of weighing with this stone — which is the whole stone — then it is prolix, and it would have been fitting for him to say "a stone with which to weigh — this is the [spelled-out] Yod, and it is twenty gerah." Why did he say "a stone with which to weigh — this is Yod; twenty gerah is the shekel — this is the [spelled-out] Yod," which is repetitive and prolix? Fourth, his saying "and the half-shekel — it is ten," which appears to have no connection.

And further, that it is the opposite of what he explained: for above he said that the explanation of "half-shekel" is "mediating," and now he says "the half-shekel — it is ten," which implies that "half" is [literally] half of a shekel, in its [plain] sense.

Now to understand this passage we must first premise that the matter of the sefirot is [that they are] ten from above to below and ten from below to above — like the image of a ray of the sun that comes and strikes a polished mirror, and the light returns and reverses back toward its source; so it is with the sefirot, for they come from above to below until Malkhut, and there is the "station" of the light, and it returns to its source by way of the journeys, such that just as they are ten from above to below, so they are ten from below to above. And this topic we shall elaborate upon in the appropriate Gate, God willing.

Now this secret is made clear from the form of the [letter] Alef, which is a Yod above and a Yod below, to indicate the source of the light from above to below and from below to above; and these are the "upper waters" and the "lower waters," as we shall explain in the Glossary of Titles, under the entry "water," God willing.

Now the Vav that is in the middle of the two Yods is Tiferet, which unites the upper waters and the lower waters; and this is the half-shekel, which mediates within the shekel — which is the complete measure, the measure of Atzilut: ten from above to below and ten from below to above — and it is mediating and central between the two Yods, which are "twenty gerah is the shekel." And now the meaning of "half the hin" and the meaning of "half the shekel" are all one [and the same] thing. And the first difficulty is resolved. "A stone with which to weigh — this is Yod": the explanation is that a "stone" is always the form of Yod, which is called "stone," and every "stone" is hinted at in the existence of Yod, as we shall explain in the Glossary of Titles, under the entry "stone," God willing.

Now it is a "stone" with which to weigh the half-shekel, for the half-shekel is ten, as we shall explain; and therefore the "stone" with which one weighs is the form of Yod, and this is ten. "Twenty gerah is the shekel — this is the [spelled-out] Yod": the explanation of what he said, "twenty gerah is the shekel — this is Yod" [in its full spelling], is that it indicates twenty, which is the two Yods — ten from above to below [and] ten from below to above.

Now its half, which is the simple [unspelled] Yod, is the "stone" for weighing; and when it is full [spelled out] it is a whole shekel, which is twenty gerah — ten from above to below and ten from below to above, as we explained. "The rich shall not give more — this is the central pillar; it shall not exceed ten," etc. The explanation: needless to say [regarding] the other sefirot, but even the "rich" one — which is rich in effluence and in inclusion more than the other sefirot — nevertheless may not add inclusion beyond ten sefirot, because they are ten and not eleven. And so it may not add inclusion beyond ten on account of its richness; rather, its richness will be in an abundance of effluence and light, or in its including many tenfold inclusions, but it will never add to the inclusion of ten. "And the poor shall not give less — this is the Tzaddik; it shall not be less than ten," etc. The explanation: Yesod — although it is called "poor" on account of its poverty [in the time of exile], as it says (Isaiah 57:1), "the righteous one perishes," etc., and it is poor and destitute — he said that, although it is poor, its poverty is not [such as] to fall below ten sefirot at all, for one must not fall short of them, in the sense of "ten and not nine"; rather, its poverty is in the diminution of its effluence or the diminution of [its] inclusion of the ten, but not that it falls short of them — only that it does not add many inclusions [each] of tenfold ten. But from the aforementioned ten one must not subtract, so that there not be less than ten; for it is impossible to say that there be a place devoid [of the ten] in any one of them — rather, they are always ten. "And the half-shekel — it is ten." The explanation: now, according to what we explained — that the "rich" one is the central pillar, which is truly the half-shekel, mediating between the two Yods which are a shekel of twenty gerah — then the half-shekel is ten, and ten is the half-shekel. And so, since the verse comes to teach us that the "rich" one, which is Tiferet, must not add beyond ten — then how did he say "the rich shall not give more than the half-shekel," when it [Tiferet] is itself the half-shekel? And how did he give a measure to the "rich" one, which is Tiferet, by [reference to] the half-shekel, which is Tiferet itself? To this he said, "and the half-shekel — it is ten." The explanation: although we explained above that Tiferet is the one called "half-shekel" because it is intermediate — with all this, "a verse does not depart from its plain sense": it is called thus by its aspect of being within the shekel and dividing it in two, and half the shekel is ten. And now he said: the "rich" one shall never add, in its existence which is [that of] the half-shekel — that is, that it divides the shekel into two and makes each of them ten by ten. Thus far the explanation of the passage. And we find ourselves learning from it the explanation of the mishnah, that "ten and not nine, ten and not eleven" comes to teach us concerning the matter of the inclusion of [things] included — that one must not add to ten, as explained.

And now let us return to explaining the rest of the language of the mishnah, which said "Understand with wisdom and be wise with understanding," etc. The commentators explained that the intent is to unite Chokhmah with Binah and Binah with Chokhmah. They further explained that the intent is to convey that the root of Chokhmah is in Binah and the root of Binah is in Chokhmah. They further explained: when you draw effluence to Chokhmah, let it be on condition that it come to Binah; and when you draw [effluence] to Binah, give it the power of Chokhmah. And according to these matters and the like the commentators explained, but their explanation is not settled. For why would [the mishnah] now warn us about these matters with Binah and Chokhmah and not with the other sefirot? For surely, just as we are obligated to unite the first three, so we are obligated to unite the seven that are below them.

And further: why does Keter not enter into this matter of union, according to some of the interpretations? Further, [the mishnah] said "test them," etc., and the commentators explained that when you test [them] well you will know that the aforementioned Chokhmah and Binah are the root of Gedulah and Gevurah; and "probe from them" means: when you probe, you will find that Gedulah and Gevurah are the root of Netzach and Hod, which extend from them. And he said "and set the matter (davar) in its clarity (boryo)": "davar" [is] Malkhut; "boryo" is like "its support," and so Onkelos translated (Exodus 21:19), and it is Yesod. "And restore the Former (Yotzer) to His place (mekhono)": "restore" (hashev) corresponds to teshuvah [Binah], to give its power to Tiferet, which is designated by the name "Former" (Yotzer); and the "place" of Tiferet is Netzach and Hod. Thus far the words of the commentators, after we have selected the choicest and finest of their interpretations. And since this matter is not settled for us — because this is not the nature of an author's language; and furthermore, what is the point of informing us now of these matters and these novel teachings? For this is the way of those who pray, not of authors, and we derive from this no instruction or novelty — therefore it seems to me to explain that "chokhmah" is the received tradition and learning that a person learns from his teacher, in the sense of "they transmit to him the headings of the chapters [outlines]." "Binah" is the analysis and the addition that a person studies out and adds of himself, from the general principles and chapter-headings transmitted to him. And now to this they referred in saying "Understand with wisdom" (havein be-chokhmah) — that is, study well what you learned from your teacher in the wisdom of the attributes, in which only chapter-headings are transmitted; and a person needs to understand from it one matter [derived] from another, in the sense of what the Sages said (Chagigah 13a): "one does not say this matter except to a sage who understands of his own knowledge."

Behold, [this means] that a person needs to liken one matter to another and to derive one matter from another, so that he will have a "generative intellect" (sechel molid) and not a "barren intellect" (sechel akar). And he said "be wise with understanding" (chakkem be-vinah) — the explanation: when you generate and liken in your intellect and understand, you must "make it wise" and ground it in the received tradition of the masters and in the brevity of their words, so that the matter is included in what is transmitted to you, whether much or little; "and do not lean upon your own understanding" [Proverbs 3:5]. "Test them" (bechon bahem) — that is, with regard to the sefirot themselves, that is, "in them," in their essence, the examination shall be only by way of "running and returning" (ratzo va-shov) and by way of humility, being mindful of the honor of your Maker, who makes the simple wise; and this is "in them." But with regard to the actions that proceed from them, the matter shall be [pursued] with intense investigation, with good knowledge, with give-and-take, and with great study. And since investigation is into the actions that proceed to us from the existence of the sefirot, he said "probe from them" (chakor me-hem) — meaning, into what proceeds from them, and not into their very selves, which is "in them," as he said above. "And set the matter in its clarity" — the explanation: establish the matter firmly and descend to the depth of the topic, so that it will be clear to you without doubt. "And restore the Former to His place" — the explanation: in any case, let your entire intent be that the King of kings, the Ein Sof, blessed be He, oversee from His "place," which are His thrones, which are the ten sefirot; and the intent is that all be [directed] toward the matter of the union of the emanated [sefirot], which unite in the Emanator, and the Emanator in the emanated. Or he means "set the matter in its clarity" in the manner that the commentators explained — that is, the union of Malkhut with Yesod, and not to separate them by believing [there to be] nine, God forbid, but rather ten together with Malkhut. "And restore the Former to His place" — for the sefirot are a "place" and a throne for Him, and He is the Lord, the Emanator, like a king upon the throne, and He is not among the count of the "throne." Thus far the explanation of the mishnah.

Now it has been explained from these chapters that the sefirot are ten, neither less nor more, and there is no doubt in this matter, God forbid; rather it is a belief [held] in the heart of all the Kabbalists.

After we have engaged, in the previous chapters, in the strengthening of our beliefs — agreed upon by all the Kabbalists — that the sefirot are ten, neither less nor more, we have seen fit in this chapter to save the student from a place of confusion and error; and it is a question that was asked of Rav Hai Gaon. And these are the words of the questioners: "Let our master teach us — for we find that the Sages [speak of] thirteen attributes [of compassion] that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, received; and for Abraham our father, peace be upon him, in a book that the Sages attributed to his name — which is the Sefer Yetzirah — there [the author] counts ten sefirot. And we need to learn from his holy mouth whether the ten sefirot are the thirteen attributes. If so, we find thirteen attributes [but] we do not find thirteen sefirot; or [are there] thirteen attributes alone and ten sefirot alone? We are in need of your instruction, and we await your answer." Thus far the words of the question.

Now the master [Rav Hai] explained to them that the thirteen attributes are derivative branches issuing from the ten levels called sefirot, these corresponding to those, together with three that are stored away, "heads of heads." "And if they are not [evident] to you as [distinct] entities, there is a tradition concerning them [handed down] by our predecessors, each from the mouth of the other, up to the mouth of the prophets, of blessed memory"; and the derivatives — which are the actions — are called "attributes" (middot), and the roots, which are "fathers," are called "sefirot," not because there is [merely a] number, etc. And we shall not copy the entire text of his answer, because we are destined to copy it and explain it at length in the Gate of Tzachtzachot (the Dazzling Lights), chapter 1, God willing. And now it is fitting that we say that the master's intent, in saying "together with three heads of heads," etc., is not that his answer to them is that there are thirteen sefirot. For if this were his intent, he would have had to resolve for them the main point of their question — namely, that [the statement] in the Sefer Yetzirah, "ten and not eleven," is not the [accepted] law. And since we see that the Gaon was not concerned to reconcile the wording nor to reject it, it appears that he indicates that the three concealed ones are not sefirot, such that we should say they are thirteen. For they are only concealed powers — manifestations subtler than the manifestation of the sefirot — as we shall expand upon there, God willing. And just as we have no difficulty from finding that there are ten of Atzilut, ten of Beriah, ten of Yetzirah, and ten of Asiyah, so the existence of the concealed ones poses no difficulty to us, because the sefirot are never anything but ten. And if we find concealed entities, they are sources for the revealed ones; and if there are revealed ones, they are a shadow to the upper ones; and they never ascend above ten nor descend below ten; and the three are sources, as we shall explain there in the exposition of the Gaon's words, God willing. There is further room for error in the Baraita of Rabbi Shimon HaTzaddik, which Rav Chamai Gaon copied in the Book of Contemplation (Sefer ha-Iyyun) that he composed, whose words are: "And these are thirteen powers, each of which has a known name, and the name of their rank, one above the other: (1) Primordial Air (avir kadmon); (2) Primeval Wisdom (chokhmah kedumah); (3) Wondrous Light (or mufla); (4) Chashmal; (5) Arafel [dense cloud]; (6) the Throne of Radiance (kisei ha-nogah); (7) the Wheel (ofan) of Greatness, called Chazchazit, the place from which the vision of the seers issues; (8) Cherub (keruv); (9) the Wheels (galgalei) of the Chariot; (10) the Encompassing Air (avir ha-sovev); (11) the heavenly curtain [pargod] — this is the Throne of Glory; (12) the place of the souls, called the Chambers of Greatness; (13) the secret of the supernal array (ma'arakhah), called the supernal Sanctuary of Holiness. And these thirteen powers are revealed as one, from the concealed supernal Keter, called Omman (Artisan)," etc. Thus far his words, as relevant to our matter. And in truth, seemingly it implies that he is enumerating the order of the sefirot, and so it is — that the sefirot are ten. The first, "Primordial Air," is Keter, for so its name is well known, as will be explained in the Glossary of Titles; (2) "Primeval Wisdom" is, literally, Chokhmah; (3) "Wondrous Light" is Binah; (4) "Chashmal" is Chesed; (5) "Arafel" is Gevurah; (6) "the Throne of Radiance" is Tiferet; (7) "Chazchazit" is Netzach, and it is one of the [sources of] true prophecy; (8) "Cherub" is Hod; (9) "the Wheel of the Chariot" is Yesod; (10) "the Encompassing Air" is Malkhut. From here onward [the list] is not among the sefirot but [consists of] levels that are below the sefirot. And some have explained that they are three kinds of "emanation" within Malkhut, and not literal Atzilut. But it seems to us that his intent is that they are three concealed sources within Malkhut — for the hint came in it [Malkhut]: just as three concealed upper ones are hinted at in Keter, so they came in it [Malkhut] revealed; and this is not the place for this matter, but rather the Gate of Tzachtzachot and the Gate of ABYA, God willing. And as for the three extra [items] in the words of Rabbi Shimon HaTzaddik, peace be upon him — which are (11) the heavenly curtain, (12) the place of the souls called the Chambers of Greatness, (13) the secret of the supernal array called the supernal Sanctuary of Holiness — it appears to us, from his language, when examined with good study, that he is not speaking of the matter of the sefirot but [of] the powers of the sefirot; and in particular, that he called the eleventh "the heavenly curtain," the meaning of which is "a place of division," and it is a veil and a screen between Atzilut and the other things below Atzilut; and he called it "the Throne of Glory," which is a throne that includes many thrones, and which is, for us, the matter designated by the term "Beriah," as will be explained in the Gate of ABYA, God willing.

Now it is known that the souls are hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory; and although in truth they are emanated from above the Throne, nevertheless they are hewn from beneath the Throne — for "hewing" is a title for Yetzirah, as we shall explain in the aforementioned Gate.

Now Yetzirah is beneath Beriah; thus the souls — the place of their hewing is beneath the Throne of Glory, that is, beneath Beriah; and therefore the level beneath the Throne of Glory is called "the place of the souls," and likewise "the Chambers of Greatness," which are, literally, the chambers of the Garden of Eden. And beneath this Yetzirah is Asiyah, which is designated by his language "the secret of the supernal array" — and they are the array of the ministering [angels] in the secret of Asiyah, who are beneath Yetzirah. This is what appears to us regarding the matter of the Baraita of Rabbi Shimon HaTzaddik.

Now the matter of the thirteen attributes is settled, and according to both this one and that one, the sefirot are never anything but ten. However, regarding the question they asked the Gaon — whether the thirteen attributes are sefirot or not — we have a proof that they are not a hint at the sefirot, in line with the Gaon's reasoning. And the proof is that they are called "thirteen attributes of compassion (rachamim)," yet among the sefirot there are attributes of Din, such as Gevurah and Hod. Therefore, what is clear to us in this is that the thirteen attributes are the twelve boundaries (gevulin), which are the twelve havayot [permutations of the four-letter name], and they are twelve; and the place that bears them, which is the Name that includes them, [together they] are thirteen. And they are in each of three places, which are Teli, Galgal (sphere), and Lev (heart), and the mnemonic is "TaGeL" [T G L]. Besides which there are yet another thirteen [attributes] that are concealed, and they are in Keter. And what is fitting to elaborate in explaining this topic will be explained in the Gate of Particulars of Names, God willing, for there is its place, in the exposition of the seventy-two-[letter] name.

Now Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, peace be upon him, is [counted] among [those holding] this view, for he counted thirteen attributes in Keter, as I shall copy his words in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 3, God willing. And likewise Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Idra wrote of thirteen attributes of compassion in Ze'eir Anpin and thirteen attributes in Arikh Anpin. It certainly appears that their view is the opposite of the Gaon's view, of blessed memory. And the exposition of the thirteen attributes does not belong here, for it will be explained in a book of its own, if God decrees [for me] life. And our purpose in this is to uphold the belief of the Kabbalists: that one must not believe in any addition to the ten sefirot nor in any [number] less than them — for it is "a tent that shall not be moved, whose stakes shall not be pulled up" [Isaiah 33:20] — ten and not eleven; and one who adds or diminishes sins and brings evil upon himself. And of God we ask that He save us from errors.

After we have verified the matter of the number of the sefirot, it is fitting that we investigate whether they are necessary from the standpoint of inquiry or not. To this we say that they are necessary for several reasons. The first: because we who believe in providence — and even in particular providence — are compelled to say that He exercises providence by way of the sefirot. For the simple One, the Cause of all causes and the Cause of Causes, is removed from change and from attributes — that is, "wise," "righteous," "one who hears," and the rest of the predicates that the philosophers have removed from Him. So too the dimensions of body and corporeality, such as "And YHVH came down," and "And the appearance of the glory of YHVH was like a consuming fire," etc., and "And I saw YHVH sitting upon a throne," etc., and "And the glory of YHVH filled the Tabernacle," and "And they saw the God of Israel, and under His feet," etc., and what is said in Daniel (7:9), "And the Ancient of Days sat; His garment was white as snow," and likewise "written with the finger of God," "the ears of YHVH," "the hand of YHVH," "the eyes of YHVH" — matters of this kind that occur in Scripture indicating limit and corporeality, and likewise indicating predicates. Now of the simple One, in respect of its aspect relative to its very Self [atzmut] and its simplicity, it is impossible to say this — unless we consider it relative to its attributes, as we shall explain in the Gate of Self and Vessels and in the Gate of Titles, with the help of God.
And so it is by way of the attributes that the changes occur, and judgment and compassion — not in His [own] aspect — as will be explained in the aforementioned Gate.

Now from the standpoint of this aspect — so that we not deny the principles of our faith in the simple One, in its very simplicity, that it is removed from the predicates that entail body and corporeal forms — and since we are compelled to believe in His providence, which too is among the principles of the religion, we therefore need to believe in the sefirot, so that the principles of our faith not contradict one another, as explained. This, then, is a reason — or reasons — compelling belief in the sefirot; and these are somewhat compelling proofs from the side of the Torah, by way of inquiry. However, by way of inquiry alone, without support and prop from the Torah, the commentators have written many further proofs; and because our way in this composition is not by way of inquiry, we have not copied them at all. Furthermore, these ten attributes — their secret and their import — have been expounded in Scripture. The first three are expounded from the words of Job to his companions, where he said (28:12), "But wisdom — whence shall it be found, and where is the place of understanding?" In this verse he set out for us the order of the first three, which are called Ayin (Nothing), Chokhmah, and Binah. First he said: Chokhmah is emanated from the first sefirah, called Ayin, and this is "But wisdom — from Ayin (me-ayin) shall it be found." And  A Y  — which is Alef = Ayin, Yod = Chokhmah — ZeH (this) is the place of Binah, [the place] by which Binah is emanated. But of the emanation of the Ayin he did not speak at all, for even the emanated is called Ayin (Nothing), all the more so the Emanator.

Now the seven [sefirot] that proceed from them are expounded in the words of David, king of Israel, peace be upon him, in the verse (1 Chronicles 29:11): "Yours, O YHVH, is the greatness, and the power, and the beauty, and the victory, and the majesty; for all that is in heaven and on earth [is Yours]; Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom." The words "Yours, O YHVH" (lekha) are a title for the first three; and Binah is called lekha, which equals 50, like the count of the fifty gates of Binah. And the letters of  L K  (lekha) are the same as the letters of  K L  (kol). And Yesod, when it receives from Binah the aforementioned fifty (Nun) gates, is called KoL — like the image of the reversing seal, from  L K  to  K L. And the reason that the fifty gates are hinted at in the word lekha and in the word kol is that the gates are 50, in the secret of Binah, which spreads down to Hod — these being five sefirot, each including ten, making fifty; and they are three over two: Gedulah-Gevurah-Tiferet (G G T) are a segol or segolta, which is 30; Netzach and Hod are a tzere or sheva, making 20 — thus  L K  (30+20) in their order. And KoL is in the secret of the reversing seal: what was above returned below. And the remaining matters of the gates will be explained in the Gate of Gates, with God's help. "The greatness" (ha-gedulah) is Chesed; "the power" (ha-gevurah) is Fear (Pachad); and then Tiferet, and Netzach, and Hod. "For all (kol) that is in heaven and on earth" — this is Yesod, the bond that binds heaven and earth. That is: it unifies Tiferet, called "heaven," and "earth," called Malkhut; and it is Yesod. And Malkhut was not clearly expounded in the verse; rather he said "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom" — because Malkhut's place is above Netzach, Hod, and Yesod, and on account of [its] diminishment it descended below. Therefore he did not wish to mention it except by way of the unification, to indicate that its place is in heaven, save that it was cast from heaven to earth; and afterward he said "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom," to set forth its hosts and its adornments in their own right; and even so he returned and unified it up to the supernal root, saying "Yours, O YHVH, is the kingdom" — "Yours" [referring to] Binah, as explained. "YHVH" is Tiferet. "The kingdom" (mamlakhah) is Malkhut, in its plain sense. And this is its manifestation together with its spouse — two kings nourished from a single Keter.

After we have occupied ourselves in the preceding chapters with the necessity of the existence of the sefirot and their number, it is fitting that we know whether one who denies the matter of the existence of the sefirot is called a heretic [kofer] or not. And we say that a person's error in this matter will be in one of two ways. The first way: one who did not know of them at all — not in the sense that, were the hidden things of wisdom revealed to him, he would deny them, God forbid, but [only] in the sense that he was not habituated to them and the gates of light were not revealed to him. This man certainly ought not to be called a heretic [kofer] or a denier. And a proof of this: for even regarding the removal of corporeality from the truly simple One, blessed be He, Rambam said, in Sefer ha-Mada, in the Laws of Repentance ch.3, that one who believes the simple One is a body and possessed of form is a sectarian [min], and he included him in the category of the sectarians (minim). And Ra'avad, peace be upon him, objected to him, and these are his words: "I say: and why did he call this one a sectarian? — when several great and good men greater than he went with this thought, according to what they saw in the Scriptures, and even more than what they saw in the words of the aggadot, which confuse the views." So Ra'avad, peace be upon him, took issue with him for saying that one who says that God is a body is a sectarian. And it is not fitting to think that Ra'avad's view, peace be upon him, is that he is not a sectarian — for surely one who corporealizes God is a sectarian. Rather, their dispute hangs on this: that Rambam, according to the apparent sense of his language, holds that one who says that God is corporeal is a sectarian, even though this error stems from his not being habituated in divine matters, and from his having chased after the plain senses of the Scriptures and the midrashim, not descending into their depth to understand their matters as they truly are. And to this Ra'avad objected, of blessed memory, and contradicted him, and said that such a man — who in all his affairs serves God and walks in the ways of the Torah in innocence, and who, through the shortness of his knowledge, believed in corporeality — is not called a sectarian, though he certainly errs, since his intent is not to do evil, God forbid. But one who recognizes his Creator, to whom the gates of the premises in the removal of corporeality have been revealed, and who does not acknowledge the truth, but is brazen and says that God is a body — this one is surely called a sectarian, even according to the view of Ra'avad, of blessed memory. And likewise we say regarding the matter of the sefirot: that surely one who did not know of them and believed in the simple One without knowledge of the sefirot ought not to be called a heretic [kofer], God forbid, nor "one who cuts among the saplings" [mekatzetz ba-neti'ot], God forbid. For if so, it would have been fitting that, when a person is able to understand the training in the commandments, they should train him in the matter of belief in the sefirot and the knowledge of them — which we do not find to be so. But on the contrary, they said that it is fitting to hide them, and that these matters are transmitted only to the modest, etc. This is not so with the matter of the existence of God, and the unity, and the matter of Torah from Heaven, and the prophecy of Moses, and most of the principles of the religion: for when the lad knows how to call "my father" and "my mother," they train him in them and reveal to him the plain sense of the matters, as our Sages of blessed memory said in Tractate Sukkah (42a): once he knows how to speak, his father teaches him Torah and the Shema. And they asked in the Gemara, "What is 'Torah'?" and they said, "'Moses commanded us the Torah,' etc."; and "the Shema" is "Hear, O Israel," etc.

Now, they chose these two verses because in them are included most of the corners of the cardinal principles of the Torah. In the verse "Hear, O Israel" is included the existence of God — namely, "YHVH." Further, that He exercises providence, and even particular providence — and this is the meaning of "Eloheinu (our God)." For although His existence is necessary in respect of the whole world entire — and He was, is, and will be, and brings into being all the beings (which is the meaning of the four-letter name in its writing); and although He is Master of all worlds, upper and lower (which is the meaning of its reading in lordship [Adonut]) — and from this His providence is necessitated as including the whole world: even so, "Eloheinu" means that He watches over us in particular. "YHVH is One (echad)" necessitates the unity. And they have already explained in the Gemara (Berakhot 13b) that a person must intend, in the word echad, that He is King above and below and in the four directions. And by this it is necessitated that He is not a body, for the corporeal cannot be found in differing places at one time. Further, the meaning of echad: [it means] not like one of an enumeration, etc., as we shall explain in the Gate of Self and Vessels, in Gate 4, ch.5, with the help of God. And in the verse "Moses commanded us the Torah" is included the cardinal principle of Torah from Heaven, and prophecy, and the prophecy of Moses — and this is "Moses commanded us the Torah," as is well known. Reward and punishment — in his saying "an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob," for YHVH delighted, for the sake of His righteousness, to make Israel meritorious and to bequeath them His Torah. And this is what they intended in saying these two verses: for the reason that, when the lad grows, he begins to roam in his thought among these words, and asks his father and his elder their reason and their matter; and they tell it to him and bring him into the matters of the corners of the Torah little by little, according to his understanding, as he is able to bear. This is what is found regarding the existence of the cardinal principles. Not so with the supernal sefirot — on the contrary, they conceal their secret from every eye, and reveal them only to the modest, the unique ones in the generation. And here, then, is proof that one who does not discern the matter of the sefirot is not, on this account, called a heretic [kofer], nor "one who cuts among the saplings," God forbid. Rather, what we may rightly say of him is that he did not merit to behold the luminaries in his days, nor tasted the sweetness of the Torah and the nectar of its pleasant sayings; and behold, he died without wisdom and saw no good. The second way: these are those to whom the matter of the sefirot and their existence were revealed, and who deny them because of the evil of their disposition — for they were habituated in external sciences, and "with the children of strangers they content themselves." And these, even if they not be called heretics (koferim) or sectarians (minim), inasmuch as they believe in all the matters of divinity — even so they are called heretics (koferim), because they deny an interpretation of the Oral Torah. And one of the three [kinds of] heretics is one who denies an interpretation among the interpretations of the Oral Torah, as Rambam wrote in the aforementioned chapter; and he also denies the words of our Sages of blessed memory. And besides what is already his, he adds to his sin a transgression: for from the denial of the sefirot, heresy will follow — for we will compel him by the premises and corners of the Torah: since the simple One is not subject to change, how does He watch over passing matters? And likewise, since He is one, how does He watch over the kinds of species — for that would necessitate multiplicity, as is known? And therefore he is compelled to believe in the sefirot; and if not, he falls into heresy, God forbid — as many have erred in [the matter of] the removal of particular providence, and in these matters, which it is not fitting to raise up in writing.

And so, perforce we compel him to belief in the sefirot, or he is called a heretic. And by this way it is necessitated that one who says he has no dealing with Kabbalah, and does not wish to direct his prayer except to the Master of the lights — as many have thought — surely is called one who errs. For if a person comes to speak of the simple One in respect of its aspect toward its [own] existence, apart from its existence and its aspect in respect of the sefirot, he is found to remove its actions altogether. For the Ein Sof, in respect of the aspect of its Self, is simple and is not a possessor of changes — that it should change from judgment to compassion, and be moved by will, and change from will to will through prayer — except in respect of its aspect toward its sefirot, which are its [acts of] providence, and through which the change of judgment and compassion occurs. And let the inquirer not press to enter, by means of these our words, within the partition, to understand the matter of the changes and the providence — for harm will reach him, and not benefit; rather, we shall explain the matter at length in the Gate of Self and Vessels, with God's help. In sum: a person is compelled to believe in the sefirot in order to be correct in the cardinal principles of the faith and in its corners, which cannot be upheld except through them — that is, by means of them — for through them the Emanator effects the changes, and from this no change whatsoever reaches Him, God forbid, as is explained at length in that lovely Gate. And of God we ask pardon.

After we have occupied ourselves with the matter of the sefirot, and the necessity of their existence, and the matter transmitted concerning them among the sages, we need to know their essence and their names — the comprehensive [naming] agreed upon among the commentators, and in particular in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him. And this is it: the first, Keter; the second, Chokhmah; the third, Binah; the fourth, Gedulah or Chesed; the fifth, Pachad or Gevurah; the sixth, Tiferet; the seventh, Netzach; the eighth, Hod; the ninth, Yesod; the tenth, Malkhut. And these sefirot are ten names that may not be erased; and the names and the sefirot are all one thing, for the spirituality of the names is the very sefirot. Keter is Ehyeh, and it is not found in Scripture except three times in one verse (Exodus 3:14): "And God said to Moses, Ehyeh asher Ehyeh (I will be what I will be); and He said, Thus shall you say to the children of Israel, Ehyeh has sent me to you." But the reason it does not appear [more] in the Torah, and other doubts in this inquiry, will be explained in the Gate of Names, with the help of God. And the name of Chokhmah is Yah, and there are many of these written: in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "My strength and song is Yah," and "For a hand is upon the throne of Yah." Repeated in the Prophets: "I shall not see Yah, Yah, in the land of the living," which is in the writing of Hezekiah. Tripled in the Writings: "From the straits I called Yah; Yah answered me with expansiveness," and many like them. And the name of Binah is the four-letter name with the vocalization of Elohim, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "Adonai YHVH, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it," and many like it. Repeated in the Prophets: "YHVH Adonai is my strength, and He makes my feet [like hinds']," etc., and many like it. Tripled in the Writings: "I will come in the mighty acts of Adonai YHVH; I will make mention of Your righteousness, Yours alone," and many like it. And the name of Chesed is the name El, and there are many of these in the Torah, in the Prophets, and in the Writings. In the Torah: "And he called it El, God of Israel," and many like it. In the Prophets: "El, Elohim, YHVH — He knows," etc., and many like it. In the Writings: "El, whose way is perfect," and many like it. And the name of Gevurah is Elohim, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And Elohim tested Abraham," and many like it. Repeated in the Prophets: "And there was a terror of Elohim," and many like it. Tripled in the Writings: "Arise, O Elohim, judge the earth," and many like it. And the name of Tiferet is YHVH — written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And YHVH said," "And YHVH spoke," and many others. Repeated in the Prophets: "Thus said YHVH," and many others. Tripled in the Writings: "YHVH said to me, You are My son," and many like it. And the name of Netzach you will not find alone, but only joined with the name of Hod — for the reason that the two of them have one name, which is Tzeva'ot. And this is not found in the Torah at all; but in the Prophets, many: "Thus said YHVH Tzeva'ot," and many others. And as for the name of Yesod, all the later commentators explained that its proper name is El Chai. But this is difficult, for El Chai is not among the names that may not be erased — for the word Chai is not holy, as it appears in Tractate Shevuot (35a), where they counted there only [the name] El. And the name El, which is the holy one, is borrowed for it from Chesed as a title, and they counted it. And among those holding this view is Rabbi Abba in the book of the Zohar, Parashat Vayikra (11a), and these are his words: "The sixth and the seventh are called Tzeva'ot. The eighth is El Chai, as it is said, 'For there YHVH commanded the blessing — life,' etc.; and this is the Tzaddik, from whom all life issues."

And as for his having counted Netzach and Hod as sixth and seventh — although they are seventh and eighth, as is known — it is because Rabbi Abba began to count the names from the name Yah, from Chokhmah, as is explained there. And he explained that the Tzaddik is called El Chai for the reason that the issuing-place of life is from him; and he said "from whom all life issues," because the root of life is above, in Chokhmah and Binah, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), "wisdom gives life to its possessors," and as we shall explain in the Glossary of Titles, with the help of God. For this [reason] he said that the reason Yesod is called by the name El Chai — although the root of life is above — is because he is their source in respect of their issuing forth; and on that account he adopted the expression "issue" (nafkin), that is, in respect of issuing.

Behold, then, that Rabbi Abba explained that the name of Yesod is El Chai. And Rabbi Elazar (there, 11b) disputed him and said that its name is Shaddai, and these are his words: "The ninth is Shaddai, for He said to the world, 'Enough (dai)' — for 'dai' is sufficiency; and sufficiency comes to the world only from the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world (yesod olam), who said to the world, 'Enough.'"

And because it was difficult for Rabbi Elazar that the name Shaddai means "He said to the world, Enough" — that is, that He set it a limit, in that its boundaries were stretching ever onward until He said to it, "Enough" — and this cannot rightly apply to Yesod, since the creation of the world was by way of the Architect, which is Malkhut, and so it is surely she who said to the world, "Enough" — therefore he said that Shaddai means sufficiency and sustenance, and the sustenance is from the side of Yesod, and it is he who supplies sustenance to the world; and this is "and sufficiency comes to the world only from the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world." And he intended to say [the acrostic] Tzaddik-Yesod-Olam, for he is the foundation that establishes the world; and this is why he doubled his expression and said, "the Tzaddik, who is the foundation of the world, who said to the world, 'Enough.'" Even so, we do not deny that the name El Chai is in Yesod, as Rabbi Abba explained — but not that it is a holy name in the manner of the other names that may not be erased, but rather a title like the other titles; and it comes in Scripture (Psalms 84:3): "my heart and my flesh sing out to El, the living God (El Chai)." And the name Shaddai is written in the Torah: "And El Shaddai will bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you"; repeated in the Prophets: "like the voice of Shaddai when they went"; tripled in the Writings: "and Shaddai will be your defense." And the name of Malkhut is Adonai, written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, tripled in the Writings. Written in the Torah: "And now, let the power of Adonai be magnified," and many like it; repeated in the Prophets: "A word has the Adonai sent against Jacob," and many like it; tripled in the Writings: "Adonai, open my lips," and many like it.
