And it has come in the Masorah that there are 134 of them in Scripture; and the reason for this you will find in Chizkuni's commentary on the Torah, at its beginning, where he said that this number corresponds to the letters of the initial and final letters of the words mizrach (east), ma'arav (west), darom (south) — to say that these three directions are shut up in the name of the Holy One, blessed be He; and likewise [the number] 134 (k-l-d) is a term of shutting, like aklidei (keys); but north is not included, for it is open, to exact [punishment] from the wicked, and in the time to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will shut it up as well, etc. — see there, and you will find reasons that follow from this inquiry. And these ten aforementioned names are palaces (heikhalot) for the spirituality of the sefirot; and that spirituality is a garment for their inner spirituality, hinted at in the four-letter name within each and every sefirah. And this matter, and others besides it, in the explanation of these names and the matters of the sefirot, will be explained in the coming Gates, with the help of God, each and every one in its fitting place.
And so this Gate is concluded; and thanks be to God, who has helped us — may He help us — forever, Selah, and ever. Amen.
The Second Gate is the Gate of the Reason for the Emanation:

On the reason why ten and not more. After we occupied ourselves in the preceding Gate with the necessity of the Emanation, and with its being agreed among the Kabbalists that they are ten, no fewer and no more, and set out their matter and their names, we have seen fit in this Gate to give a reason for their being ten, and for the matter of the Emanation as a whole, in general, with the help of God.
Chapter One:

As we were reveling in the garden of delights that is the books of the sages of this wisdom, we found that the sage Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat, in his book Minchat Yehudah (fol. 9b), wrote, on the reason for the ten, one reason in the name of Rabbi Azriel, with its rebuttal beside it. And these are his words: "Know that every point comes with three diameters [kotarim] — length, breadth and depth — and when you multiply them by one another, in the manner of a square number, the three make nine; and with the place that bears them they are ten." Thus far the words of Rabbi Azriel, of blessed memory. And Rabbi Yehudah objected to him, and these are his words: "This reason does not seem good to me, on two grounds. The first: the premise is not true, because the diameters mentioned have quantity, and the point has no quantity, for it is the end of the line. And further: would it be good in the eyes of YHVH that the diameters mentioned, by which body is defined, be attributed to the Emanation? For in divinity, body [geshem, which also means 'rain'] 'is over and gone.'" Thus far [his] words.

And because his words are somewhat obscure — particularly in the first difficulty, where he says "the point has no quantity," etc. — we have seen fit to explain his intent. The matter is this: every corporeal thing has length, breadth and depth, and there is no corporeal thing in the world that lacks these three, for they are the dimensions of body [gidrei ha-guf, 'what defines a body']. Were one to conceive of two of the dimensions of body alone, namely length and breadth without depth, it would be called a plane [shetach], meaning something like color spread [shatuach] over the face of paper, of which length and breadth can properly be said, but not depth; and therefore it is called a plane. And when we conceive of one dimension of body alone, namely length without breadth, it is called a line [kav], meaning a line of length, stripped of breadth and all the more of depth. And when we conceive of the negation of all three dimensions of body, that thing is called a point [nekudah]: that is, it has neither length nor breadth nor depth. And this is not because it could actually exist so; rather, it is called a notional point [nekudah tzurit] — that is, the notion [tziyur] of the negation of the dimensions of body, and not that it actually exists. With this premise the intent of Rabbi Yehudah will be understood, in objecting to Rabbi Azriel that his words contradict themselves: for he said "a point comes with three diameters," and this is impossible, since a point has neither length nor breadth nor depth, but is "the end of the line" — meaning, as we have explained, that it is the end of the line, which is likewise the negation of length; so the point turns out to have no diameters at all. And his statement that it is the end of the line is not agreed among the masters of astronomy [ba'alei ha-tekhunah]. For some say that two points or more, gathered together, make a line; and some say that even if all the points in the world were gathered, they would not make a line: since the point has no length at all, it is impossible that length should come to be through it. But this is not our principal concern.

Now Rabbi Yehudah resolved his two objections to the view of Rabbi Azriel by way of number, in Rabbi Azriel's defense; but since the thing is neither seemly nor acceptable, we shall not copy it here. It seems right to us to argue in Rabbi Azriel's favor, and to say: it is true that the Emanation is neither body nor corporeality. Nevertheless, body and corporeality proceed from it. And just as the masters of the Kabbalah held that the four elements — water, fire, air and earth — are hinted at in the sefirot (Gedulah being the element of water, Gevurah the element of fire, Tiferet the element of air, and Malkhut the element of earth), not because these are literally elements, God forbid, but because they are the root of the elements, and the elements are created from their root: so it is with the dimensions of body. The point is not that there is literally body above, nor that the dimensions of body can properly be said of the sefirot; rather, since body is created from them and they are its root, the dimensions of body are found in the roots as titles. Therefore we may properly speak, above, of "length, breadth and depth," meaning the power by which length is made, the power by which breadth is made, and the power by which depth is made. And likewise each of these three powers performs three further actions, so that they turn out to be nine; and that which brings the existence of body into being, before it comes into its dimensions, is a tenth power. Thus ten powers are necessary above, and these are the ten sefirot. And it is not that Rabbi Azriel's view is that the dimensions of body exist above, Heaven forbid. Further, it seems that the difficulty was none at all to begin with, for Rabbi Azriel did well in likening the Emanation to the dimensions of body, since permission for this has already been given.

And indeed Sefer Yetzirah took this very way in saying "depth of height and depth of below, and height and below, and east and west, and south and north" — these are the dimensions of body; and yet Sefer Yetzirah did not refrain from applying the likeness to divinity, since they are a parable and a likeness for the subject under discussion. And as for the second difficulty, that the point has no quantity: this is no objection. For there is certainly no point that does not have dimensions; and if we said above that the point has no quantity, that is only the notional point, which does not actually exist, whereas a point that actually exists has diameters. If so, this is no objection.
And further: because the Emanation is not body or corporeality, he referred to it by the term "point," which is not a body — since the Emanation is the root of body and of its dimensions.

And further, he referred to the Emanation by the term "point" to say that, just as the point is unified in its parts and admits of no parts at all, so the Emanation admits of no parts; and even if we speak of parts in it, it is all parable and likeness. Thus far what has seemed right to us to argue in favor of Rabbi Azriel. And now we shall write what Rabbi Yehudah wrote on the reason for the Emanation, and these are his words: "Since the Emanation comes in a point, we must perforce acknowledge that this point has a beginning, a middle and an end [rosh, tokh, sof]. We must acknowledge an end, since we see that, had [things] been created from the side of the power that has no end, they would go on without end and would exist forever; and that was not the intention. And since it has an end, it therefore has a beginning, for there is no end without a beginning and no beginning without an end. But beware of thinking, when I say 'beginning, middle and end,' that a beginning, middle and end in quantity are meant, Heaven forbid; rather, [they are meant] in respect of power, for there is a difference between the cause and the effect. And since each of the three extremities mentioned in the point includes the three — for in the beginning there are end and middle, and so in the middle, and so in the end — they come to nine, when we multiply three by three in the manner of a square number; and the place that bears [them], etc." Thus far [his] words.

These are some of his words, in brief; and he brought many passages from the Zohar as proof. But since the passages are no proof at all for his words, we have not seen fit to copy them. And the difficulty that should be raised, whether against his words or against the words of Rabbi Azriel, peace be upon him, is this: since the reason for the ten is the point, which has three, each including three — then we too may say that each part of the three in each of the three parts itself includes the three, and so they mount up without end, from three to three. And if we do not wish to include them [in one another] in this way, then the first inclusion, by which we make three into nine — whence do we have it? This is certainly very strained: so much so that, on account of it, there are those who wished to combine the two views, and said that every point has depth, length and breadth, and each of these three has an end, a middle and a beginning [sof, tokh, rosh], making nine, and the place that bears them makes ten. And I am able to object to the holders of these three views, for I see no place for these things: since it turns out that bodies and limit are what necessitate the existence of the Emanation. And it is not acceptable to say that, because these are necessary dimensions, the sefirot were compelled to be of this measure; for it is the sefirot that acted and begot the world and all created entities. Indeed, if the sefirot were sixteen, the dimensions could exist as sixteen things, four by four. Who ever saw fit to make the bringing-about of the form of the father necessary on account of the existence of the form of the son? Would you say that Reuben had to have hands so that his son should have hands — or, again, that Reuben must have three hands so that his son should have three hands? How can we make the form of the cause necessary on account of the form of the effect? For in truth the cause is the principal thing and the effect is secondary to it; and how can the effect be what necessitates the form of its cause's existence? I wonder at this.

And further, as to the words of Rabbi Yehudah, who said that the point has an end, a middle and a beginning, and that each of the three has an end, a middle and a beginning: this too does not come out well. For a middle cannot have an end and a beginning: if it had an end and a beginning it would not be a middle; and of that which is a middle, "end" and "beginning" cannot properly be said, since its beginning is the first beginning and its end is the last end. For "end" and "beginning" here are not a quantitative end and beginning, but the cessation of the power, or its beginning. And how can one say that there is a power that has a cessation of its power, or a beginning of it, other than its final cessation or its first beginning — that is, its very own beginning and end?

And further: since "beginning" and "end" mean nothing but the cessation of the power or its beginning, as has been explained, then, since the end is the cessation of the power, how can we speak, in that cessation, of a beginning and a middle? For it is nothing but cessation — the power has ceased — and in cessation there is no beginning and no middle. (Though some of this can be resolved, with strain.) And as with the difficulty he himself raised against Rabbi Azriel — how can the diameters of the corporeal be attributed to the Emanation, "for in divinity," etc. — is it any easier on his own view? How can cessation of power and beginning of power occur in the Emanation? For of divinity no lack of power can properly be said, God forbid, for it is perfect with the utmost perfection. Perforce we must answer this in one of two ways. The first: it is necessary because there is a difference between the Ein Sof and the emanated, like the difference between cause and effect; and so some cessation of power can properly be said of it, since it is necessarily not exactly like the Emanator, having descended from Him and being emanated from Him. And this is no deficiency in the Emanator, God forbid, nor in the emanated; rather, because it is emanated and an effect, it must descend a grade from its cause. This is due to the superiority of the Emanator over the emanated, and for this reason cessation of power can properly be said of it, in a certain respect. Or we may say that there had to be a limit in their action, in order to fulfil the intent of the Emanator, which was that created entities should be finite and subject to cessation. If so, then according to the words of Rabbi Azriel too we may say that limit was necessary in the Emanation, for these reasons. First: because the First Cause is the utmost negation of cessation, both in notion and in quantity, altogether; whereas those emanated from Him are necessarily limited somewhat, in the measure of their descent from before Him, by a notional limit and not a literal limit. Yet relative to the Emanator, who is their cause, from whom we are obliged to negate limit and cessation and all such things, the emanated must have a difference from Him, like the difference of the effect from the cause.

And further, second: so that the created entities that proceed from the emanated should be limited. And this is His power, blessed be He: for just as the world was created Something from Nothing [yesh me-ayin], so the Ein Sof, King of kings of kings, emanated the emanated, from whom there would proceed finite actions, so that created entities would be limited. And the inquirer into this must bring his mind to understand, and establish it and support it and direct it toward the truth. Let him not think that our intent in this is to set a limit either to the Emanator or to the emanated, Heaven forbid and forfend. Rather, the intent is this: after we have negated body and limit and quantity and cessation of power and finitude and end from the pure and holy Emanation, with the utmost negation and distancing, we are obliged by absolute necessity to rise yet higher, to a more exalted and more choice grade, in the case of the Ein Sof, the Emanator, King of kings of kings. And that is why they called Him Ein Sof ['without end'], for the reason mentioned. And few words on this matter are good and seemly; of this and the like it is said (Proverbs 27:26), "Lambs [kevasim] are for your clothing" [which the Sages read: things that are the hidden matters (kivshono) of the world should be kept under your clothing]. Nevertheless, we have seen fit to prove the matter conclusively from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 70, fol. 130a), and these are his words: "The supernal Keter, although it is a primordial light, a clear light, a refined light, is dark before the Cause of Causes." Thus far [his] words.

The meaning is: although it is a clear light, etc. — the utmost of purity, and without limit, and we are obliged to negate density and limit from it — nevertheless we are obliged to believe that it has density and limit, and a cessation of light and of power, relative to the Emanator who is its cause. And that is why he here referred to the Ein Sof by the expression "Cause of Causes": the intent is to establish the matter by absolute necessity, for He is the cause of all the causes, and therefore He must necessarily have a rank above them all. For if we were to strip the Emanation of every deficiency whatever and raise it to the most perfect grade possible, a denial of the existence of a First Cause would follow: since Keter would be at a rank than which there is no higher, what then would be the rank by which the Emanator rises above it? Therefore we are obliged to leave room in which to raise the Emanator above all the emanated, even while we raise the emanated as far as is possible. And this is a thing a person must contemplate; let him not be hasty to reply.

Rabbi Yehudah wrote yet another reason, and wrote that it is more satisfactory than the reason of Rabbi Azriel that we copied in the preceding chapter; and these are his words: "The all-inclusive number is ten, and there is none besides it. For everything above ten returns to the units — whether on the side of the units, like eleven, twelve, thirteen, or on the side of the tens, like twenty, thirty, forty, which are multiples in the series of the tens. And since the Emanation enters into number, it is fitting that it should take the most inclusive number there is." Thus far [his] words.

As for his saying "since the Emanation enters into number": the meaning is that they had to have number so that created entities should have number and limit, as we explained above. But the difficulty that can be raised is this: what causes the all-inclusive number to be ten and not twenty, or a hundred, so that the return of the ranks does not begin [only] from twenty upward? We would answer that the cause of this is that the sefirot are ten; for if the sefirot were twenty, the number too would run to twenty. And this is certainly true; and it is a more satisfactory and more acceptable account that the sefirot be the principal thing and number secondary — and not the reverse, that number should be ten for no reason, and that this should be the cause of the Emanation's being of that number.

And further: the sefirot are a cause prior to all created entities, and they are the causes of all that is from them and below. How, then, can number, which is posterior, be the cause of the sefirot, which are prior? This is certainly very strained. Yet although we reject these answers as the reason for the Emanation, we do not deny that it is true that number and the Emanation have a relation and a great affinity. For number is ten, and it rises from ten to ten without end, and never rises beyond ten; and so it is with the sefirot.

And further: numbers are ten, and from ten they rise to a hundred, and from a hundred they rise to a thousand — and that is elef ['thousand'], which is one [Alef], in the secret of the return of the matter to complete unity. So it is with the sefirot, in all of which [all are included]: for ten times ten is a hundred, and when we include them once again they are a thousand, that is, Alef, in the secret of pele ['wonder'], which is the return of things to their source, in the secret of the unity. And there are several other great principles that depend on number, which are principles of the Torah, as we shall write in the Gate of Permutation, with the help of God. And we cannot think of anything in the world that resembles the Emanation more than number does. Likewise we do not deny that it is true that the Emanation is three [sets] of three each, and an all-inclusive power: that is, three, which are Chesed [lovingkindness], Din [judgment] and Rachamim [compassion], with three in each of them. In Chesed there are an end, a middle and a beginning [sof, tokh, rosh]: namely Chokhmah the beginning, Chesed the middle and Netzach the end. Likewise in Din: the beginning is Binah, the middle Gevurah and the end Hod. And likewise in Rachamim: Tiferet the beginning, Yesod the middle and Malkhut the end. And the supernal Keter includes them all, as we shall explain at greater length in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter twenty-five, with God's help. And this matter is deep, as we shall set out at length there. But for all that, we shall hold truthfully to what is true: that these things do not suffice at all as a reason for the Emanation, as explained above. Rabbi Menachem Recanati, of blessed memory, wrote yet another reason, for the seven sefirot of the Structure [binyan], one by one, in his book Ta'amei ha-Mitzvot [the Reasons for the Commandments], in the discussion of the Self and the vessels; and Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat, of blessed memory, copied his words: "And now we shall explain how the world needs these seven extremities, which are Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod and Malkhut. The beginning of the Structure is Chesed, for there can be no structure without it: that is, by this attribute the Holy One, blessed be He, whitens the iniquities of Israel. And in Sefer Yetzirah this attribute is called 'she who whitens the iniquities of Israel'; and she pardons them for what is done from the side of Gevurah, for the evil inclination flows from there. And this sefirah is emanated from Binah, which is above it. But the first three are intellective and are not called attributes, and we are not at present engaged in explaining them. And this is a great lovingkindness [chesed] that the Holy One, blessed be He, does with His creatures: that He passes over [their iniquities] one by one, the first each time, and is reconciled to them, even though strict justice does not warrant it. Therefore the world cannot endure without this pillar. And in Sefer ha-Bahir I found this: The attribute of Chesed said, 'All the days that Abraham was in the world I did not need to do my work, for Abraham stood there in my place and kept my charge. For this is my work: I acquit the world, even when they have been found liable.

"'And further, I turn them back and put it into their hearts to do the will of their Father in heaven. All this Abraham did.' Further, the world needs the second pillar, which is Din [judgment], the opposite of the first attribute we mentioned. Were it not for this pillar, punishment would not reach the wicked, and every man would rob and kill his fellow with none to exact payment from him. Therefore the world needs to be governed by this pillar, so that payment may be exacted from the wicked. And this sefirah was emanated from the Chesed we mentioned, and it is called 'fire from water,' meaning fire that came out of water; and as water is the opposite of fire, so the actions of this attribute are the opposite of the action of the other attribute. And these two are called 'the arms of the world,' as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:27), 'and beneath are the arms of the world.' Further, the world needs a third pillar, which is Tiferet. It is the intermediate attribute; it receives from both of them and stands between the two. And the world's need for this attribute is because the first two attributes are not enough for the world. For if one who has become liable were judged by the second attribute, which is the attribute of judgment, it would judge him without pity, being the attribute of harsh judgment, and it would likewise [punish] the meritorious and the good, above, altogether. And if he were judged by the attribute of Chesed, even his few iniquities would not be remembered against him, even in this world. Therefore the world needs the intermediate attribute, like a person who joins two things together and unites them in a single subject, in order 'to give to each man according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds': so that if the righteous have sinned, payment is exacted from them in this world, and if the wicked have performed commandments, their good reward is paid to them in this world. And this attribute is called 'east,' for from there light went out to the world; and the sphere of the sun corresponds to it, for the attribute of day flows from it. Further, the world needs a fourth pillar and a fifth pillar, which are Netzach and Hod. They flow and are emanated from the Gedulah and the Gevurah that we mentioned above, as it is said (Psalms 16:11), 'pleasantness at Your right hand, Netzach' — meaning that Netzach is on the right, set directly beneath Chesed, and Hod on the left, set directly beneath Gevurah.

"And Netzach has the sense of victory [nitzuach]: that is, by this attribute lovingkindness and merit are victorious over the accusers. And for this one must give thanks to YHVH, and this is Hod, in the sense of thanksgiving [hoda'ah] to the Name, who founded this pillar; for without the help of YHVH a person could not stand before the Satan. Further, the world needs a sixth pillar and a seventh pillar, which are Yesod and Malkhut; they are the likeness of male and female, and all flows into Malkhut, which is called Shekhinah and the Assembly of Israel [Knesset Yisrael], for all the sefirot dwell [shokhenot] in her; and we have already explained this above. And therefore our Sages, of blessed memory, called her 'bride' [kallah], and in the Song of Songs too she is called 'bride,' because she includes [kelulah] all. And she is in the west [ma'arav], as our Sages, of blessed memory, said, 'the Shekhinah is in the west,' because there all is mingled [mit'arev]." Thus far [his] words on the reason for the Emanation. And although it is true that most of what he says is right, nevertheless these things do not suffice as a reason for the Emanation. For once judgment and punishment, lovingkindness and reward, are found in the two attributes Chesed and Gevurah, and the intermediate attribute is Tiferet, what further need is there for the other sefirot? Why should the victory over the accuser and the evil inclination not lie in Gevurah — as in truth it does? For so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained: that a person's prevailing [gover] over his inclination is from the side of Gevurah; and we shall treat this at length in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter three. Likewise thanksgiving, on his account, is not an attribute that acts, but only that a person should give thanks to the Name; and was it necessary to emanate a sefirah just for the thanks that a person owes to YHVH? I wonder at this. Further, why Yesod and Malkhut? Since Chesed and Din come together in the intermediate [attribute] and are united, what need is there of male and female at all, for the sake of mingling? For the powers have already been mingled in the intermediate [attribute].
And further: in this manner we cannot give a reason for the first three at all, as he said explicitly.

And further — God forbid — is the hand of the Emanator too short to emanate one emanation only, that is, a single sefirah in which there would be the power of punishment, of reward and of the intermediate? And there is no rebuttal from the wording of the mishnah (Avot 5:1), "By ten utterances the world was created. And could it not have been created by one utterance?" etc. For, on the contrary, the mishnah means the opposite of what he said: that although the world was created through differing things that indicate judgment, compassion and the intermediate, it could nevertheless have been created by the power of a single utterance, that is, a single sefirah. This shows that it is not beyond His power for the power of all ten to be in the power of a single sefirah. That is the meaning of "And could it not have been created by one utterance," etc.: it is certainly speaking of the creation of the world as it now is. And as for its saying "but rather to exact payment": the meaning is not as Rabbi Menachem supposed. Rather, it concerns finitude — or [what proceeds] from that which is not finite — or something else, as we shall explain at length in the coming chapters, with the help of God. Therefore this reason does not at all satisfy our will or quench our thirst.

After we have written, in the preceding chapters, all the reasons that the commentators wrote, whether many or few, and have raised our points against them as Heaven has shown us, we have resolved to speak on this matter as it falls to our lot. And before anything else we say: "I see the men, but the objection I do not see." For this question must take one of two ways. Either the question of the reason for the ten is put to us — that is, whence do we have proof, from the Torah or from investigation, for our tradition; or the question is put to the Emanator, the Ein Sof, King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He: why did He emanate ten and not some other number? And we shall speak to each of these. If the question is put to us — that is, whence do we have support for the tradition that they are ten, so that we should not say they are twenty, or five, or one — it is no question to begin with. For we have proof upon proof in the Torah of Moses, which reveals these treasured secrets to us and enlightens our eyes in them: in the creation of the world by ten utterances; in the giving of the Torah by ten Commandments; and King David, peace be upon him, in the ten kinds of praise in the psalm "Praise El in His sanctuary," with which he sealed his book. And this matter has already been explained in tractate Rosh Hashanah (fol. 32), for we read there: "These ten Kingships [Malkhuyot] — to what do they correspond? Rabbi said: to the ten praises that David spoke in the book of Psalms. — But there are many praises! — Those of which it is written, 'Praise Him with the blast of the shofar.' Rav Yosef said: to the Ten Commandments that were spoken to Moses at Sinai. Rabbi Yochanan said: to the ten utterances by which the world was created. — Which are they? The 'And He said' of Genesis. — But those are nine! — 'In the beginning' is also an utterance, as it is written, 'By the word of YHVH the heavens were made.'" Thus far [its] words.
In truth this passage is, on the face of it, difficult as regards Rabbi Yochanan, who answered, "'In the beginning' is also an utterance."

For "In the beginning" hints at Chokhmah, which is called "beginning" [reshit], and the large Bet hints at it. If so, even though "In the beginning" is also an utterance, there are still [only] nine; and this is the difficulty. For then what was troubling the questioner? If his difficulty was that Chokhmah is not in the count, there would be eight, and that is the objection he should have raised. And if his difficulty was that Keter is not in the count, then why was he satisfied when he was answered "'In the beginning' [is also an utterance]," etc.? He should have objected: even though "In the beginning" is also an utterance, still, with "In the beginning" there are nine, for "In the beginning" is Chokhmah. This is a general question about the utterances mentioned in this passage. And likewise, from this difficulty one could prove the view of Rabbi Shem Tov ben Shem Tov, author of Sefer ha-Emunot, whose words we shall copy in the Gate of Whether the Ein Sof is the Keter, chapter three. This is the Da'at view: he holds that Keter is not in the count of the sefirot, but that the ten sefirot run from Chokhmah downward; and since the count pressed him, he said that a further sefirah was newly added to it, called Da'at, which is below Chokhmah and Binah and above Chesed and Gevurah. We shall treat the matter at length there. Now on his account it turns out that the utterances begin only from Chokhmah, and even so there are nine without "In the beginning," which is Chokhmah, and ten with "In the beginning," which is Chokhmah. And because of the ruin that would follow from this passage, before we raise further points about it or explain anything in it at all, it is fitting that we look to setting this matter right. And we say that this [view] is impossible. For since Rabbi Shem Tov admitted with his own mouth that Da'at is what is mentioned in the verse (Proverbs 3:20), "By His knowledge [da'at] the depths were split," and likewise in what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah fol. 12; and there it reads "by ten things the world was created," three of them being wisdom, etc.), "by three things the world was created: by wisdom [chokhmah], by understanding [tevunah] and by knowledge [da'at]" — it is compelled by the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that [this] Da'at is the manifestation of Tiferet that is concealed between Abba and Imma [Father and Mother]; and this is what is called BeN-YaH ['son of Yah'], through which Chokhmah and Binah are united, as we shall explain these matters at length in that Gate.

Accordingly, we should ask: what distinguishes this Da'at — which is the concealed manifestation of Tiferet, emanated between Abba and Imma — that it should effect an utterance of its own, from the other manifestations of the sefirot, which did not effect utterances, although their coming-to-be preceded the coming-to-be of this Da'at? Take the manifestation of Binah concealed within Chokhmah: just as Chokhmah itself acted, the concealed Binah ought also to act. Likewise the manifestation of Gevurah concealed within Binah, and the manifestation of Chesed concealed within Chokhmah: each of them ought to have effected one utterance, besides the utterance that belongs to it in its revealed manifestation, as with Da'at and Tiferet. Nor can it be said that the reason Da'at effected an utterance of its own is that Da'at is the manifestation of Tiferet with its mate at its side — they being the manifestation of "the two great luminaries" — and that because they were united the two together effected one utterance, like the other sefirot, whereas after the moon made her accusation and was diminished and driven out, the luminaries were divided in two, and Tiferet went back and effected an utterance of its own, and Malkhut an utterance of her own. For if so, why did Tiferet not effect an utterance of its own from the outset, and Malkhut one of her own, even while they were united in the utmost union? For it cannot be denied that they were two sefirot. Otherwise — if they are counted as only one sefirah — it turns out that before the diminishment the sefirot were nine and not ten, since Malkhut and Tiferet are one sefirah; and likewise, when she returns to her first place, they will be nine. And this is impossible by the law of this wisdom, as explained in the preceding Gate.

And further: the ten Commandments and the ten utterances are one matter, as is evident from the passage we copied above. And so it is evident in the Zohar, Parashat Yitro (fol. 93b), and these are its words: "These ten sayings of the Torah are the sum of all the commandments of the Torah, the sum of above and below, the sum of all the ten sayings of 'In the beginning.'" Thus far [its] words.

It said "the sum of all the commandments of the Torah" because Rashbi, peace be upon him, holds that the six hundred and thirteen commandments are included in the ten Commandments, as is explained in Parashat Yitro, and likewise included in the ten utterances, as is evident in Parashat Bereshit and in the Tikkunim. That is why it said that the ten Commandments are the sum of the commandments. And it likewise said that they are the sum of the ten utterances: meaning that whatever is made clear from the ten utterances of the account of Creation is made clear from the ten Commandments of the giving of the Torah, to the eyes of the discerning. Now we say: since the ten Commandments and the ten utterances are all one, how can it be said, in the case of the Commandments, that [Tiferet and Malkhut] were united and that the Shekhinah was driven out? For certainly, once she was united in the coupling she was not diminished, so long as she was in her husband's bosom. And if she was below, why are they ten? For Da'at was by then concealed, and it was not fitting for it to speak a Commandment [dibbur], since it had already been concealed and the matter had not returned to its tikkun.

And further: can we say that, had there been no diminishment, the utterances would have been only nine? I wonder at this; for the world would then have lacked, from its perfection, everything that belongs to that one utterance.

And further: since Da'at includes Malkhut and Tiferet, then, as to the utterance that it spoke, by which that creation was created — why did it not create everything that was possible by the power of Malkhut and everything that was possible by the power of Tiferet, seeing that it is the manifestation of their union, which is their being two great luminaries? And why was there still a creation left over for Malkhut and Tiferet afterward? Was the power of Da'at lacking, when it is more perfect than both of them?

And further: we have several clear proofs that "In the beginning" is the utterance of the supernal Keter. First, in Sefer ha-Bahir, and these are its words: "What are the utterances? The first is the supernal Keter, blessed is it and blessed," etc.; "Chokhmah is the second, as it is written," etc. Thus it counted the supernal Keter among the utterances, and it is the first of them all.

And further: the difficulty is no difficulty to begin with, and proves nothing. For although the word "In the beginning" [bereshit] is in Chokhmah, the utterance is nevertheless in Keter. And because of the subtlety of Keter and its nearness to its source — so that, of the four-letter name, nothing was attributed to it but the thorn of the Yod; and it is likewise called Alef, from the word pele ['wonder'], and it is called "a wondrous and covered Amon" [amon: 'nursling' or 'master craftsman'] — although the Bet of bereshit is the hint at Chokhmah, its thorn nevertheless points to Keter. And so Rabbi Akiva explained, and these are his words: "They say to the Bet, 'Who created you?' and it points with its thorn to the Alef." The meaning is that the Bet itself — which is Chokhmah to the beings [havayot], and which is not the start of the Emanation but a second emanation — has a thorn behind it pointing to the Alef, as though indicating to those who ask it "Who created you?" (that is, whether it was emanated by something emanated or by a first Emanator); and it shows with its thorn that it is a second emanation, and that the Alef, which is Keter, preceded it. And so it can now properly be said that the utterance "In the beginning" is in Keter, although the word bereshit hints at Chokhmah, since Keter too is somewhat hinted at in it, as we explained. And the point is that the whole Emanation is included in the verse "In the beginning," to indicate of it [Keter] that it is the Emanator — that is, by the power of the Ein Sof — and yet Keter itself is the Emanator and the agent that speaks the utterance. And so we find that most of the utterances include all ten; and that is why a hint at Chokhmah came in the word bereshit, although the principal part of the utterance is in Keter. Nor is this surprising: for the blessing of the Patriarchs is in Chesed, and yet Chesed is not mentioned in it until "God of Abraham" — and even "God of Abraham" is in Chokhmah — and it is not mentioned in itself except in the words "the great God," apart from the closing formula. So it is with the utterance "In the beginning": granted that the word bereshit is in Chokhmah, the principal part of the utterance is nevertheless in Keter, which is concealed, as is its way; and yet it came as a hint in the thorn of the Bet, as we explained — and what is meant is the Chokhmah-within-Keter.

And further, apart from this, it may be said that the Bet itself hints at Keter. The support for this is that the Bet of bereshit is the Alef of Avgitatz, which is the forty-two-letter name, as we shall explain in the Gate of Particulars of Names, with the help of God; and Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained that the Alef of Avgitatz is the hint at Keter, and these are his words (in Tikkun 70, fol. 116): "The Alef of Avgitatz is Keter, wondrous, an Amon, and covered."

Thus he testified explicitly that the Bet of bereshit is in Keter. And close to this is the view of the Ramban, of blessed memory, in Parashat Bereshit, and these are his words: "And the word bereshit hints at Chokhmah, which is the beginning of beginnings, as I have mentioned; and therefore the Jerusalem Targum rendered it 'with wisdom' [be-chokhmeta]. And the word is crowned with the crown of the Bet." Thus far [his] words.

And the meaning of his words is that the Bet hints at Keter, because it is a house [bayit] for all the sefirot. And this is evident from his wording, for he says "and the word bereshit hints at Chokhmah": he means the word bereshit — not the Bet, but the word itself — as he concludes, "which is the beginning [reshit]," etc.; he did not say that it is called bereshit, but reshit alone. And when he brings proof from the Targum, which rendered "with wisdom" [be-chokhmeta], it is not that [the Bet] is literally Chokhmah; rather, the Bet of bereshit is a prefix. For the word reshit is Chokhmah and the Bet of bereshit is Keter; and that is why he said, "and the word is crowned with the crown of the Bet."

From all this it appears that this passage gives no compelling proof for the view of Rabbi Shem Tov, of blessed memory. But it still remains our duty to explain what is found to conflict with this passage in the Zohar, Parashat Vayikra. For in this passage it said that "In the beginning" is the tenth utterance, whereas in Parashat Vayikra (fol. 11b) Rashbi explained that there are ten utterances apart from "In the beginning." And these are his words: "Rabbi Shimon said: It is written, 'Ten, ten the spoon, by the shekel of the sanctuary.' Why 'ten, ten'? Ten for the account of Creation and ten for the giving of the Torah: ten utterances in the account of Creation and ten utterances in the giving of the Torah. What does this tell us? That the world was created only for the sake of the Torah; for as long as Israel occupy themselves with the Torah the world endures, and whenever Israel neglect the Torah, what is written? 'If not for My covenant by day and by night, I would not have set the laws of heaven and earth.' Come and see: ten utterances for the account of Creation, as we have learned, 'By ten utterances the world was created'; ten utterances for the giving of the Torah, these being the Ten Commandments. It is written, 'I am YHVH your God,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let there be light, and there was light.' This (is) the faith of the Holy One, blessed be He, [who] is called 'light,' as it is written, 'YHVH is my light and my salvation,' etc. It is written, 'You shall have no other gods before Me,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters,' etc. 'Let there be a firmament': this is Israel, who are the portion of the Holy One, blessed be He, and who hold fast to that place called 'heaven.' And this is the secret: once Rabbi Yeisa the Elder asked Rabbi Ila'i, saying: All the other nations the Holy One, blessed be He, gave over to great appointed rulers; where are Israel? He sent back to him: 'And God set them in the firmament of heaven.' And he sent him a good answer. 'In the midst of the waters': amid the words of the Torah. 'And let it divide between waters and waters': between the Holy One, blessed be He, who is called 'a well of living waters,' and idolatry, which is called 'broken cisterns that can hold no water,' which are the bitter waters, etc., foul and stagnant. Therefore holy Israel divide between waters and waters. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not take the name of YHVH your God in vain,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the waters under the heaven be gathered to one place.' Come and see: whoever swears falsely by the holy name, it is as though he separated the Mother [Imma] from her place above, and the holy crowns are not settled in their places, as it is said, 'and a whisperer separates the Chief [aluf],' and the 'Chief' is none other than the Holy One, blessed be He. And it is written, 'Let the waters under the heaven be gathered to one place': do not make a separation through a false oath. 'To one place': as is fitting, in the place of truth, and not in another place, for falsehood. And what is falsehood? When the waters go to another place that is not theirs. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the earth sprout grass, herb.' When did the holy earth grow great and become crowned [it'atrat] with her diadems [itraha]? You must say, on the Sabbath day; for then the bride is joined to the King, to bring forth grasses and blessings for the world. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven.' What does this tell us? That these luminaries are 'your father and your mother': 'your father' is the sun, 'your mother' is the moon. And the sun is none other than the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, 'For YHVH Elohim is a sun and a shield'; and the moon is none other than the Assembly of Israel, as it is written, 'and your moon shall not withdraw.' Therefore all is one. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not murder,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the waters swarm with living souls.' And you: do not kill a human being, who is called by that name, as it is written, 'and the man became a living soul.' Do not be like those fish, of whom the great swallow the small. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not commit adultery,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'Let the earth bring forth living souls after their kind.' From here we learn that a man must not be false with another woman who is not his mate; and therefore it is written, 'Let the earth bring forth living souls after their kind': that a woman should bear only from her own kind. And who is her kind? Her mate. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not steal,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'And God said: Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed.' What I have given you and entrusted to you shall be yours; and you shall not steal what belongs to another. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'And God said: Let us make man in our image.' Against one who is in the image of the King, do not bear false witness; and whoever bears false witness against his fellow, it is as though he bore [false] witness above. It is written in the giving of the Torah, 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife,' and in the account of Creation it is written, 'It is not good that the man should be alone.' See, your mate is there before you; therefore 'you shall not covet your neighbor's wife.' And these are the ten utterances for the account of Creation and the ten utterances for the giving of the Torah; and this is what is written, 'Ten, ten the spoon, by the shekel of the sanctuary': they were weighed as one, in a single balance. And for this reason the world stands and peace is found in it." Thus far [his] words.

And from it, it appears explicitly that among the ten utterances of the account of Creation, "In the beginning" is not an utterance at all; and this is certainly strained. And in order to understand this matter we shall first set down another passage, from the Tikkunim, and through it this perplexity will be cleared up, with the help of God.

In the Tikkunim it is implied that the work of the utterances was not done by any of the first three; for the first utterance, which is Keter, is "Let there be light"; the second utterance, Chokhmah, is "Let there be a firmament"; and the third utterance, Binah, is "Let the waters be gathered." And these are its words (in Tikkun 42, fol. 79): "Bereshit: there [in that word] is ish ['man'], of whom it is said, 'and Jacob was a whole man [ish tam]'; and this is the third day, for there were three craftsmen up to this point: the first day, the second day and the third day, each of which brought forth its craft. To the first day spoke that wondrous and covered Amon, that grade which is called Ayin ['Nothing'] and includes three sefirot — Alef, Keter; Yod, Chokhmah; Nun, Binah — etc. It told each of the three days to bring forth its craft. It said to the first day, 'Let there be light'; at once it brought forth its craft and made it, as it is written, 'and there was light.' And they have established that there is no 'being' [havayah] except through making [asiyah]. The Alef of Ayin, which was flying in the air [avir], brought forth light [or]; the Yod brought forth the firmament; the Nun of Ayin brought forth the dry land, as it is written, 'And God said: Let the waters be gathered,' etc." Thus far [its] words.

From it, it appears explicitly that those who acted were the craftsmen, which are the six days, and that they acted at the utterance of the first three, which are Ayin. And among the things that should also be understood about these utterances is that they are ten; and although they are ten, we know that there is no creation and no action except through the six days alone, which are: Gedulah, the first day; Gevurah, the second day; Tiferet, the third day; Netzach, the fourth day; Hod, the fifth day; Yesod, the sixth day. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained: that the whole work of Creation was included in and done through these days, in Malkhut, and Malkhut brings the things out into the light in completeness. And these are his words in Parashat Terumah (fol. 127): "'Of the trees of Lebanon': these are the planted trees that the Holy One, blessed be He, uprooted and transplanted in another place; and these are called 'cedars of Lebanon,' as it is said, 'the cedars of Lebanon that He planted.' And this palanquin was built and completed only through them. Again, 'of the trees of Lebanon': these are the six days of Creation. Each and every day arranges in this palanquin the arrangement that is proper to it. The first arrangement: there flowed from the right side the primordial light that was stored away, and it was taken from the right side; and there entered into this palanquin a certain image, in the likeness of this light, by means of a certain Foundation [Yesod], and it performed its service in it. Afterward this palanquin brought forth a certain image in the likeness of this light. And this is the secret of what is written, 'Let there be light, and there was light.' Since it said 'Let there be light,' why is it written 'and there was light'? Scripture needed only to write 'and it was so.' What is 'and there was light'? It is that this light brought forth another light that was proper to it. And this is the first day of those trees of Lebanon. The second arrangement: there flowed from the left side the separation of the waters, in a flow of mighty fire; it was taken from the left side and entered into that palanquin and performed its service in it, and it separated the waters on the right side from the waters on the left side. Afterward that palanquin brought forth a certain image in its likeness. And this is the secret of what is written, 'between the waters that are under the firmament and the waters that are above the firmament; and it was so.' And this is the second day of those trees of Lebanon. The third arrangement: there flowed from the left side and from the right side a certain third day, which makes peace in the world; and from there fruits were drawn. And this one performed its service in this palanquin and brought forth kind after its kind: a kind for many works, the kind that was proper to it, and all the grasses and herbs and trees, in their many powers. And its image remained there, and that palanquin brought forth a kind in that very likeness. And this is the third day, which includes two sides, of those trees of Lebanon. The fourth arrangement: the light of the sun flowed and shone, to give light to this palanquin within its darkness; and it entered into it to give light, but performed no service in it until the fifth day, when this palanquin brought forth that service of the light that had entered it on the fourth day; and that palanquin brought forth in the very likeness of that light. And this is the fourth day, one of those trees of Lebanon. The fifth arrangement: there flowed a certain current of the swarming of the waters, and it performed its service, to bring forth the light of the arrangement of the fourth day; it performed its service in this palanquin and brought forth kinds after their kind, those that appear in that very likeness. And this day performed that service more than all the other days. And all remained in suspense until the sixth day, when this palanquin brought forth all that was stored away in it, as it is written, 'Let the earth bring forth living souls after their kind.' And this is the fifth day, one of those trees of Lebanon. The sixth arrangement: this is the day on which this whole palanquin was arrayed; it has no tikkun and no strength except from this day. When this [day] came, it arrayed this palanquin with many spirits, with many souls, with many maidens fair to behold, such as are fit to dwell in the palace of the King. It too was arrayed in the beauty [of] all the other days that had gone before, and it arrayed them in one craving, in desire [ra'ava], in joy: a tikkun of above and below. Then this palanquin was sanctified with supernal sanctities and crowned [it'atar] with its diadems [itrohi], until it rose in the ascent of the diadem of rest and was called by a supernal name, a holy name, which is Sabbath: the rest of all, the craving of all, the cleaving of all, above and below as one. And then it is written, 'King Solomon made himself a palanquin of the trees of Lebanon.'" Thus far [his] words.

And although the passage needs a long explanation, as will be given in Sefer Or Yakar, with God's help, it is nevertheless explicitly implied in it that all the utterances and the creations were through the six days: "Let there be light, and there was light" is in Chesed, etc. It turns out that, even if we say that "In the beginning" is an utterance, nothing at all is left for the first three. Therefore we must clear the stumbling-stones of the difficulties from these passages and set this discussion on its proper footing. And before anything else we say that it cannot be denied that the creations of the account of Creation were in six days, as in "and there was evening and there was morning, one day," "a second day," etc.; which shows that, although there were ten utterances, they were all nevertheless included in the six days. Now let us consider: if it is true that "In the beginning" is an utterance, whether in Chokhmah or in Keter, how can what is said there be right — "and the earth was formlessness and void [tohu va-vohu], and darkness," etc.? Would it be good in the eyes of YHVH for us to say that, when Malkhut was in Chokhmah or in Keter, the husks [kelipot] surrounded her there, namely formlessness, void and darkness? This is certainly very strained; for who put a husk up above? So the matter must certainly be this: that the Torah made known to us, before anything else, the existence of the Emanation, in the order of its emanation, in general. And this is the meaning of the verse "In the beginning": the concealed Keter, with the "beginning" [reshit], which is Chokhmah, "created" — that is, emanated — "Elohim," which is Binah; "et the heavens": these are Chesed and Tiferet. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained: that the word et comes to include Chesed, and "the heavens" is Tiferet; "and et the earth" is Gevurah, by the inclusion of et, and "the earth" is Malkhut. And Netzach, Hod and Yesod are included in Gedulah, Gevurah and Tiferet. And then it said "and the earth was formlessness and void," etc., which is to tell us of the existence of Malkhut and her chariots, good and evil. And after that it told us of the actions of these sefirot in Malkhut. And because the first three are concealed and have no revealed action, their action and their utterance were drawn forth through the three Patriarchs, who are the three craftsmen: Chesed, Gevurah and Tiferet. Therefore "Let there be light" is the first utterance, and it is drawn from Keter, through Gedulah, to the palanquin. [And the second utterance, "Let there be a firmament," is drawn from Chokhmah, through Gevurah, to the palanquin; and therefore, etc. See Asis Rimonim and the Pelach.] And that is why the matter of the firmament that divides between waters and waters is found at times hinted at in Chokhmah, in the secret of the upper waters and the lower waters with the firmament in the middle, as we shall explain in the Glossary of Titles, with God's help. And the third utterance, "Let the waters be gathered," is from Binah, through Tiferet. And this is the general sense of the passage of the Tikkunim. And now we say that the fourth utterance, which is on the third day, namely the utterance "Let the earth sprout," is drawn from Chesed through Tiferet, the third day. And the utterance "Let there be luminaries" is drawn from Gevurah — as is known, "luminaries" is written defectively [me'orot without the letter Vav], which is from the side of Gevurah — and it was done through Netzach, the fourth day. And the utterance "Let the waters swarm" is drawn from Tiferet through Netzach, in Hod. And this is hinted at in the passage from Terumah that we copied above, which said, "the fourth arrangement: the light of the sun flowed," which is the manifestation of Tiferet. And the reason is this: because Tiferet includes right and left, it received three utterances — from Chesed, from Gevurah, and one of its own. And because it inclines toward Chesed, it effected one utterance, that of Chesed: this is the utterance "Let the earth sprout," which is the second of the third day and the fourth of the utterances, and belongs to Chesed. And it handed over to Netzach the two [other] utterances, namely the fifth, which is Gevurah's, and the sixth, its own. Netzach effected the fifth, Gevurah's, and handed over to Hod the sixth, Tiferet's. And because judgment is complete only together with compassion, the light of the sun did not shine through Netzach, and the action of Netzach was not complete, until the fifth day came, which is Hod, on which the sixth utterance was done, which is the utterance of Tiferet. And this is what it said in the passage from Terumah, "the fifth arrangement … and it performed its service, to bring forth the light of the arrangement of the fourth day," etc. And Yesod, which is the sixth day, because it includes Netzach and Hod, brought forth three utterances, corresponding to Netzach, Hod and Yesod: the utterance "Let the earth bring forth" corresponding to Netzach, the utterance "Let us make man" corresponding to Hod, and the utterance "Behold, I have given" corresponding to Yesod. For the saying "Be fruitful and multiply" is not an utterance but only a blessing. For if you do not say so, there would be a full ten utterances, and how could he say "those are nine"? Rather, on this view, certainly nothing is called an utterance except an utterance of creation, and this one is an utterance of blessing. And because fruitfulness and increase belong to Yesod, this blessing was given on the sixth [day], which is Yesod. And with this the Sabbath day, which is Malkhut, was sanctified, and she was completed and "the city was built on its mound." And once she was complete she spoke her own utterance, which is "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him," etc.; for through the coupling the blessing would flow, as is evident in many places in the Zohar. So it now turns out that, for the utterances themselves — which are what acts — to hint at the ten sefirot, the utterances are only nine. For the utterance "It is not good" is not literally [the utterance of] Malkhut, but the actions of Malkhut; and the utterance of Malkhut is the one that was decreed from the mouth of Yesod, for Yesod emanated Malkhut. And because, in the passage of the Talmud in Rosh Hashanah with which we were dealing, the intent was that the ten Kingships are literally the ten utterances, he raised the difficulty and said "those are nine." For the utterance "Let there be light" is Chokhmah, as is explained in many places in the Zohar, and it comes out by the power of Keter. And what is meant is not Chokhmah proper; rather, of the utterances drawn to Malkhut, that which was drawn from Keter was the manifestation of Chokhmah, and that which was drawn from Chokhmah was the manifestation of Binah. That is why he objected "those are nine": for the utterance drawn from Malkhut, which is "It is not good that the man should be alone," is not Malkhut but what is drawn from Malkhut; and so the hint of the utterances to the sefirot themselves is only nine. And to this he answered, "'In the beginning' is also an utterance": for although it is the existence of the Emanation, the matter was together with Keter, and it is impossible that Keter not be included there, as we explained. And now what is found in the Zohar, Parashat Bereshit, and in the Tikkunim will be seen to be right: that this utterance hints at times at Keter, at times to Chokhmah, at times to Binah, at times to Malkhut (which is also called "beginning" [reshit]), and at times to Da'at; for it is an utterance that includes the existence of the whole Emanation in general, as we explained. And with this we have discharged our obligation in this matter for the present, so that the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, should not conflict with one another, and should not conflict, God forbid, with what is explained in the Gemara in these passages, so as not to give an opening to those who speak falsehood. And each one shall come to his place in peace, and rest upon his couch.

And now, having cleared the stumbling-stones from the vineyard of this passage in the preceding chapters, we shall examine it closely a little, and afterward explain its meaning briefly, with the help of God. What should be examined is this. First, the order of the sages: it put Rav Yosef before Rabbi Yochanan, although Rabbi Yochanan preceded him by a long time. Second: since the Commandments, the utterances and the praises all hint at the ten sefirot, what are they disagreeing about? Third: its saying "the ten praises that David spoke in the book of Psalms" is needless length, for certainly David spoke praises nowhere but in the book of Psalms; so much so that this very length almost made room for the error by which he was challenged, "But there are many praises!" — for the questioner understood, from the words "in the book of Psalms," that the whole book was meant. Fourth: its saying "the Ten Commandments that were spoken to Moses at Sinai": why did it go on at such length? Are there any others? And what further needs examining in its wording will become clear as we proceed, with the help of God. Now this passage is to be understood with what we already have from the Tikkunim, where Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained that the Kingships are in Malkhut, the Remembrances in Tiferet and the Shofarot in Binah. And even if the later commentators have other explanations of this, they all agree that the Kingships are in Malkhut. And the one who asked already took it as given that the ten Kingships are certainly in the ten sefirot. But he was in doubt whether they are the ten sefirot included in Malkhut itself, in the way that each one includes ten, as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter two, with the help of God; or whether they are the ten sefirot proper, but in their manifestation as they pour their effluence into Malkhut; or whether we should say that they are the sefirot literally in their own place. And should you say that they are called "Kingships" and so must be in Malkhut, since their name testifies to them: we would answer that they would be ten Kingships in the sense of the Malkhut within each and every sefirah, in its own place. And along these lines we shall explain the Remembrances and the Shofarot, as explained. And this is what it means by "These ten Kingships — to what do they correspond?": since they are ten, I know that their number testifies that they correspond to the ten sefirot; but the question is, in which aspect of them, of the three aspects we have mentioned? And on this the three sages were divided, one saying this and another that. Rabbi answered that they correspond to the ten praises that David spoke in the book of Psalms. And by the length of his wording, "that David spoke," he had in mind what our Sages, of blessed memory, have already explained: that all that David said in the book of Psalms he said only in correspondence to Malkhut, which was his attribute.

Thus he had in mind the first aspect, which is the ten sefirot included in Malkhut, as we explained. But the questioner did not grasp the fine point of the phrasing in his saying "in the book of Psalms," and took it as meant to indicate a place; and so he objected, "But there are many!" And he was answered that only those in which the shofar is mentioned were meant; and these are at the end of the book. "Praise El in His sanctuary" is Keter. "Praise Him in the firmament of His strength" is Chokhmah. "Praise Him for His mighty acts" is Binah. "Praise Him according to the abundance of His greatness" is Gedulah. "Praise Him with the blast of the shofar" is Gevurah. "Praise Him with harp and lyre" is Tiferet. "Praise Him with timbrel and dance" is Netzach. "Praise Him with strings and pipe" is Hod. "Praise Him with sounding cymbals" is Yesod. "Praise Him with clashing cymbals" is Malkhut. And all of these are in Malkhut, as is evident from their being in the book of Psalms, which corresponds to Malkhut. And Rav Yosef had in mind the second aspect, namely that what is meant by the ten Kingships is that all the sefirot pour their effluence into Malkhut; and this is what he meant in saying "to the Ten Commandments," etc. For it has been explained that at the giving of the Torah each and every attribute poured one of the Commandments into the sefirah of Malkhut, and Malkhut revealed that Commandment and showed it to Israel. And this is the meaning of (Exodus 20:15) "And all the people saw the voices": they saw the voices coming to Malkhut, so that Malkhut might speak the Commandment by the power of each and every sefirah. And this is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, meant in the book of the Tikkunim (in the Introduction, fol. 10), and these are his words: "And on the seventh day the Torah was given: this is the Righteous One, the foundation of the world; and at his grade Malkhut spoke with them. And they have established it: [as] with ten kings, lest they be unable to speak with one mouth, He touched the house [bayit] and included in her all ten." Thus far [his] words.

The meaning is clear without our examining his wording closely now, so as not to go on at length. And further, [it is clear] that He spoke from the side of Malkhut, for she was the one speaking, by the power of each and every sefirah that pours its effluence upon her. And this is what Rav Yosef meant in saying "the Ten Commandments that were spoken to Moses at Sinai": he meant that they were spoken to him by means of "Sinai," which is Malkhut, as explained. Nor is it surprising that they are ten apart from Malkhut; for Malkhut has an aspect [in which she is counted] with the ten, and an aspect in which she receives from the ten, in that she receives from herself — in the secret of the manifestations Yod and Heh within her, as will be explained in the Gate of Manifestations. And with this the wording of Rashbi, peace be upon him, becomes exact, when he said "He touched the house [bayit]": for the manifestation Bet in Malkhut is the manifestation Heh, and these are lower grades in her relative to the aspect of the Yod, as will be explained in the Gate mentioned. And that is why he said "and included in her all ten": for even Malkhut must be included with her.

So Rav Yosef had in mind the second aspect, which is the ten sefirot pouring their effluence into Malkhut. And Rabbi Yochanan had in mind the third aspect, which is the aspect of the sefirot proper, in their own place. And this is what he meant in saying "by ten utterances the world was created": these are the sefirot themselves, in their own place. And what is intended with regard to Malkhut is that, when we are at the Kingships, we should direct our intention to the ten sefirot in their own place, or to the Malkhut within each and every sefirah, as we explained above.

The matter of "those are nine" has been explained above. And he answered, "'In the beginning' is also an utterance": for although it speaks of the existence of the Emanation, it nevertheless has the existence of an utterance. And the proof of this is "By the word of YHVH the heavens were made": meaning that the existence of the emanation of "the heavens," which are Tiferet — their emanation is from Keter, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Order of the Emanation, with the help of God.
And it said "by the word" [bi-devar], the language of utterance, to teach that the existence of the Emanation is referred to as utterance.

Thus from this passage it appears explicitly that the ten Commandments, the ten utterances and the ten praises, by their existence, are faithful witnesses in our holy Torah to the existence of ten sefirot, without any hesitation whatsoever — apart from what we wrote in the preceding Gate, in chapter one, with God's help. And no question at all remains on this for our tradition, to say that perhaps they are twenty or five.

Having shown in the preceding chapter that there is no room to demand a proof for our tradition, since we have a decisive proof, as explained, we now say that there is likewise no room to ask the Emanator for a reason why He emanated ten, and not twenty or five or the like. (Nor, indeed, does the question arise, for there is a refutation of its very premise.) What we ought to investigate is this whole Emanation: why was it emanated? And with our answer to this, everything will be settled. And it is this. The intent of the Emanator, King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, was to bring within limit things that are not within limit. That is: the Emanator is not finite, and the Emanator's intent in creating this lowly world was that the world should be finite, perishing and passing away. And for this reason the Emanation was necessary: so that, through the emanated being emanated and the grades chaining down, grade after grade — emanated from Emanator, created from emanated, formed from created, made from formed — the grades would at length reach the passing-away and destruction in which they stand. For there is a created thing that "came to be in a night and perished in a night," and there is one that, "if it stand a day or two," will not endure. And now, how shall the clay say to its Maker, "Why thus and not thus?" He saw in His wisdom that finitude — the coming-to-be and passing-away of created entities — could not be reached unless the number of the emanated were ten. For if they were fewer than ten, created entities would not descend to that grade of descent, because of their nearness to the source. But now that all that was possible in the Emanation has been emanated, it follows of necessity that the grades that chain down from them descend to finitude, because they are as far removed from the root as is needed to arrive at finitude. And we do not mean to say that the Emanation is limited or finite, God forbid. We mean that the actions that proceed from them effect a finite work, like the work of this world, which comes to be and passes away and has limit and measure, being wrought by the agents through the entities created from the emanated. And the need for finitude and limit in the lower ones was explained by our Sages, of blessed memory, in the Mishnah, when they said, "By ten utterances the world was created. And what does this teach? Could it not have been created by one utterance?" That is: it was not impossible, God forbid, for this world to be created by a single utterance that would include all the things and grades and creations and beings that have now come to be. For although some actions are through Chesed and some through Gevurah, and so with all of them, the power to create by a single utterance alone would not be lacking on that account; for the power of all of them is in each one of them, as is known — each including ten, as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter two, with God's help. And the reason ten utterances were needed is "to exact payment": meaning that through ten utterances created entities descended to finitude. For had they not been finite, a person would live forever and would not receive punishment for his iniquities, and the side of impurity and the husk would spread through the world, and the damage would not be rectified. So too the righteous would be sunk in this world and would not see the good. Therefore the world had to be finite and limited, in order to exact payment from the wicked and to give a good reward to the righteous. And the meaning of "who destroy the world that was created," etc., is that they destroy the world, and have the power to bring it to an end, because it is finite and was created by ten utterances. And so too the righteous sustain it; for were it not finite, the righteous would not sustain it nor the wicked destroy it. For this reason it had to be created by ten utterances — that is, the emanation of ten grades — so that it should be finite: the wicked man perishes and passes away and returns to his dust and is rectified, and the righteous man departs in honor to greet the face of his Father in heaven and to eat the fruit of his deeds. Yet there is a difficulty with this reason. If the cause of the Emanation was to bring the lower ones to passing-away and destruction, so as to reward those who do righteousness at all times and to punish the wicked, as explained, then after the resurrection — which is not a time of reward and punishment, nor a time of deeds, as is known — what reason is there for the Emanation? For wickedness will already have ceased from the earth, and it is the time of permanence. Shall we say that the purpose of the Emanation lasts only until the time of the resurrection? God forbid: certainly not. For the principal state of the world and its perfection are then, as is known; and then, certainly, will be the perfection of the Emanation and its shining. And the same difficulty arises with the holy palaces, in which a person is judged according to his deeds, to be rewarded or punished, as will be explained in the Gate of the Holy Palaces, with God's help. If so, in the time of the resurrection, when there is no rewarding or punishing or judging or bringing of charges against human beings, what will become of the palaces? Shall we say that they will be for nothing, and that each and every one will cease from the work that they were doing? Yet this is no question; for it is possible that they will be united, each with the next, one within another, "each one cleaving to his brother"; and in the time of their oneness and union there is no judgment in them, and the sparks are swallowed up in their sources, and they take their pleasure in abundant peace, as is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Pekudei, on the palaces. And for this reason too it cannot be said that the purpose of the Emanation is to reward and to punish, to judge and to bring charges against the guilty and the innocent. For then we would ask: after the resurrection, when human beings are no longer judged according to their deeds but enjoy what they toiled for on the eve of the Sabbath [that is, in this world], it would turn out, God forbid, that they [the emanated] exist for nothing. Therefore we say that this was not the principal purpose of their emanation, even though reward and punishment do proceed from them under the supernal providence, as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Governance and in the Gate of Self and Vessels. Rather, the principal intent was to make His divinity known to what is other than Himself, as we shall explain in the second reason in this chapter, and we shall add further explanation in chapter seven, with the help of God. And so it turns out, on the contrary, that as long as the world is in ruin from the filth of the serpent and the husk, the emanated are not united as they should be, and His divinity is not revealed, and knowledge among the people of the children of Israel has come to an end and is finished — until He has compassion from heaven and the world emerges from the filth of the serpent and is rectified as it should be. Then the world will return to its tikkun, and His divinity will be revealed among those below, rightly and properly, and human beings will grow stronger in knowledge of Him. And then it is said (Jeremiah 31), "And they shall no longer teach, each man his neighbor," etc., "for they shall all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them." And then the light of the Torah, its treasured things and its secrets, will be revealed, rightly and properly, and the emanated will be united in complete union; for the verse will be fulfilled that is written (Zechariah 14), "And YHVH shall be King over all the earth; on that day YHVH shall be one and His name one." And from the mishnah of the ten utterances nothing can be inferred [against this], for it may be explained thus: "By ten utterances the world was created" means that all ten sefirot acted in the creation of the world, although it could have been created by the power of one, namely Keter, which is called "one utterance," as explained in the Zohar; "but rather in order to," etc. — that is, so that they could effect actions in different aspects, whether of judgment or of compassion; for Keter has no judgment in it, only simple compassion, as is known. And this mishnah does not mean that the emanation of the emanated was for the sake of the world, God forbid; it is a reason for their action below, in the lower world, although the first sefirah has the power to effect everything. There is also another reason, close to the preceding one. The Emanator, King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He — it is His attribute to pour effluence upon what is other than Himself, and that His good effluence should do good to created entities and pour upon them from His attributes: lovingkindness, for example, through the attribute of Chesed, and so with all the sefirot. And He saw fit to emanate this Emanation and to reveal His greatness to the eyes of the created entities, so that He might be recognized by His created entities and apprehended a little, through His holy and pure Emanation. And it belongs to the attributes of His goodness that His will is to reveal His exaltedness to the lowly.
