And all is made in this manner below, until [it is found] that a human being in this world is kernel and husk, body and spirit; and all is the tikkun of the world." Thus far [its words].

Now, when you contemplate this passage well, you will understand the saying of the masters of Kabbalah, who called YHVH, blessed be He, "a soul to souls" — for He, blessed be He, is a soul to His attributes, which are called "souls"; for the upper [one] is a soul to that [one] below, and each [is a soul] to its fellow; and they are unified in a complete, true union.

And the matter of the parable of the soul is this: that, just as the soul of a person is one, and we cannot apprehend its truth except by its actions that appear in the limbs of the body, so — to draw a distinction [of] a thousand thousands of thousands, without end — we cannot apprehend Him, blessed be He, except from the side of His actions performed by means of His attributes. And just as there is no action for the limbs of the body without the soul, for it is their life and their cause, so there is no action for the attributes without the will of their Possessor, blessed be He, for He is the cause of their endurance. And just as the soul is one, and its powers are bound up in it and are the soul itself — except that it has differing names according to the origins of its actions, and therefore it is sometimes called "vital" (chiyyunit) and sometimes "natural" (tiv'it) and sometimes "psychic" (nafshit), [these] being powers chained-down from the very self of the simple soul — so the sefirot are unified in the Self of the Creator, blessed be He, and the multiplicity and the variation is in respect of the actions chained-down from the unity of the Creator; not that there is any variation in Him, but [only] in respect of the recipients. And therefore our Sages of blessed memory (Berakhot 10[a]) likened the soul to the Holy One, blessed be He, in five things." Thus far [his words].

And he further prolonged with proofs from Rav Chamai and Rabbeinu Hai Gaon, of blessed memory, and Rabbeinu Bachya, of blessed memory — that is to say, that they all agree with his view. And in truth, neither the words of the Zohar nor the words of the commentators agree with his view, [and] all the more [is there no] necessity for that view; for with a little examination a person can contemplate that all his proofs — the wind will carry them all away, and there is no substance in them. And in truth, we have copied [only] the most nearly-approaching of his proofs to his view. And not enough [is] this, but that he prolonged against Rabbi Menachem and nullified some of his proofs in a tongue not soft but [in] bone-breaking [fashion]; and even so, let us copy here some of his answers to the difficulties of Rabbi Menachem. He resolved that number does not befall Him, blessed be He, from the side of His Self, but [only] from the side of the division of the aspects; and likewise the division of the attributes, and branch and root, and judgment and compassion, and right and left — all these things are said of Him, blessed be He, and of His Self, and there is no deficiency in His Self, for they are not said of Him, blessed be He, from the side of His absolute Self, but [only] from the side of what is examined in differing aspects. And understand this. And we have no need of his view; for how could we say it [otherwise]? — since it is well known in all the books of Kabbalah, and he too will admit this, that the sefirot are emanated and not created; and it is known that everything of which "emanation" is said is the power of the Emanator in the emanated, and the emanated is not separated from the Emanator; and if so, all that is said of the sefirot is literally said of the Creator, blessed be He. And how can he divide [and say] that they said [it] of the sefirot and not of the Creator — since it is His Self, blessed be He? And he already touched upon this and magnified the difficulty, and answered in the aforementioned way; and what he answered is no answer to this difficulty. And how shall that which he said in Sefer Yetzirah be settled — that they are in a wondrous unity, "like a flame bound to a coal"? And how shall we also resolve the rest of the passages that he stated above?

And further, [in] that, in what he resolved, he returned to the perplexity: for if we say [there is] division in His attributes and multiplicity, then they would necessitate multiplicity in Him, blessed be He, when He is described by them, since they are distinct from Him.

And further, [in] that the parable of the soul that he brought above — which is "equal to all the delights," etc. — is the opposite of his intent: for since the sefirot are not the Self of divinity, how do they spread from Him, their root being one? — for, according to his view, they are separate from Him. And the passages that he brought are the opposite of his intent, and a proof for our words. The first passage: "but is it not written, 'I, YHVH, have not changed'; if so, how do they turn His attributes?" — since His attributes and He, blessed be He, are all one thing, [then] how do you say that they turn [them]? Know that the Tanna said only "compassion into judgment," for if not so, what was difficult for him? Rather, certainly, since the attributes are His Self, therefore he found it difficult, [in] that even [of] the attributes it is not fitting to say they "turn" [them]. And as for the matter of all the passages, the resolution [is] that all the things he said — judgment and compassion, right and left, north and south — all these things are from the side of His aspect, not from the side of His Self; rather, from the side of the hiding of His face He performs judgment from His Self, and then we say that He is "judgment"; and when He emanates, the intent is whitened toward compassion, and then we say that He is "compassion." Thus far the words of Rabbi David. And even so, he wished to overturn the proofs and the passages; and since this matter neither raises nor lowers [anything] for our view, we have seen [fit] to abridge. And in truth, most of his objections against Rabbi Menachem have no place. For Rabbi Menachem said that what they said — that they are the Emanation and the power of the Emanator, etc. — is specifically [in reference] to His providence that spreads within His sefirot, but not [to] the sefirot [themselves]. And likewise, that which he objected from the matter of the parable of the soul that Rabbi Menachem set forth, etc. — his intent is not as he explained in the words of Rabbi Menachem; rather, the intent of Rabbi Menachem was to resolve, regarding the matter [that] the attributes are ten and the actions are without end — and to this his intent was to say that each and every attribute performs a thing and its opposite, like the soul, for if not so, it would be fitting that the sefirot be without end, like the actions, which have no end; and this is certainly a mighty difficulty for Rabbi David. And when we are precise in the words of Rabbi Menachem, we find this matter explained, and these are his words: "and the sefirot are things equal to a thing and its opposite." And the intent is that the sefirot themselves sometimes punish [and] sometimes reward; and the reason is that the one who fulfills the commandment of the covenant, which is dependent on Yesod — that attribute will surely give him good reward for his labor, and his reward will be by its means, as we find (in the Zohar, Miketz, 197) regarding Joseph the Righteous — because he fulfilled the commandment of guarding the covenant, he ate the fruit of his deeds in this world, and merited kingship, and to sustain the whole world, in the manner of Yesod, which nourishes and sustains the world. And likewise, if a man sins in this commandment and profanes his covenant, behold, by means of Yesod will his punishment surely be. And regarding this matter our Sages of blessed memory said (Sotah 8b), "with the measure that a person measures, it is measured out to him" — the intent [being] that, according to the blemish blemished by his hand, so will his punishment be, by means of that attribute. And we shall not trouble ourselves with the explanation of this matter here, because it is appointed for the Gate of Essence and Governance, with God's help. And likewise, that which he objected against Rabbi Menachem — that if they are vessels, how is He, blessed be He, described by them? — this too is no difficulty; for according to him, is it well [resolved]? — if they are aspects, how is He described, etc.? Rather, what is there to say [but] that they are in respect of the recipients, in the manner of the sun that melts and dries, etc., and it is in respect of the recipients; and also, according to this [view], in divinity, etc., as is explained from within his words — likewise, according to the words of Rabbi Menachem, we shall resolve that they are in respect of the aspects of the sefirot, not in respect of Him, blessed be He; and although He is described by them, the intent is [His] being [the one who] acts by means of them. Thus far what we have seen [fit] to explain in the words of Rabbi Menachem and Rabbi David, without the pursuit of length, but [in] utmost brevity. And we shall not trouble ourselves with the settling of the passages from within which they necessitated their proof, because neither side of this inquiry disputes with our intent.

And further, [in] that all those passages incline to this side and to that side, and there is from them no necessity, neither for this [view] nor for that, as will be seen from them by light examination.

After we have, in the preceding chapters, set forth these two arrays — namely the view of Rabbi Menachem, that they are vessels, and the view of Rabbi David, that they are Self — let us now rouse, in this chapter, our short and weak opinion upon them. The first array, which was arrayed in chapter 1 — the view of Rabbi Menachem, and the view of Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat following after him — and it is this: that the sefirot are the vessels of the craftsman, [for him] to perform by means of them, as he wills, a thing and its opposite; and the good actions and their opposites are all chained-down from the attributes, which are His vessels, and not from His Self, God forbid. And there is [reason] to rouse [an objection] against this view. Behold, it is known that the knowledge of the Name, blessed be He, is not like the knowledge of the rest of the created [entities]; for they know with a knowledge outside themselves. The example of this [is] a person who knows a form among the forms, or some thing that is depicted in his mind: behold, in any case there will be three things. One: the knowledge [faculty] that was devoid of that form before his knowing it — that is one; and the knowledge by which he knew and recognized that form — that is two; and the known form — that is three; and they are called the knowledge, the knower, [and] the known. And the knowledge of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not so, God forbid; rather, He is the knowledge, and He is the knower, and He is the known, as will be explained at length in the Gate of Essence and Governance, in ch.13, with God's help. And if so, since this premise is true and fitting to be fixed in the heart of the believers, how can our saying be valid that the sefirot are not His Self? — for behold, God forbid, He would be knowing by a wisdom outside Himself, God forbid, God forbid; and likewise, how would He be understanding by a Binah outside Himself, God forbid? And in this manner we infer regarding the rest of the sefirot attributed to the rest of the actions. Further, according to his view, that the reward and the punishment are chained-down from the attributes — for of divinity it cannot be predicated, neither light nor darkness, neither judgment nor compassion, etc. — if so, it is found, accordingly, that the attributes are the rewarders and the punishers by their imprint [teva], which their Emanator impressed in them, as he said, "a parable [of] a king who commanded one of his servants," etc. — if so, according to this view, God forbid, there is in divinity no capacity of the rewarder and the overseer, but [rather] YHVH has abandoned the earth into the hand of the attributes; and if a man sins, his prayer before the Emanator will not avail to emanate good to him and to forgive his offense, since his reward and his punishment do not depend on Him, but [rather] let him pray to that servant whom the king appointed over the reward and the punishment. For if we should wish to say, according to his view, that when a person prays to the Cause of Causes, He receives his prayer and commands the servant to do good to him and to remove his evil from before his face — if so, it would be found that by His command and His will are the life and the good and the death and the evil, the reward and the punishment, and He changes from will to will: before his prayer He willed his destruction and to punish him, and now He wills his endurance and his life and his good. Rather, what have you to say, according to his view? — [that] the life and the good and the opposite are all handed over into the hand of the attributes, which is the faithful servant likened [to] above; and with this, God forbid, His providence, blessed be He, is removed from the world, and likewise our worship before Him is removed — for before Him all are equal in [respect of] good, the righteous like the wicked, since there is in His will no examination [distinction] between good and evil, God forbid. And these things, and the like of them, are the demolition of faith, God forbid, and not its establishment. And it is clear to us that Rabbi Menachem, of blessed memory, was of those steeped in perfect faith. Further, there is [reason] to be precise [in objecting] to this view: that since the Self of divinity is not the rewarder and the punisher — for the reason that no change of will is found in Him — if so, accordingly, He is devoid of the capacity to do good and to do evil, for He removed His capacity and handed it to that servant. For if you do not say so, according to his view, but [say] rather that it is within His capacity to reward and to punish, it is found, accordingly, that there is in Him a change of will, for from the change of will follow the reward and the punishment and the judgment and the compassion. And since He has no change of will, it is found that it is not within His capacity to judge for liability or for merit; for the liability follows from the will of judgment to do evil to that liable man, to destruction, and the merit and the reward follow by reason of the change of His will toward the doing-of-good and the success of that upright man; and as a person changes from the good way to the evil way, so the judgment changes upon him, and as he changes from the evil [way] to the good [way], so the judgment changes toward him, whether for good or for evil. It is found, accordingly, that this matter does not depend on His knowledge and His will — but rather, the one whom He [finds] good from his beginning, He does good to him, even if he changes to evil; and the one who [is] evil at his beginning, He does evil to him, even if he changes to good — and all these things are against uprightness and righteousness. And now it would be found, accordingly, God forbid, that the whole Torah was not given by God, but by His servants — for in it is written reward and punishment, and in particular in the verse (Deuteronomy 28:63), "and it shall be, just as YHVH rejoiced over you to do you good and to multiply you, so YHVH will [cause others to] rejoice over you to destroy you and to annihilate you" — for these are nothing but the words of a servant among His servants, since there is in God no change of will, neither to do good nor to do evil; and likewise the majority of the fundamentals of the Torah. And may the Compassionate One save us from this view! For this is nothing but the view of the philosophers, who speak of God [in] error, fabricating from their heart deception and falsehood; and of them it is said (Psalms 139:20), "who speak of You with wicked intent (li-mzimah)," etc. — for they exchange their glory for shame. And surely we have to believe that this is not the intent of the pious Rabbi Menachem, of blessed memory; rather, surely another spirit was with him, and the hand of his tongue fell short in his transferring [it] from the intellect to the mouth and from the mouth to the pen — for it is known to all who see his books, his piety and his uprightness; and "if the animal of the righteous — the Holy One, blessed be He, does not bring a mishap by means of [it], the righteous themselves all the more so." Rather, surely the correct [thing] is to believe that this was not his intent, according to the plain sense understood from his words, God forbid.

And further, there is [reason] to object against the masters of this view, the like of these and these; but it is not fitting to prolong [discussion] in these matters, for the honor of our Fashioner. And even this it would not have been fitting to raise in writing, except in order to remove the weak of understanding from error, God forbid; and may God atone. And [now] to the second array, which Rabbi David, of blessed memory, arrayed, and [in which] he wished to rely on the view of Rav Hai and Rav Chamai and the author of the Ma'arekhet — and it is that the sefirot are the Self of divinity; however, the multiplicity is not from His side, blessed be He, but [only] from the side of the aspect of His actions toward us, in the likeness of the sun — for so he explained at the end of his words, when one examines [them] in his book. And regarding this matter we say: "how this man neither ails nor feels, and as though sleeping and lying down he said it!" For since the existence of the sefirot is [merely] the aspect of the actions, in the likeness of the sun, as explained — if so, why should it be necessary that Malkhut receive from Tiferet, and any [other] attribute from another besides it, since they are [merely] from the side of the aspect of His actions, blessed be He, and they are all grasped in His Self, in the likeness of the light of the sun, as explained? If so, it cannot be validly said of Him that the attribute of His being a dryer needs the attribute of His being a melter — for this would not be necessary in order that its fellow be emanated from it and this one draw sustenance from that, since they are all equal in [respect of] good: Keter equal to Malkhut, and Malkhut to Keter, and likewise all of them. It is found, accordingly, that the matter of the channels, and the grades of the worlds, and their binding and their union one with another, and likewise the order of their emanation, is nullified — for they have no order, since they are all bound in Him like one man, in the likeness of the sun, whose attributes are bound up in itself, not an attribute in [another] attribute, as explained.

Now Rabbi David wished to support himself from what is said in the Zohar, "this is kernel to that and that is husk to that" — and it is opposed to his words in every [respect], as explained; for according to his view there is no attribute that needs another besides it, or [else] they would all be kernels or all husks. And likewise he wished to support himself from the words of the Geonim and the commentators; and his view does not agree with any one of them, as is explained to the examiner in their books, of blessed memory. Further, it is difficult: for according to this view, the whole intent of prayer and the commandments and the unification of the worlds, one with another, is nullified.

Now he aimed to establish the corner[stone] of unity — and the like, [which] he [had] demolished; for the intent of the verse "Hear, O Israel," etc., is to unite the sefirot together, and in the word "one" (echad) to unite Malkhut with all of them, and all of them with Malkhut, and to raise her by way of the rungs by which she descended. And according to his view, neither "the diminishment of the moon" nor "and the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun" is applicable there.

And further, if so — since the sefirot are [there only] when you examine [them] in respect of their actions — then the sefirot are not found except at the time the actions are performed. The example: you find the existence of the sefirah of Chesed [in] its performing the action of Chesed; and when its action is removed, that attribute is removed; it is found that sometimes they are ten, when He performs all His actions, and sometimes they are five or two, all according to the measure of His actions; and sometimes, too, they ascend above ten, when His actions are multiplied in this world. And even if it is possible to settle, with some strain, a few of these our questions, even so the words of truth are recognizable.

And further, there is [reason] to be precise: that, according to his view, [in] that the sefirot are only from the side of the examination of His actions toward the recipients — if so, it is found that the sefirot are not found in the true existence; and if so, what is expounded in the Zohar regarding the matter of the sefirot and the subtlety of those worlds, and in particular in the Idra of Naso and in the Idra of Ha'azinu — toward which, surely, the yearning of the soul is directed [and] nothing [else] — [would be void].

And further, [in] that it is explained in several places in the Zohar regarding the matter of the soul and its emanating, by means of its deeds, from the sefirot to the worlds, and its ascent to cleave, by way of its deeds, to its honored roots, which are the sefirot. And according to his view, that the sefirot are only as [stated] above, behold, it will not cleave to anything at all — for they are not sefirot except in respect of the actions, in the likeness of the sun, of which we cannot say that there is in it the existence of attributes; and likewise in divinity there are no sefirot, God forbid; and by what would the souls be unified? Can we say that they would be unified in the divine Self [itself]? — this, surely, [is] not [so]. And these things, and the like of them, are the demolition of the wisdom and its cessation. And now, where is the one who counts, and where is the one who weighs? — [every] concealed inquiry among the inquiries of the wisdom is rejected, [and] the majority of its corners[tones].

And behold, Rabbi David demolished a wall in order to bring in a mat — for, on account of one perplexity in which he was perplexed in the wisdom, he demolished the majority of its corners[tones]. Thus far has reached what we have seen [fit] to rouse against the view of Rabbi Menachem and Rabbi David; and with this, this chapter is concluded.

After we have already set forth the view of Rabbi Menachem and Rabbi David and have roused ourselves against them with a strong hand, we shall now come, in this chapter, to explain the view of Rashbi—may peace be upon him—in this inquiry. And first of all, we shall not deny that these men are at peace with us in their proofs, whether the sefirot be Self or whether they be vessels; and these and those are the words of the living God, and the law is in accordance with them—though not for their reasons, as shall be explained. Therefore we shall not be concerned to refute their proofs at all, for they are all men of our peace, and they shall come in peace and rest upon their couches, each man coming in peace to his place. It is true that our Maker, who forms all, the Ein Sof, the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One blessed be He—of whom it is not apt to say "may He be blessed," nor "may He be praised," nor "may He be glorified," and the like, because He is not blessed by any other, nor praised, nor glorified by another; rather He is the One who blesses and praises and glorifies and gives life, from the first point of His Emanation to the lowest point, from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice. And before the formation of the world He had no need of the Emanation, as was explained in the preceding Gate, and He was concealed in His holy and pure simplicity. And even though He emanated this holy and pure Emanation, no letter, vowel-point, or figure is apt to Him; for even Keter, the beginning of the Emanation, is denied any name or figure—how much more so, a fortiori, the Emanator, the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One blessed be He. Of Him we are unable to speak, nor to depict, nor to predicate—neither judgment nor compassion, neither agitation nor irritation, neither change nor limit, nor any attribute—not before the Emanation and not now, after the Emanation. However, what is fitting for us to know is that at the beginning of the Emanation the Ein Sof, the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One blessed be He, emanated ten sefirot which are of His Self, unified with Him; and He and they are all a perfect unity. And these sefirot are a soul, and they clothe themselves in ten sefirot designated by names, which are vessels—as though we were to say that the ten sefirot which are Self are a kernel and a soul to the ten sefirot which are vessels. And this matter will be well understood when we look to the spheres, which all the sages agreed to be bodies; though they are living and eternal, they are corporeal and refined, and a divine power is set in each one of them, the power that revolves it, and that power is its soul, and it is the one that recounts the glory of God, as in the words of the Psalmist (Psalms 19:2).

And behold, in truth they are two kinds of spheres, unified as one: the first, the corporeal spheres; and the second, the power that gives them life, which is the divine power overflowing upon them, spreading forth within the spheres. So too can we liken it in the sefirot—with however many distinctions of difference. And in truth the vessel is not called "Chokhmah"—I mean the outer sefirah, which is a garment to the middle one; for it is the middle one that is called Chokhmah in truth, and this is a garment to it, to display to the peoples and the princes the beauty of its soul that acts within it. Likewise Binah is not the outer sefirah—I mean the vessel, which is a garment to the middle one; rather the soul that enters into it and is hidden within it is Binah in truth, and the outer is a garment to it; and so for the rest of the sefirot. And therefore there will be no change in the Emanator, nor division in Him, such that it would be apt to say of Him that He is divided into parts by these parts of the ten sefirot; for the change and the division are not in Him, but only in the outer sefirot. And we may set forth a fine parable, so that this matter may be received in the mind of the discerning. The parable is to water, which is divided among vessels, and the vessels differ in their color—this one white, this one red, this one green, and so all of them.
For when the water spreads forth into those vessels—though the water is simple, free of all color—behold, it appears in the colors of those vessels and changes to their color.

And behold, in truth that change of color does not belong to the water; rather, by means of the differing vessels it changes to that color accidentally, not intrinsically—and that accident is in relation to the beholders, not in relation to the water itself. So too is the matter with the sefirot. The vessels are the sefirot designated to us as Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet (ChaGaT), and they have a color according to their action—white, red, and green; and the light of the Emanator, which is the Self of the ten lights spreading forth within the ten sefirot, is the water, which has no color at all, for they are simple, free of all change and all action, and they effect the change only by means of the vessels that change in their action. And there is no change in the Self that spreads forth within them intrinsically, but only accidentally, to the eye of beholders—I mean according to the recipients, not according to themselves. And let us set forth yet another, more fitting parable: the parable of the ray of the sun that passes through a window and, in the course of its passage, [passes] by way of ten lanterns of ten differing colors, and the light shines toward their surface.

And behold, in truth the light of the sun takes on no color at all; and yet, in the course of its passage through the lanterns, it changes by reason of the change of the lanterns, and the light is found shining toward their surface, inward, in the color of the lanterns. And in truth the change does not belong to the light as an intrinsic possession, but only in relation to its aspect toward the beholders. And precisely this is the matter with the sefirot. For the light that clothes itself in the ten sefirot, which are the vessels, is the Self—likened in our words to the ray of the sun—in which Self there is no change of color at all, neither judgment nor compassion, neither right nor left. However, by means of its spreading forth within the sefirot, which are the lanterns differing in their color, by them are judgment and compassion adjudged; and the light that shines toward the surface is the governance that flows from it, precisely by means of its sefirot, according to the change of its sefirot, which are the vessels—they change and alter the action according to the will of the light, to illumine or to darken; and the light that changes does so accidentally, not by an intrinsic change belonging to the light. And it is known that according as the lanterns or the vessels grow greater, so their light and their soul and their inner sefirah grow greater.

And behold, the limit was only in the limited vessels. And in saying "limited," the intent is only the limit that is bounded in action toward us—but not that there is any limit in them, God forbid; and in relation to the Emanator there is no limit, even in the action that flows forth. And this change is no intrinsic change, God forbid; for even in the sefirot the change is not intrinsic. And the change is in relation to the investing of the Emanation in Creation, and of Creation in Formation, and of Formation in Action, and by means of them the change is effected, as shall be further explained, God willing. And the truth is that their power lies in their soul—to enlarge or diminish them, to establish them and to support them, as is His will. And in saying "to enlarge or diminish," I mean: to raise up that which is emanated tenth so that it may become equal to the sixth, as in the matter of the union of Tiferet and Malkhut; or to diminish, as in the matter of "Go and diminish yourself," as shall be explained in the coming Gates, God willing.

And behold, there are now two kinds of sefirot, and both are united in the utmost union. The first is like a wheel within a wheel, and it is the soul and the true sefirot, the power that truly acts—and it is the spreading-forth of the Self and the power of our Maker. And the second is the vessels, which are the emissaries of their soul to the actions. And we may set forth a fine and true parable, which makes known every detail of this inquiry: the parable of the soul that spreads forth within the body and acts by means of it. And it is known that the limb of the hand—the actions of the hand do not depend upon it, for there are many who have hands and yet do not have the power of their action, because the vitality and the soul do not spread forth into that hand; thus the action is found to depend principally upon the soul that illumines within that hand.

And behold, in truth we may say that there is no change between the soul of the hand and the soul of the eye; and yet their action is not the same, for this one's action is seeing and this one's action is touch. But the action depends upon the inner soul in truth, and is altered by means of the outer limb according to the appearance of the action; and the change of action is not in the soul, but rather in the hand or in the foot, in the partnership of the soul with that limb that performs that action.

And behold, when we ask: what is the definition of the foot or the hand?—it is aptly [answered], in truth, only by the power of the soul that overflows [into it], since it is the power of walking or the power of grasping. And so is the matter with the sefirot, which are like the likeness of body and soul: the soul is the Self that spreads forth within the sefirot and gives them the power to perform a thing and its opposite; and the change of the actions depends upon the existence of the sefirot, which are the vessels—such that, God forbid, when the overflowing light (which is the souls, the sefirot of the Self) gathers in, the others remain like a body without a soul. And what is fitting for us to know is that when the abundance of the shining light gathers in and does not shine within them as is fitting, God forbid, then the world is in judgment, until destruction. And to this matter there are divisions upon divisions, without end. Yet we shall rouse [attention] to some of them, and from there the discerning one will go forth to draw an analogy to many aspects beyond them. And before we explain the matter, let us set forth a parable: to a story atop a story, and a story atop a story, up to ten; and the stories have an aperture in the middle of each one, this one opposite that, and by way of the uppermost the light of the sun and its ray enter through those apertures into all the stories, and it shines toward their surface, inward. And when, the world being in stillness and tranquility, [this] indicates that those apertures correspond one to another, until they draw in the light of the sun's ray. But if, God forbid, it should arise in thought that one of those stories inclined to one of the sides, and the light of the sun is withheld from the story whose aperture inclined to the side and does not receive the sun's ray—then surely that story is found in great darkness, together with all those below it, according to the place where that defect falls. And behold, in truth the darkness is not from the absence of the light, nor is its darkening in the light itself; rather it follows from the poor preparedness of the recipient. And now, after we have roused [attention] by this parable, it is fitting to look into the thing signified, and we find that the sefirot shine from the light of that soul which spreads forth by way of the channels; and if, God forbid, one of the sefirot is blemished, surely the light will not shine by way of that sefirah, and it will gather upward, because the Holy One blessed be He does not cause His Presence and His providence to rest except in a perfect place. And when that sefirah is blemished by reason of the evil of the deeds of human beings, the sefirah will turn its face away from looking toward the place of light, by reason of its shame and disgrace at the evil deeds of human beings and that blemish; and the light is found to depart, and the apertures are stopped up, and the channels are broken, and darkness and judgment come to be.

And behold, this is not by reason of the light; rather, by reason of the hiding of the face of compassion, the supernal shining light departs, and that sefirah remains of itself darkened, and Gevurah clothes itself within it—even though it be of the attribute of Chesed or of compassion. And with this introduction one may understand the first passage that we cited in chapter 2, in the words of Rabbi Menachem, of blessed memory—"And YHVH rained down … not as a judge," etc.; for the reversal by which the upright one turns judgment into the attribute of compassion is by means of the appearance of that light, in superabundance beyond the accustomed, and then the concealed roots are changed and judgment is sweetened, as shall be explained in the Gate of Essence and Governance, God willing. And the reversal, by the wicked one, of the attribute of compassion into the attribute of judgment is, God forbid, by means of the hiding of the shining light, through his blemishing above, in the honored roots, as shall be explained in the said Gate. And with this introduction that passage and the like of it may be understood. However, the matter of the blemish and its existence above by means of the deeds of human beings will be explained in the Gate of the Soul, and this inquiry is not now germane to the case before us.

And behold, the matter of Self and vessels has been well explained, and all our words will be borne out from within the words of Rashbi—may peace be upon him—in many places, in the coming chapters, with the help of Heaven.

After we included, in the preceding chapter, the whole of our intent in the matter of this lovely inquiry, we come, in this chapter, to compel this matter from within the discourse of Elijah to Rashbi and his companions in the Sefer ha-Tikkunim (in the Introduction, fol. 15). And these are his words: Elijah opened and said: Master of the worlds, You are the One, but not in number. You are the Highest over all the high, Enclosed tighter than all the enclosed; no thought grasps You at all. You are the One who produced ten tikkunin, and we call them ten sefirot, with which to govern enclosed worlds that are not revealed and worlds that are revealed; and by them You are covered from human beings. And You are the One who binds them and unites them; and because You are within, whoever separates one of these ten from its fellow, it is reckoned to him as though he had made a separation in You. And these ten sefirot proceed in their order: one long, one short, and one intermediate. And You are the One who governs them, and there is none who governs You—neither above, nor below, nor from any side. Garments You arrayed for them, from which souls fly forth to human beings. And several bodies You arrayed for them, which are called "body" relative to the garments that cover over them; and they are called, in this tikkun: Chesed, the right arm; Gevurah, the left arm; Tiferet, the body; Netzach and Hod, the two thighs; Yesod, the conclusion of the body, the sign of the holy covenant; Malkhut, the mouth—the Oral Torah we call it. Chokhmah is the brain, it is the thought within; Binah is the heart, and of it is said, "the heart understands." And of these two it is written, "The hidden things belong to YHVH our God." The supernal Keter is the crown of Malkhut, and of it is said, "declaring the end from the beginning"; and it is the pate of the tefillin. Within, it is Yod-Heh-Vav-Heh, which is the way of Emanation; and it is the watering of the Tree in its arms and its branches, like water that waters a tree, and it grows by that watering. Master of the worlds, You are the Cause of Causes and the Cause of causes, who waters the Tree by that welling; and that welling is like a soul to the body, which is life to the body. And in You there is no likeness and no image, of anything within or without. And You created heaven and earth, and brought forth from them the sun and the moon, the stars and the constellations; and upon the earth, trees and grasses and the Garden of Eden and herbs and beasts and birds and fish and cattle and human beings—so that by them the supernal ones might be made known, and how the supernal and the lower ones are governed, and how the supernal and the lower ones are distinguished. And there is none who knows You at all. And apart from You there is no unity among the supernal and the lower ones, and You are known as Lord over all. And each of the sefirot has a known name, and by them the angels are called; but You have no known name, for You are the One who fills all names, and You are the completeness of them all. And when You depart from them, all the names remain like a body without a soul. You are wise, but not with a known wisdom; You understand, but not with a known understanding. You have no known place, except to make known Your might and Your power to human beings, and to show them how the world is governed in judgment and compassion—which are righteousness and justice—according to the deeds of human beings. Judgment is Gevurah; justice is the central pillar; righteousness is the holy Malkhut; the scales of righteousness are the two supports of truth; the just hin is the sign of the covenant. All this is to show how the world is governed—but not that You have a known righteousness which is judgment, nor a known justice which is compassion, nor any of these attributes at all. End of his words, for we have no more. And even though it is evident from within it that the end of the passage is missing, nonetheless from his words a great light has gone forth to us, toward what we want in this Gate.

And behold, Elijah, of blessed memory, intended in this passage to explain, in most concise fashion and in words that hint, the bulk of the fundamentals of the divine wisdom. And he explained the principle of the Ein Sof in His simple unity, and the matter of the Emanation, and the inquiry into Self and vessels, and the reason for the Emanation, and the number of the sefirot and their necessity—and all this in fitting eloquence, great in quality and small in quantity, words suitable and as if from the mouth of their Speaker, and according to the measure of their hearers: Elijah was speaking, and Rashbi—may peace be upon him—and Rabbi Yehudah and the rest of the esteemed companions, together with the pious and the righteous who are in the Garden of Eden, were listening. For so is that holy book, the Sefer ha-Tikkunim, as is explained within it.

And behold, he said "Master of the worlds"—the intent is toward the Ein Sof; and he called Him "Master of the worlds" because he wished to speak concerning the matter of the world and its Emanation, and therefore he called the Ein Sof "Master of the worlds."

And further, "Master of the worlds" is as if [to say] "the Necessarily Existent"; for from the existence of the created entities a person comes to affirm that the world has a Governor, and therefore it is apt to call Him "Master of the worlds." And the intent of "You are"—that is, You are the Necessarily Existent—refers back to "Master of the worlds" aforementioned; and this is what he said, "Master of the worlds, You are." And he dwelt upon the word "are" (hu), whose meaning is "the Necessarily Existent." "One, but not in number": this matter is understood by what is customary in the mouths of the masters of the faith when they say "one, but not like the one that is counted." And its meaning is that the counted one has many fellows; for although we say "one," nonetheless there is another such that this "one" is like it, except that the prior is "one" and the one that comes after it we designate by the name "two"; and yet between the one and the two they are equal. This is not so with the Master of the world, who is one and has no second; and He is also not like the one of a genus, which includes many species, nor like the one of a species, which includes many individuals; but rather a "one" whose like in oneness there is none in the world.
And further, the definition "one" is apt only of a thing apprehended in essence and bounded on all its sides, as when one says "one man"—here, by the word "one," he bounds it.

And behold, when we say "one man," we bound the man on all his sides, and his essence is apprehended. But not so the definition "one" in the Godhead; for it is not apt of Him on the side of affirmation—to affirm that He is one by an affirmative definition "one"—but rather the intent is on the side of negation, that He is one in the sense that there is no second. And this is what Rabbi Solomon ibn Gabirol intended in his prayer when he said, "You are one, and in the secret of Your oneness the wise of heart are astonished"—for they did not know what it is. The intent is that the "one" is not apprehended by any apprehension at all; rather, the word "one" is aptly [said] of Him, may He be blessed, on the side of negation, not on the side of affirmation. And this is the intent of Elijah in saying "You are One, but not in number"; for the counted one has apprehension in it, whereas His oneness, may He be blessed, is not aptly [described by] "one" except in the manner explained. And this is the intent of the founders of the faith in saying "one, but not like the one that is counted"—I mean, that the "one" is only by way of negation, as explained. And this is what is intended in the Sefer Yetzirah when it says: "Ten sefirot of belimah; their measure is ten, which have no end. Their end is embedded in their beginning, and their beginning in their end, like a flame bound to a coal. For the Lord is one and there is no second to Him; and before One, what can you count?" End of its words.

And the intent is that he counted ten sefirot, and said of the ten that they are belimah, which means "without essence"—as explained in the third Gate, chapter 4; see there. And because he counted ten, and number is a limit, therefore he said "their measure is ten, which have no end." And the intent is that they are without measure, for in relation to their aspect toward the Emanator they have no limit; but in relation to their action that flows toward us they have a limit, for they are the agents of limit. And because number indicates multiplicity, he united them in the utmost union and said "their end is embedded in their beginning, and their beginning in their end"—I mean, united in a true union, in their binding of head to end and end to head.
And the matter of "their end is embedded in their beginning" will be explained in the Gate of the Reversal of the Light, chapter 1.

And the matter of "like a flame bound to a coal" means: just as the flame is bound to the coal—for a person cannot depict a flame without a coal, and the binding and union of the flame with the coal is necessitated—so the sefirot, each is bound to its fellow like the coal to the flame that issues from it. And he compelled the matter from what is said above, that "the Lord is one, ruling over them all." And the intent is that the Ein Sof rules over them and governs by means of them, over them all, for "the Lord is one and there is no second to Him." And by this he gives the reason for the unity in the sefirot: that since the Lord is one and has no second, it was therefore necessitated that the garment in which He clothes Himself and by which He is revealed—namely, the ten sefirot—be united in the utmost union; and this is what he said, "for the Lord is one," etc. And the reason he said "and there is no second to Him" is to indicate what we said: that the intent of the word "one" is only to negate duality, not to affirm; and therefore it is fitting that His sefirot too be united. "And before One, what can you count?" This means: "one" applies, on the side of affirmation, only to Keter; and the reason is that it is "one." And it does not [mean] to negate that there is a "one" like it, for there is one more exalted than it—namely, the Emanator, blessed be He, who precedes all. But the name "one" is aptly [said] of Keter because it is the first of the Emanation, and before it nothing whatever was emanated; and [of the Emanator] even the name "one" is not aptly [said]. And this is what he said, "and before One, what can you count?"—meaning: since Keter is "one," number does not apply to that which precedes the One. And it is found that there is no "one" except in Keter, and above Keter "one" does not apply, for the reasons we have said. And a disclosure of this explanation is found in the Tikkunim (in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, fol. 112b), and these are its words: "All the calculations and gematrias of the boundaries—these are the appetizers to wisdom; for in the supernal Keter there is no boundary and no number, as it says in the Sefer Yetzirah, 'and before One, what can you count?' The head of all boundaries is Chokhmah," etc. End of its words, as relevant to our matter. And the intent is that number and reckoning apply only to Chokhmah, which is second, and number is apt of it, for since we add one to one, behold it is a number—though it be not a whole number, nonetheless it is already a number. But from Keter and above there is no number, because Keter is "one" and is no number at all; and how much more so from there and above, where there is no number "one"—for the One is no number, how much more so that which precedes the One. And this is what he said, "and before One, what can you count?"—meaning: before the One, which is the supernal Keter, what can you count? And let us return to the words of the passage: "You are the Highest over all the high"—meaning, He is highest over all the high ones, Keter; He is the cause to them all, and they are all effects from Him. And because he said "highest" and the word "You"—all of which would seem, God forbid, to make Him apprehended in place and grasped in essence (by saying "You," which indicates essence, and by saying "highest," which indicates place), and this is not among the [proper] attributes of God, for He is not apprehended in place, nor grasped at all—therefore he said, "Enclosed tighter than all the enclosed; no thought grasps You at all." "Enclosed," etc., is to indicate that He has no place, God forbid, but rather He is enclosed tighter than all the enclosed—meaning, that even in relation to the enclosed ones He is enclosed and concealed from them, for they do not apprehend Him at all. And even in relation to the incorporeal ones He is devoid of bodily existence—as if to say that the separate intelligences are, in relation to Him, like the corporeal ones, by reason of the abundance of His concealment and His not being corporeal. And to the word "You," which indicates apprehension of essence, he said, "no thought grasps You at all." The intent is that there is no apprehension of His essence and His very Self at all; for even a slight grasp in thought is not in Him at all, God forbid. And after he had soared in [describing] the heights of the Emanator in brief words, he began to speak concerning the matter of the Emanation, saying, "You are the One who produced ten tikkunin." This means: He emanated ten emanated ones, and called them "tikkunim" because in them is the tikkun of the Emanator, by reason that in them the Holy One blessed be He reveals His power and His might, as we shall explain, God willing; or he means, because in them is the tikkun of the world, for the world is impossible without them, and they are the ones that govern it by the power of the Emanator revealed within them. "And we call them ten sefirot": this means, the ten tikkunim aforementioned we designate as sefirot. And the reason is that it is from the language of "sapphire" and from the language of "illumination," because by them the revealed and the concealed things are illumined—as is known, that by means of the sefirot is the illumination of all the worlds. And this is what he said, "to illumine by them the enclosed worlds that are not revealed and the worlds that are revealed." For the reason for the Emanation of the ten tikkunim is so that the Ein Sof might illumine, by means of them, the upper and lower worlds; for were there no sefirot, the worlds would not suffice to receive the effluence from the Ein Sof, by reason of the abundance of His exaltedness; and now, by means of the sefirot, they receive the effluence and the illumination from Him and from His greatness. And the reason is that the cause of the Emanation is on account of two things—though they are one, as explained above in the Gate of the Reason for the Emanation, chapter 6: whether because He wished to conceal Himself, so that the created entities might be finite; or because He wished to reveal Himself, so that the created entities might be able to apprehend His greatness, blessed be He. And to this he directed his words, toward the two reasons, in saying "to illumine," etc.—for they would not be able to be illumined, nor to apprehend His Self, nor to take pleasure in His radiance, except by means of the sefirot; and this is the revelation. [And] whether because He wished to conceal Himself, so that the things might be finite—he said, "and by them You are covered from human beings," for by them He is concealed from them, and the things descended from before His presence, by means of intermediaries, to coming-to-be and passing-away and the lowly, base composition—like the composition of the children of earth and the like. And this is what he said regarding the first reason, "to illumine by them the worlds"; and regarding the second reason he said, "and by them You are covered from human beings"—meaning, in relation to revelation, the principal revelation is in the concealed worlds; but the concealment, its principal [locus] is for human beings and the lowly of this composition. But in relation to the upper worlds, He is revealed to them more, to each one according to its measure. "And You are the One who binds them and unites them"—for the binding of the sefirot and their union is by the power of the Ein Sof hovering over them. And for this reason there is one who designates Him by the name  Y A H D V N H Y, indicating the union, as Rashbi—may peace be upon him—explained concerning it at all the length required. And at this he hinted here in saying, "And You are the One who binds," etc. And his saying "who binds and unites" is to hint at two unions that there are in the sefirot: the first is the binding they have in relation to their union and binding one to another; and the second is the union—that is, coupling—which is apt only of four sefirot: Chokhmah and Binah, Tiferet and Malkhut, as shall be explained in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 3.

And behold, these two unions are by the power of the Ein Sof, which unites and binds them. "And because You are within," etc.—by this he intended to explain the matter we are explaining, namely the matter of the Self that spreads forth within the vessels. And this is what he said, "and because You are within," for the Self of the Ein Sof spreads forth within them in the manner of the soul that spreads forth within the body, as we explained in the preceding chapter. And [the passage] proceeds to this inquiry, to explain to us how, if a person sins and blemishes the sefirot, "God judges him"—even though He is without attributes; and likewise, if he acts righteously, what it effects for Him. And the reason is: although the blemish is in the sefirot, nonetheless, because the Emanator clothes Himself in them, [the offender] forfeits his head to the King. And the parable for this is to a person who tears, with malice, the garments of the King—and all the more so when they are upon the King; even though he did not touch the King Himself, nonetheless he has touched the honor of the King, and has forfeited his head to the kingship. So is the matter with the sefirot: by reason that the Ein Sof, blessed be He, clothes Himself in them, it is fitting that the one who blemishes them, God forbid, should be liable as though he had touched the King Himself. And this is what he said, "and because You are within, whoever separates," etc. The matter of separation and parting is the matter of the "cutting," as explained in the preceding chapter in the parable of the stories. "And these ten sefirot proceed in their order"—by this he intended to indicate to us that the order of their standing is according to the order of their emanation, this one above that, by way of cause and effect, even though [more] shall be said of this in the Gate of the Order of Their Standing, God willing. And we saw fit to divide this passage into two chapters, in order to give space between the contiguous [portions], so that the one who studies may be able to grasp the matter of the chapter in its totality, by reason of its being brief.

"One long, one short, and one intermediate"—the intent is to explain to us that the Chesed and the compassion and the judgment are all by means of the sefirot, not in the Emanator. And this is what he said, that the sefirot proceed in their order, and their order is "one long and one short," which indicates the attributes, as we shall explain, God willing; and all of it is on the side of the emanated ones, who are the bounded, not the Emanator. And the intent in saying "long and short" is not "long and short" in any truly bounded length and shortness, God forbid; but rather the intent is: "long"—from the side of the line of Chesed, where there is long-suffering even to the wicked; and "short"—I mean short of patience, that is, given to fury, which is the line of judgment; and "intermediate"—which is the line of Rachamim that mediates between the two, namely Tiferet between Gedulah and Gevurah, and Yesod between Netzach and Hod. And all is included in "long, short, and intermediate"—that is, Chesed, judgment, and compassion, which is the inclusion of the whole Emanation, as we shall explain in the Gate of Essence and Governance, God willing. "And You are the One who governs them"—the intent is that, although he said that the change of judgment and compassion and the other changes are on the side of the sefirot, not on that account do we attribute the action to them; for the action is only by means of the Governor, the Emanator, who is the soul that spreads forth within them—namely, the ten sefirot that are Self, as explained in chapter 4. For by means of the power that hovers over them, governing them like a shepherd his flock, and inclining them to whatever He wishes, there is none who governs them but Him, and none who saves but Him—like the likeness of the soul, whose actions are by means of the soul, and whose changes are by means of the body, as explained there. And it is found, accordingly, that the Chesed and the judgment and the compassion are in relation to them, who are subject to change, while the power for the action is the Self. "Garments You arrayed for them"—meaning that they are like garments to that which is within them, as in the matter of the body, which is a garment to the soul. And he compelled this matter from the matter of the soul, and said that the souls are emanated from the sefirot; and as the soul is to the body, so is the Ein Sof to the sefirot. And this is what he said, "from which souls fly forth"—that is, the emanation of the souls is from the sefirot. And although their emanation is from one place—namely, the sefirot—and therefore it would be necessitated that human beings be in one uniformity, by reason of the uniformity of their soul; and even if they differ according to the grades of the sefirot, nonetheless the changes would not multiply, by reason of the fewness of the sources—I mean, the source of the emanation of the souls, which are but ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefirot—nonetheless the souls were differentiated by reason of their partnership with the body, until no person resembles his fellow.

And behold, these changes are in the aspects of the body, even though the soul has no changes. And so is the matter with the sefirot, which are the sources of the souls, which are a garment to the Emanator; and although the Emanator has no changes, nonetheless the changes are in the aspect of the emanated ones, who are a garment to the Emanator. Or he means "Garments You arrayed for them"—that is, the Emanator further created ten other sefirot, which are garments to the sefirot. And the sefirot, in relation to the garments—which are the other sefirot—are as the Ein Sof is in relation to the sefirot in which He clothes Himself; for just as the Ein Sof, blessed be He, is not at all subject to change, so the sefirot, which are vessels to the soul, are not intrinsically subject to change, by reason of their nearness to their source, they being the first emanated ones; therefore the ten sefirot of Creation were necessitated. And the Emanation, in relation to Creation, is as the soul that spreads forth into the vessels. And to the second ones, called Creation, there is yet a garment, called Formation, to which Creation is as the soul within the body—for in Formation the changes are more particular than in Creation. And likewise, the relation of Creation to Formation is as the relation of the Emanation to Creation.

And further, by reason of their nearness to their source, the third array—which is Formation—required a fourth array, which is Action; and by means of the chaining-down of these garments, the limit and the changes and the cessation and the finitude are effected. And the matter will be explained in the Gate of ABYA, God willing. And let us return to the explanation of the passage: for the Emanation, which is ten sefirot, are vessels in relation to the soul that spreads forth within them; and yet the soul and the vessels are united in a complete union; and the Emanation is a soul to Creation, and Creation a body to the Emanation, and Formation as a kind of garment to the body—for just as the garment covers the body and clothes it, so Formation is a garment in which Creation clothes itself, as explained there. And this is what he said, "and several bodies You arrayed for them"—meaning, You arrayed for these sefirot, further, garments in which the bodies clothe themselves to effect the changes; for even those bodies have yet a garment in which they clothe themselves—namely, Formation, which is the garment of Creation. And this is what he said, "which are called body relative to the garments that cover over them"—meaning, those bodies are called "body" in relation to another garment in which that body clothes itself, namely Creation, which is a body to the Emanation; and to this Creation there is a garment, which is Formation, as explained. And this explanation is the principal and correct one. And to indicate precisely that they are like the likeness of the soul in the body, he said that the Emanation is designated, in its totality, by the limbs of the body. And this is what he said, "and they are called, in this tikkun," etc.: Chesed, the right arm; and Gevurah, the left arm; and Tiferet is the body that is between the two arms; and from it extend the thighs, which are Netzach and Hod, this one to the right and this one to the left; and the covenant, "the Righteous One, Foundation of the world," Yesod, extends from the extension of Tiferet; and Malkhut is the mouth. And by reason that the order troubled him—for it would have been fitting that Malkhut be in the order of the lower sefirot, not above them all, as the mouth—therefore he compelled the matter, that it is called the Oral Torah because it is dependent upon the mouth. And afterward he returned to explain the first three, and said that Chokhmah is the brain, and therefore it is called "thought," for thought is in the brain; and Binah is in the heart, and proof of this is from what the Sages, of blessed memory, said—"the heart understands"—they hinted that the heart is from Binah. And because the thought and the understanding that are in the heart are hidden actions of the body—for you have in the body no actions more hidden than the thought and the understanding that are in the heart—and because, in the supernal Form, the brain in which is thought and the heart in which is understanding are Chokhmah and Binah, therefore of them it is said (Deuteronomy 29:28), "The hidden things"—which are the thought and the understanding—"belong to YHVH our God"—which are Chokhmah and Binah, called "YHVH our God," which are the thought and the understanding of the heart, which are hidden. "The supernal Keter is the crown of Malkhut, and of it is said," etc.—meaning, now he comes to explain, concerning the matter of Keter, why Malkhut is called "mouth," which is above, in the head, embedded in the skull, which is Keter; and therefore the head is called "the crown of Malkhut," by reason that the two of them are united—"crown of Malkhut" in the secret of "declaring the end from the beginning" (Isaiah 46:10): "beginning" is Keter, and "end" is Malkhut, and its extension and its emanation are from the supernal Keter. And this is the reason that he placed the seven sefirot of the structure before the first ones: because the explanation of the mouth, which is Malkhut, is settled only from within the explanation of Keter, as explained. And there are versions in which is written "the skull that lays no tefillin." And it appears to me that it is possibly a scribal error, and that the principal correct version is "skull" alone; and its meaning is the cranium in the head, which hovers over the brain, and it is Keter, which crowns Chokhmah, and it is above all. But if we do read it [as "the skull that lays no tefillin"], its explanation is thus: that below Keter there is the skull of Zeir Anpin, which lays tefillin—which are four passages, four lights: "Kadesh"—Chokhmah; "Ve-haya ki yevi'akha"—Binah; "Shema"—Chesed; "Ve-haya im shamoa"—Gevurah—and these are the tefillin on the head of Zeir Anpin. However, on the head of Arikh Anpin there are no tefillin, because there is no emanation above its emanation; and therefore it is called "the skull that lays no tefillin."

And this matter will be explained in the Idra, in the Sefer Or Yakar. "Within, it is Yod-Heh-Vav-Heh"—he has already explained above that within the sefirot is the Self, and the sefirot are a body to the soul that spreads forth within them. And therefore, after he explained the matter of the Emanation in the form of a body and a fitting parable, he came to explain the Self that spreads forth within them. And it is already well known that the four-letter name, though its basis is four letters, amounts to ten letters in its plene spelling—which are ten sefirot; and they are the sefirot that spread forth within the vessels. "And it is the watering of the Tree," etc.—meaning, as we explained in chapter 4, that it is within the power of the Self to enlarge the sefirot and to add to them, to enlarge them and to diminish them according to the will of their Emanator, as is explained in the passage of the Ra'aya Mehemna that we shall explain in chapter 8. And therefore he called the Self "the watering of the Tree"; for just as the water enlarges the tree and makes it grow, so the inner Emanation enlarges and gives life to the vessels that clothe the Self. And this is what he said, "and it is the watering of the Tree in its arms and its branches, like water that waters a tree, and it grows by that watering." And this is the effluence itself, as we shall explain, God willing. "Master of the worlds," etc.—he needed to dwell upon this to indicate that the four-letter name in its plene spelling, which is the watering of the Tree, is the Self, the innerness of the sefirot, which spreads forth from the Ein Sof into the midst of the sefirot. And the Self is the soul to the sefirot, the vessels; and they are alive by reason of the inner sefirot, like a soul that gives life to the body. "And in You there is no likeness and no image," etc.—he comes to explain to us that the existence of the actions, and the judgment and the compassion effected by means of the Self that spreads forth, does not belong to the Self as a possession; rather the action is performed accidentally by means of the Self, and intrinsically by means of the vessels—like the likeness of the water that is in the vessels, and the likeness of the light that spreads forth in the lanterns, which we mentioned above. And therefore he said "and in You"—meaning, in the Ein Sof above, before its spreading forth in the sefirot, there is nothing: not in action, not accidentally and not intrinsically. And the actions are after the spreading-forth of the sefirot of the Self within the vessels. And this is what he said, "and in You there is no likeness and no image, of anything within or without"—meaning, neither of the actions that are in the Self nor of the actions that are in the vessels. And now this will in no way be apprehended from all that we apprehended of the view of Rabbi Menachem; for according to our view the principal providence and governance is by means of the sefirot, which are the Self that spreads forth within the vessels. And that Self and the Ein Sof are all one unified thing—except that there is a distinction in our apprehension of Him, between before His spreading forth and after His spreading forth: I mean, the Ein Sof, blessed be He, in His aspect before the Emanation—in which aspect no action whatever is to be adjudged—or in relation to His aspect after the Emanation, when He was revealed and shone by way of these sefirot, and then the Self spreads forth within the vessels. And the revelation that was revealed, and before its revelation, are all one and unified—like the likeness of the water unified in the spring even after its spreading forth, and like the likeness of the ray of the sun in its source. "And You created heaven and earth," etc.—meaning, now, in the manner we have explained, it is apt that the creation of heaven and earth and the rest of the created entities was by means of the Self of the Godhead, not by means of the vessels, as would arise in the mind from the side of inquiry, which is the view of the inquirers—as they say, that He has removed His providence from this world, as explained in chapter 3; rather the creation was in truth by means of the simple Self, and yet from this there followed for Him neither multiplicity nor change, as explained. And therefore he was abundant in mentioning the matters of creation, saying "heaven and earth," etc.; for although these are many things differing one from another, with all this no multiplicity is necessitated in Him, God forbid. "So that by them [the supernal ones] might be made known"—the intent is that by means of the creation, in which he was abundant in the matters of the actions, [it is] to make known by them the supernal things, for from the lower things we recognize the supernal—as he said (Job 19:26), "and from my flesh I behold God"; and by them a person recognizes the Godhead. And after a person discerns the supernal from the lower, he returns from above to below and recognizes the greatness of the lower, which are suspended from the supernal; for so is the order of the apprehension of the hidden things—from the later to the prior, and afterward from the prior to the later. And the matter is that He emanated His Emanation first, and within it spreads forth the Self; and after the Emanation, Creation; and after Creation, Formation; and after Formation, Action—all this to make known His greatness and His existence in the world; for from Action we discern Formation, and from Formation we ascend and discern Creation, and from Creation we ascend and discern the Emanation, and from the Emanation we recognize the Self that spreads forth; and afterward we recognize the binding of the things in the First Cause, for we know and recognize the binding and union of the Self with the Emanation, and the two of them are united in a firm bond in the Cause of all causes; and from there we recognize and know the binding and union of Creation with the Emanation, and from Creation we know and recognize the binding and union of Formation with Creation, and from Formation we know and recognize the binding and union of Action with Formation—all one, unified, like a strong and mighty chain and a jointed lampstand. And all this is in what is emanated and created and formed and made from Him; but in His Self there is no apprehension, except that we know and recognize that all is suspended upon Him, like an amulet on the arm. And this is what he intended in saying, "and there is none who knows You at all"; for there is none who can apprehend His exaltedness at all, but only that we recognize and know that He is Lord of all, and that from Him all is drawn, in a chain of will and love, and not by compulsion at all—only by benefaction, from cause to effect; and He is the cause over all. And this is what he said, "and You are known as Lord over all"; for the apprehension of the human intellect concerning Him is the chaining-down of the worlds from Him, from cause to effect, and He is the cause over all. "And each of the sefirot has a known name"—I mean, as was explained in the first Gate, and as will be explained in the Gate of the Four-Letter Name, that the names and the sefirot, in existence, are all one thing; and the name that bounds the sefirah includes the sefirah in the existence of its spirituality. And he said "a known name," that each sefirah has a name of its own, this one not like that, just as their actions are not the same. "And by them the angels are called"—for those names which belong to the sefirot, sometimes the angels appointed over the actions of the sefirot are called by them, as will be explained in the Gate of the Palaces, chapter 15. And he was lengthy in this to say that, although the relation of the sefirot to Creation is as the relation of the Ein Sof to the sefirot, and likewise the relation of Creation to Formation, as explained above, nonetheless the matters are not equal. For the Ein Sof is not called by the name of the sefirah, whereas the angel is called by the name of the sefirah, and the sefirah by the name of the action—as in the matter of Gevurah, Gabriel. But not so the Ein Sof, for He Himself is not called "mighty," since He has no descriptions. And from this we may draw an analogy to the havayot and the names that may not be erased: for the sefirah and the angel are called by one name, because they are bounded by that name or that havayah. But in the Ein Sof there is no havayah or name that bounds Him. And this is what he said, "but You have no known name," because there is no relation of the actions in Him, and He is not subject to change, nor bounded by a limit, nor finite, such that He should be designated by a name of action, or by a havayah and name. "For You are the One who fills all names"—as is known, that He is the Self that spreads forth within the sefirot and fills and gives life to them, and is their root, like the likeness of the soul that is the root of the body. And this is what he said, "and You are the completeness of them all," for their completeness is in their power, and their power is the Self that spreads forth. And to indicate that He is the soul and that the action depends principally upon Him—and even though the actions are performed by means of the sefirot, as I explained—therefore he said, "and when You depart from them," etc.: meaning, that upon the departure of His Self that spreads forth within the sefirot, the vessels remain empty, without benefit, like a body without a soul, God forbid. "You are wise, but not with a known wisdom"—he was emphatic to say that, although the sefirah is called "Chokhmah," the intent is not that He is wise by means of this Chokhmah; and likewise, though He is called "understanding," it is not that He understands by means of this Binah; rather, on the contrary, He is the source of Chokhmah and Binah, and Chokhmah and Binah are vessels to His wisdom and His understanding; and it is not that the sefirah is literally His wisdom and His understanding, for then He would be found wise by a wisdom outside Himself. And He is the vitality of Chokhmah and Binah, and they are emanated from Him—as the Ra'aya Mehemna explained, in a passage that will be explained in chapter 8, where it said "wise of Himself," etc., "for Chokhmah is not called wisdom of itself," etc. "You have no known place, except to make known," etc.—meaning, it is not that, because we say He is wise with Chokhmah and understands with Binah, it would be necessitated from this that His source and His Presence are in Chokhmah and Binah, God forbid; for He is not subject to place, and Chokhmah and Binah and the rest of the sefirot do not bound His greatness and His exaltedness, for He is not grasped in limit and place. And even though the Emanation is the place of His Presence, this is that He contracted Himself to show the peoples His glory, so that they might be able to apprehend some of His greatness. And the measure of the phrase "You have no known place" is: because place necessitates limit and corporeality, for that which is grasped in place is a body, possessing limit; and the matter is not so in the Emanation; for the Ein Sof is not grasped in place, and even if He clothes Himself in the Emanation and is revealed in it [in] some of His greatness, it is in order to show the peoples and the princes that they might know Him. And this is the reason for the Emanation, as explained in the second Gate, God willing. "And to show how the world is governed in judgment and compassion"—meaning, He revealed His Emanation to show His governance to the inhabitants of the world; and as he concludes, the matter of righteousness and justice is in the sefirot in relation to human beings—not that any attributes whatever are grasped in Him; and the attributes are in Him accidentally, and intrinsically in the sefirot. Thus far has our poor intellect reached in the explanation of the passage that includes the bulk of the corners of the wisdom. And we entreat the face of the one who studies, that in this passage he labor at the doors of contemplation, once and twice and three times, and he will find for his soul repose in this matter, as explained.

We have yet a sound proof for this inquiry from within the words of Rashbi—may peace be upon him—(in Zohar Chadash, portion Va'etchanan, fol. 67), in the passage [of the Measuring Line]. And these are his words: A light that does not subsist in [another] light engraved and brought forth the spark of all sparks, and it struck within the desire of desires, and was concealed within it and not known. At the time when this desire wished to expand, this spark, concealed within that desire, issued forth in a manner that is seen and not seen, [yet] did not abide so as to subsist in that manner. When this desire expanded, this spark struck—showing color and not color—and entered into this expansion and issued forth in its colors, and ascended and descended and stood, in [its] ascent, within the desire and the expansion. The desire struck its expansion in an enclosure that is not known, and brought forth subtle lights, included as one. When these subtle lights wished to issue forth—the spark in which are lights—it struck against that expansion and was distanced (another reading: was pressed); and from within the distancing (another reading: the pressing) those subtle lights issued forth and were heard as one. Then this spark showed its colors in them, and they were all colored as one—white and red, green and black; and it tarried within it twelve months. Afterward they were uprooted from there and transplanted in another place. And this spark ascends and descends; and this is called the Botzina de-Kardinuta (the Hardened Light). This [light] arrayed and struck within all the plantings of lights, and says to it, "Grow!" Then it brought forth the wellsprings of that first expansion; and it darkened and gave light to them all, and they were enlarged by this Botzina de-Kardinuta. He who gives light, gives light, and it ascends and descends and expands in all directions. And then it is called the Measuring Line; and the measure abides above and below. The Measuring Line is the Botzina de-Kardinuta, the Enclosure of all enclosures; a shining measure that arrayed beauty for all—that beauty which issues from the first simplicity, it arrayed them. By it they abide, to measure above and below. Whoever merits this and knows it merits to know the wisdom of his Master. Happy is his portion in this world and in the world to come. End of his words.
