But in "bringing everything," which is the return of the things to the source, a person has no power to raise them and to root them except in the completed work alone, as we have explained. "In thirteen kinds of substitution": meaning, to set the things in their source, which are the thirteen attributes of compassion that are included in Keter; for there is the concealment of all things, and there is the end of apprehension, for there they are concealed. And they are called "kinds of substitution" because they differ from one another; for the attributes are not equal, but differ from one another; and they are the very thirteen sources that are in Keter. And with this the matter of arrangement and permutation and reading and combining and letter-reckoning has been explained; and they have been explained [only] a little, for a great matter is included in it, and in our poverty there is none among us who would attain a little of the little, until YHVH have compassion from heaven. And by the way, some of the words of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, peace be upon him, have been explained. And nonetheless we shall not withdraw our hands from his words, in that he said, "And they are exalted," etc. Meaning: these pillars are exalted in the loftiness of number, without end, through the branches that branch out in reading and combining and letter-reckoning: when we combine them, and readings are made from them, and they are combined, and afterward we reckon them in reckonings, they rise without end. And by this we can hint a little. And from there the discerning one can understand that these pillars are not of the same value when we consider them two by two—for they make a choicer light than when we consider each one by itself; and likewise if we consider them three by three, they will rise to a light more and more pure and choice than when we consider them two by two. And so they rise without end, by way of arrangement and permutation, and by way of reading, and by way of combining, and by way of letter-reckoning. An example of this: let us picture in our mind that these 620 pillars of light are 620 letters, and we divide them two by two and permute those words according to the permutation that they can bear; again we divide them [into groups of] three letters and permute them; again we divide them into fours and permute them; until they come to be 620 letters together, one word; and we permute it by way of permutation, [and] the number of its words will rise without end. And this is what he said: "in the permutation of the height of their stature." The explanation: "the height of their stature" is their arrangement [tikkun]—at times two by two, and here is one arrangement; and three by three, here is another arrangement; and so for all the numbers, until their arrangement is 620 letters; and afterward they are permuted; and by this their subtlety rises without limit. And this is "in the permutation," that is, permutation; "the height of their stature," that is, arrangement; "and to their subtlety there is no end," as we have explained. And when the inquirer wishes to grasp the force of the exaltedness of these pillars, let him contemplate with his intellect their rules, which we shall set out in the Gate of Permutation; and there he will understand with his intellect how the order of permutation [goes], and its matter, and how it rises to what the mouth cannot say and the ear cannot hear. Certainly then he will grasp the force of their exaltedness, that to their subtlety there is no end. And the reason for his saying "and to their subtlety there is no end": the intent is that these many aspects are by reason of the subtlety. For subtlety and emanation are discerned in this: when two effects are unified together, they will be the manifestation of another aspect, other than the one effect's being alone. And the reason is that, when two are unified, it is the cleaving and the union of the effect with its cause, and an added rank increases in the cause and in the effect: in the effect, because of its nearness and its union with its cause; and in the cause too, because the cause needs the effect, as the mother needs the infant, so that her milk may increase. And in such ways, many and many more: for even if the effect is unified with what is not its cause, it cannot escape one of the two—either it is above it or below it; and in any case it is the completeness of their union. And likewise if three letters are unified, it is a higher rank, and their light increases, because the cause and the effect have been unified in their upper cause, and the like. And therefore, the more the letters increase, the more the lights increase and the aspects increase. And the reason is that the effects, on account of their subtlety, are unified from the side of this aspect and from the side of that aspect, and so for many aspects; and such is their matter, on account of their subtlety. And he said that they are further exalted "in reading, combining and reckoning": for when we picture before us 620 letters written in their order in one word, how many readings and combinations and reckonings we can bring forth out of that word! And from them he will know and recognize their exaltation and their rank.

And behold, it has been explained that Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah already mentioned arrangement and permutation, in what he said: "in the permutation of the height of their stature." And if the inquirer goes deep, he will see that this agrees with what we explained of it in the preceding chapter—for these and those are the words of the living God, and all rises to one place. For by means of permutation, too, the aspects are reversed: for the last is made first and the first last, and the end middle and the middle end, and the head middle and the middle head; and further, three aspects are discerned that are reversed, from male to female and from the one that pours forth to the one that receives. And this is the very permutation, with respect to the inclusion, in that each one is included in its fellow, as we shall explain in the Gate of Permutation, blessed be the Name. "There goes forth the wellspring of the flame": meaning, in arrangement and permutation, and in reading and in combining and letter-reckoning, they spread out into many, many matters, all of them going forth and spreading out from the wellspring of the flame, which is the source. And it is possible that the wellspring of the flame is the ember, namely Yod, which is Chokhmah, and from it is the spreading-out of the flame, namely Heh-Vav-Heh; for so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained, and we shall explain it in the Gate of Titles, under the entry "ember" [gachelet]. And the reason is that from Chokhmah is the spreading-out of the things from the source, and from there the flame goes forth to branch out, which is "beyond searching out and beyond number"—meaning the spreading-out of the branches from the source beyond searching out and beyond number, as we have explained. And he said "from the light that is concealed," whereas in Sefer Ma'ayan ha-Chokhmah it says "to the light that is concealed." And the matter is that, since in Sefer Ma'ayan ha-Chokhmah he said "to set all things," etc., which is the return of the things to the source, as we have explained, therefore he said "to the light that is concealed." And here the intent is to draw out and bring forth the things from the wellspring, as he said, "There goes forth the wellspring," etc.; therefore he said "from the light that is concealed," which is Keter, which is concealed even from imagination and thought. And "the darkness that is hidden" is the First Cause, Emanator of all the emanated. And it is called darkness because to our apprehension it is darkness, for there is no apprehension of it, just as there is no apprehending in darkness; and to show this matter he calls it "hidden darkness," for it is darkness by reason of the hiding. And he said that with the increase of the effluence from the hidden darkness into the concealed light, then the branches are exalted and multiply without end, in the secret of their shining into one another; and then they are included without end, in the secret of arrangement and permutation and reading and combining and letter-reckoning, as we have explained—"which is the manifestation known to the discerning." "In thirteen kinds of substitution": meaning, that we have no knowledge except of the source, the wellspring of the flame, which is from Chokhmah downward—that is the revealed; for Keter is concealed and is not apprehended. And he said that the manifestation in which it is apprehended is in thirteen kinds of substitution, meaning thirteen attributes, which are also in Keter; and by means of them there is some apprehension and intellection, because by means of them the action of Keter, in the secret of thirteen, is revealed in thirteen, and thirteen in thirteen, down to the last grade. And they called them "substitution," meaning attributes that differ from one another; and so it is explained in Sefer Ma'ayan ha-Chokhmah: "and the substitutions are attributes, and the attributes substitutions." "Which are revealed and concealed, laid upon Keter literally": meaning, these attributes are revealed in the secret of the boundaries, which are twelve, and the power that includes them is thirteen; and they are in the Teli, the sphere and the heart; and these are thirteen that are revealed. And they are concealed in the secret of the exalted source, which are the thirteen that are in Keter; and by means of the revealed we know the concealed. And this is what he said: that they are revealed and concealed and laid upon Keter—meaning that they are literally in Keter, not below; rather, the attributes are in Keter itself, in its manifestation, and they are sources for the thirteen attributes, which are three times thirteen in the Teli, the sphere and the heart, as we explained in the Gate of Particulars of Names, in the seventy-two-letter name. And he explained that the thirteen kinds of substitution are  M Tz P Tz, etc. And he said that they are laid "upon" Keter, and not "in" Keter, because they are [so] with respect to this emanated one's being unified with the Emanator. Thus far reaches what our Maker has graciously granted us in the explanation of this passage of Rabbi Nechunya. And concerning Keter and these thirteen attributes, there are those who explained that they are thirteen sources; and we have explained them at length, and for love of brevity we shall not copy them here.

After we have occupied ourselves in the preceding chapters with the matter of Keter, we shall come in this chapter to explain the two that are emanated from it, and they are Chokhmah and Binah. And concerning their essence—whether they are judgment or compassion—the commentators disagreed. There are those who wrote that Chokhmah, relative to Keter, has some judgment in it, and relative to Binah it is compassion; and this matter we shall explain further on. And there are those who wrote that it is simple compassion, and judgment is from Binah downward. And some explained the reverse, and said that Binah is compassion and Chokhmah judgment; and it is a strange view, strange in the extreme. And these are his words: "When the will and the thought arose that the world be created, that will and delight is the revelation of the thing; and that will the Kabbalists titled with the term 'thought.' And when that thought was emanated, the thorn of the Yod of the proper name [shem ha-etzem] became known; and that light sparks into Keter in sparks numbering keter [620]; and they are white sparks, white in the extreme; and by this light all the lights sparkle, and it includes them all. And wisdom required the emanation of another spark, called Chokhmah, from the light described; and when this light became known, the body of the Yod of the proper name became known; and that light sparks into the thirty-two paths of Chokhmah. And wisdom required the emanation from this light of thirty-two sparks, and they are red sparks, red in the extreme; and therefore they are called the thirty-two paths of Chokhmah. And wisdom required the emanation from this light of a third light, called Binah; and when this light spread out, the first Heh of the proper name became known; and that light sparks into fifty sparks, and they are sparks that incline to the red and to the white, and they are called, in the mouth of the sages, the fifty gates of Binah." Thus far his words.

And behold, they explained that Chokhmah is more judgment than Binah, in that of the thirty-two paths of Chokhmah he said that they are red sparks, red in the extreme, and of the gates of Binah he said that they are blended of judgment and compassion, being sparks that incline to the red and to the white. Further, they explained: "One path is drawn from Chokhmah to Chesed, for [otherwise] all those outer powers would be nullified, since from Chesed craving is not revealed; and you already know that Chokhmah is judgment; and this is clear." Thus far his words.

And this view is certainly among the astonishing ones, so that one may say: who brought them into this view? And it seems to me that they entered into it on seeing that Gedulah precedes Gevurah—and it is Chesed and white—and after Gedulah Gevurah was emanated, which is judgment and red; and afterward Tiferet was emanated, which stands between the two of them to tip the balance between the red and the white, and it is a color of red and white mixed. That is to say: as is the matter of these three, so is the way of the first three; for the first three are roots, and the three patriarchs are branches to them, and from the branches we judge concerning the roots. And therefore they said that Keter, the first of the Emanation, is the old one and the white, and therefore it is called the Ancient of Days, which is the power of whiteness; and it corresponds to Gedulah. And what follows it, which is Chokhmah, corresponds to Gevurah, and it is red. For just as after the whiteness of Chesed the redness of Gevurah was emanated, so after the whiteness of Keter the redness of Chokhmah was emanated. And just as after Gedulah and Gevurah, which are the extremities, the arbiter was emanated, which is in the middle between the two of them, so between Keter and Chokhmah Binah is in the middle between the two of them. And the proof of this is that it is called Binah from the term "the man in between" [ish ha-beinayim] (1 Samuel 17:4), whose meaning is that it stands between the two extremities. Therefore they said that it has fifty sparks inclining to the red and to the white. And likewise Tiferet is last to the two extremities and tips the balance between the two of them. This, at first sight, appears to be what compelled them to this view. However, the undoing of this proof will be explained in the Gate of Arbiters, with God's help. Further, we found a great man who was enticed after this view, and he is Rabbi Todros ha-Levi, the author of Ma'arekhet ha-Elohut: for in the Array of the Names and Attributes, at the sefirah of Chokhmah, he wrote that it is "judgment, war, might," and at the sefirah of Binah he wrote "complete compassion," etc.

Behold, he explicitly holds as [the view] above. And Rabbi Yehudah Chayyat, in the commentary on the Ma'arekhet called Minchat Yehudah, explained "judgment, war" [thus]: "Because Chokhmah is the first portion [reshit] that was separated from the dough; from this side came change and opposition and judgment," etc. "For since there are cause and effect, there is opposition: for the cause gives and the effect receives; and therefore lack cleaves to the first effect and is with it; and from there spread forth all kinds of opposition—impurity and purity, and peace and war, judgment and compassion. For from the side of the one that pours forth there will be compassion, and from the side of the one that receives judgment comes. And because of this—since Chokhmah is the beginning of judgment from the side that we have said—therefore it is called judgment, although the judgment in it is in potential, relative to the strong judgment of Gevurah, which is in actuality. And because of the relation that it has with it in judgment, there is one who said that in the intention of 'Holy, holy, holy,' one must, at the second 'holy,' intend Chokhmah bound with Gevurah, as he will say in its place, with the help of Heaven. And in the book of the Idra: 'There is the Adam of Beriah, who is Keter, ancient of all the ancient ones; he turns to the right, to Chesed, and rides on a lion, and grasps, and makes engravings. And there is the Adam of Yetzirah: he is Chokhmah; he rides on an ox, and turns to the left, and casts fire into his mouth, and depicts depictions. And there is the Adam of Asiyah, who rides on an eagle, and he is Tiferet; and he turns to the east with his face, and makes colors in the light of the face,' etc.

Behold, it is clear from this that Chokhmah is bound with Pachad [Fear], and Binah with Tiferet. And the view of the author of Sefer ha-Orah is that Chokhmah is compassion and Binah judgment, the reverse of the view of the Rav. And I come to make peace between them, and say that from the side of its face, which faces Keter, it is compassion, and from the side of the back it is judgment relative to the face; and therefore Binah, which is emanated from its back, is judgment." Thus far the words of Rabbi Yehudah. Further, Rabbi Yehudah explained, at the entry Binah: "'Complete compassion'—and the honor of the Rav remains in its place; but there is no complete compassion except Keter. And it is plain that Binah, from the side of the back of Chokhmah, has judgment in it, as the author of Sefer ha-Orah wrote. And therefore its name is YHVH with the vowel-points of Elohim; and therefore south [and] north spread forth from it; and from the power of the judgment that is in it a straight track goes from it to Gevurah. And in the book of the Zohar, and these are its words: 'And from the side of Abba, the supernal Chesed holds; from the side of Imma, Gevurah hangs; and the male child between them.'" Thus far the words of R. Yehudah.

And he further added many proofs brought from the book of the Zohar, and we did not wish to elaborate. And now, what shall we say on seeing Rabbi Yehudah act as one who shuts his eyes to the passage that he copied above from the Idra to prove the view of the author of the Ma'arekhet? For from there is proof that Keter is at the right, over Chesed; and Chokhmah at the left, over Gevurah; and Binah at the middle line, Tiferet. And almost from this very passage it is explained that Binah tips the balance between Keter and Chokhmah, and that such is the secret of the order of their standing—Keter at the right, Chokhmah at the left, Binah in the middle—as some of the commentators wrote, and we copied it in the Gate of the Order of Their Standing. Therefore the view of these sages is that Keter is at the right and Chokhmah at the left: this one the root of Chesed, and that one the root of judgment. And according to his view, which he imagined he could tip, from the passage and from the Kedushah, toward the view of the author of the Ma'arekhet—that Chokhmah is at the left, judgment—if so, what difficulty did he have in Binah's being compassion, at the middle? For so he explained in the passage: "The Adam of Yetzirah: he is Chokhmah; he rides on an ox and turns to the left." And since from here, in his opinion, there is proof that Chokhmah is judgment, at the left, then we too shall say: since he said of the Adam of Asiyah, "he rides on an eagle, and he is Tiferet," etc., then Binah is at the middle, compassion. And likewise is the matter with the Kedushah: since he proved that the second "holy" is to draw from Chokhmah to the left, Gevurah, so that Chokhmah is judgment, then we too shall say that, since the third "holy" is to draw from Binah to Tiferet, Binah is compassion like Tiferet; and Binah turns out to be at the middle line, in Tiferet, and it is more compassion than Chokhmah, which is at the left. Further, we wonder at R. Yehudah, who meant to impose a compromise between the author of Sefer ha-Orah and the author of the Ma'arekhet when their views are the reverse of each other: for to the author of the Ma'arekhet, Chokhmah is judgment and Binah compassion; and to the author of Sefer ha-Orah, Binah is judgment and Chokhmah compassion. And he wishes to impose a compromise between them, saying that Chokhmah is judgment because it is emanated from the side of Keter: from the side of the face that faces Keter it is compassion, and from the side of the face that looks toward Binah, which is the back, it is judgment. And how, by this thing, can he set right views that are opposites? Two opposites cannot both be true. And according to his ruling, Binah turns out always to be more judgment than Chokhmah, as in the view of the author of Sefer ha-Orah, since the back of Chokhmah is face toward Binah. Further, the compromise that he imagined he was making is the words of the book Sha'arei Orah, as we shall copy in this Gate, chapter 10. And how is it possible, in a matter of views that are opposites, to contrive to make peace between two opposites? For a compromise is the middle view that unites the two views, not a ruling that tips toward one view and denies the other.

And further, that he wished to reject the view of the author of the Ma'arekhet on the ground that in Binah there is the name YHVH with the vowel-points of Elohim—this is no proof. For who tells us that its name is so on account of south and north spreading forth from it? Let us say that its name is so for the reason that it is compassion and judgments are aroused from it, as we shall explain.

And further, Rabbi Yehudah explained at the beginning of his book that the Emanation came like a point of three by three: that Chokhmah emanated Chesed and Netzach, and Binah Gevurah and Hod. If so, how did south and north spread forth from it, since this is not his view?

And further, he proved [his view] from the straight track that [goes] from Binah to Gevurah. But what proof is that? It is possible that the author of the Ma'arekhet holds that the straight track is from Chokhmah to Gevurah; and the proof is from the passage that he himself adduced, from the Idra, and likewise from the explanation of the Kedushah, that the thought [goes] from Chokhmah to Gevurah. Or we may say that he holds that the first three are in the form of the shuruk, one above another, for so he wrote explicitly; and from the track there is no proof at all.

And further, even if we say that there is a straight track from Binah to Gevurah, it is no proof, as [is shown by what] the other commentators wrote, whose view is like the view of the author of the Ma'arekhet, and who hold that Chokhmah is literally at the right and Binah at the left. And these are their words: "In the channel that is drawn from Chokhmah to Chesed: because outside the chariots of Chesed there are husks that suck from Chesed; and were it not for the effluence of Chokhmah drawn to Chesed, all those outer husks would be nullified, for from Chesed craving is not revealed; for Chokhmah is judgment and fire." Thus far their words.

Behold, he said explicitly that Chokhmah is over Chesed, and nonetheless he said that Chokhmah is judgment and Chesed compassion, and that, were it not for the effluence of Chokhmah, the power of Chesed, which is compassion, would nullify the husks by its compassion. And of the channel drawn from Binah to Gevurah he wrote the reverse: that were it not for the effluence of Binah, the husks would destroy the world, etc. So the proof of Rabbi Yehudah is no proof at all. However, the compelling proof is from several other passages that are in the Zohar, and they are known and famous to those who know knowledge: that Chokhmah is in the secret of whiteness, in the secret of simple compassion; and so they called it "a white tallit" in some places; and the thirty-two paths are simple compassion, and there is no doubt in this. And even if in the Torah they are [expressed] with the name Elohim, which indicates judgment, the reason is because of Binah, as we shall explain in the Gate of Paths, and as we proved from the passage in the Gate of the Order of Their Standing that Chokhmah is at the right; and such is the view of the commentators. And according to this, when we come to get to the bottom of their view, it turns out that there is nothing to this matter. Is there, God forbid, literally a right and a left above? Rather, right and left are titles for judgment and compassion. If so, how is it possible to say that Chokhmah is judgment, except that it stands at the right? If it is judgment it is not right, and if it is right it is not judgment. And likewise with Binah: if it is compassion it is not left, and if it is left it is not compassion; for two opposites cannot both be true. And it is not apt to say "this is right and this is left"; rather, Chesed is the right and judgment is the left. And now, according to this, how can "right" be true when we say "right and judgment," as the commentators whom we copied above explained?

Further, according to the view of the author of the Ma'arekhet, that the order of the first three is in [the form of] the shuruk, one on top of another, it appears that he wished to explain their being one above another as the middle line—neither Chesed nor judgment, but intermediates, which are compassion; and he contradicts himself. For if you do not say so, then what was his intent in [setting] the order of the first three one above another? Are they, God forbid, possessors of place? Rather, certainly his view is that they are one above another, and that there is in them no inclination toward judgment, which is the left, nor toward Chesed, which is the right, but they are intermediates between judgment and Chesed, that is, compassion. And now, this is nothing but that they were confused about the order of the first three, [taking it] like the order of the second three in the matter of the arbitration, and did not understand that Da'at is the third, and Chokhmah and Binah are the extremities, as we shall explain in the Gate of Arbiters. And according to this, everything turns out to be in proper order: for just as Gedulah is first, Chesed, and after it Gevurah, judgment, and between the two of them, afterward, Tiferet the arbiter—so is the matter with them: Chokhmah at the right, Chesed; Binah at the left, Gevurah; and Da'at, after the two of them, tips the balance between the two extremities. For Keter is the root of the three lines, which are the line of Chesed, the line of Rachamim, as we shall explain in this Gate, with God's help. And as for the matter of those that incline toward judgment, the left, and the right, Chesed, we have already spoken at length in the Gate of the Order of Their Standing. And to come to a compromise between these views is a vain exercise, for they do not enter into agreement at all. And the truth is that Chokhmah is compassion, as we proved earlier and in the Gate of the Order of Their Standing. And the passage from the Idra that R. Yehudah brought to the aid of the author of the Ma'arekhet is no proof at all; and likewise from the place whence he came, from the matter of the Kedushah: for the first "holy" is in Keter, to pour forth effluence to Gedulah; and the second "holy" in Chokhmah, to pour forth to Gevurah; and the third "holy" in Binah, to pour forth to Tiferet. The intent in this is that, to weaken the power of judgment and Gevurah, we draw effluence to it from Chokhmah; and so is the matter with the depictions, for all is to weaken the power of the fire. And Rashbi was exact in the wording of the passage, in that he said "and casts fire," which he did not say in the others; for the intent is a taking that is not its way—a new action. Further, we can say it in another way: [why] in all of them he did not say "casts fire into his mouth": for the intent is that these depictions cannot be depicted except by means of Gevurah, to strengthen them and to make them firm; and they are only a taking of a little fire, like a writer who takes ink with the pen. And for their concealment, their effluence from Chokhmah was necessary; but not that this passage proves that it is judgment. And by these ways we can resolve everything that comes into our hands to overturn this matter. And this matter is proven: that Chokhmah is compassion, and it is the root of Chesed, and there is no stammering in this matter. And the honor of those who disagree remains in its place; "they shall enter in peace, they shall rest on their beds" (Isaiah 57:2). Further, we explained that in Chokhmah there are thirty-two paths; and the first to reveal this inquiry are the author of Sefer Yetzirah, and Sefer ha-Bahir, and Rashbi, peace be upon him, and likewise all the Kabbalists. And they called these sparks "paths," which indicates concealment, as it is written, "Ask for the paths of old" (Jeremiah 6:16), and likewise, "A path that the bird of prey knows not" (Job 28:7), and likewise, "a path in the mighty waters" (Isaiah 43:16); for "path" indicates concealment. This is not so with Binah, whose [sparks] are called "gates," for they are a gate and an entrance by which to enter into the palace.

And behold, the sparks that are in Keter are called "pillars," for they are hard like pillars of marble, so that the eye has no power over their outside nor over their inside. And the paths—a person apprehends the inner [part], but with great difficulty. And the gates are open and intelligible; on the contrary, they are open, to enter into a thing more inner than they. And so is the matter with the branches of these attributes: Binah is an opening and a gate through which to understand the inwardness; and Chokhmah is revealed and concealed; and Keter is concealed altogether. Thus far reaches the occupation with the attribute of Chokhmah. And these paths, on account of their great length, we have removed to a gate of their own, which will be called the Gate of Paths.

After we occupied ourselves in the preceding chapter with the matter of Chokhmah, whether it is judgment or compassion, and concluded that it is complete compassion—and likewise, by the way, we explained the view of the commentators concerning Binah, and most of them likewise agree that there is judgment in it—"I know neither chilak nor bilak; I know the Mishnah": and these are the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the book of the Zohar (Vayikra, fol. 10b), and these are his words: "We have learned: YHVH, which is called Elohim—because that river is compassion, and because judgments are aroused from it, letters of compassion are written and it is pointed Elohim." Thus far his words.

We learn from his words that Binah is compassion, although judgments are aroused from it; meaning, although it pours forth effluence into Gevurah, where judgment is, yet in its own self there is no judgment. And we have further proofs, stronger than this. The first is from the Zohar (Chadash, Song of Songs, fol. 73c), and these are its words: "Song of Songs. By the mouth of Elijah it was decreed, with supernal permission. 'Song of Songs' is the praise of praises to the King whose peace is His, because it is a place that requires joy, for there is no agitation and no judgment there. For the World to Come is all joy, and it gladdens all. And therefore it sends gladness and joy to all the grades. Just as an arousal of joy needs to be aroused from this world upward, so joy and gladness need to be aroused from the world of the moon toward the supernal King. And therefore the worlds stand in one pattern, and arousal rises only from below to above." Thus far its words.

And the explanation: "by the mouth of Elijah"—in the commentary on the Song of Songs there are at least two explanations of each and every verse: one that Rabbi Shimon would explain, and one that Elijah would explain. And above, another explanation of the verse [was given], and this explanation Elijah explained; and this is his intent in "by the mouth of Elijah," etc. "With supernal permission": the intent is that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave permission to come and reveal the concealed secrets that were revealed among the righteous in the academy on high. "'Song of Songs' is the praise of praises," etc. The explanation of the measure of the verse: "Song"—the praise of praises. "Of Songs" [ha-shirim]—as [if it were] "of the princes" [ha-sarim]. "Which is Solomon's" [asher li-Shlomo]—"the King whose peace is His," to the one whose peace is His; that is, Binah, the King whose peace, which is Tiferet, is His: King, Binah; and peace, Tiferet. And the reason that he titles Binah with the word Shlomo in this verse is that the one who sings this song is Malkhut, as we shall explain; and the reason is so as to be unified with Peace, which is her husband; and this union is by means of Binah, and therefore the song is to Binah, for the reason that the Peace is His. "Because it is a place," etc. It was difficult for him: granted, according to Rabbi Shimon, who explained in another explanation that this song is sung to Malkhut, so that by means of it she may ascend to the union by way of the grades mentioned there—that is well, for she needs the praise in order to ascend on high, as he explained there. But according to what Elijah now explains, that this song is said to Binah, it is difficult: what need has this grade of this song? And to this he answered that the reason is "because it is a place that requires joy," and by means of [the song] the gladness is aroused to pour forth, as he goes on to explain. And he explained that the reason it "requires joy" is that "there is no agitation and no judgment there"; the intent is: neither agitation, which is harsh judgment, nor judgment, which is soft judgment. "For the World to Come," etc. It was difficult for him: how can our saying that there is no judgment in Binah be true, since the judgment of strong Gevurah is emanated from it, as we explained in the Gate of the Order of the Emanation, chapter 6? And if so, there must be judgment there. To this he proved that there is no judgment there, for the reason that this sefirah is called the World to Come—and it is the World to Come, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles. And since it is the World to Come, there is in it neither agitation nor judgment, just as in the World to Come there is neither irritation nor agitation nor judgment, but all is compassion and gladness and joy. "And it gladdens all." Meaning: it is called the World to Come [olam ha-ba, "the coming world"] because it comes and pours forth effluence below; and he intended this in saying "and it gladdens all," for it is what sends gladness and effluence and joy to all the sefirot. "And therefore," etc. Meaning: it was difficult for him: how can we say that it sends gladness and joy, etc., since we see that Gevurah sucks from it, and it pours forth Gevurot to it, and it is called "doer of mighty deeds" on this account? To this he proved, with a complete proof, and said, "And therefore," etc.: if its principal pouring-forth were that it pours forth judgment, then the seven days of the Structure, which suck from it, ought to be judgment; but we see that most of them are Chesed and compassion. If so, its pouring-forth must principally be compassion and gladness. And this is the thrust of the wording "And therefore," etc.: meaning, because it is gladness it pours forth gladness to all the sefirot; for if not so, it would not pour forth compassion to them. And as for the wonder—since it is compassion and its pouring-forth is compassion, how are judgments aroused from it?—we have already resolved [it] a little in the Gate of Channels, chapter 2, and we shall speak of it at length in the coming chapters. And at times Gevurah receives compassion from Binah: for when Binah pours forth to Gevurah from the side of the channel that is from her to Gevurah alone, then she pours forth judgment to it; but when Binah receives in the channel that she has from Keter by means of Chokhmah, and pours forth into Gevurah, then Gevurah is washed in the milk of the mother, which whitens it. And a matter like this is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Mishpatim (fol. 122b), and these are its words: "When Gevurah spreads out and the eyes blaze in red color, Atika Kadisha shines His whiteness, and it blazes in Imma, and she is filled with milk and nurses all; and all the eyes are bathed in that milk of Imma that flows and goes forth continually. This is what is written: 'washed in milk' (Song of Songs 5:12)—in the milk of Imma that flows continually and does not cease." Thus far its words.

And the explanation of "When Gevurah spreads out and the eyes blaze": for it is already known that Gevurah has in it many powers and branches spreading out below, all of them acting in Gevurah; and he said "when Gevurah spreads out," which is the power of judgment poured forth into the powers of Gevurah, and it effects judgment. "And the eyes blaze": meaning, the eyes are powers of judgment, and most of them are judgment, as is proven in the Idra. And he said "blaze" in the secret of the flaming-up of judgment and Gevurah. And he said "in red color" because there is in the eyes a color of compassion, namely the whiteness that is in them; and if they were blazing and receiving effluence and shining from above, then they too would act in compassion; and this is not what is intended, but rather the strength of judgment. Therefore he said "blaze in red color," meaning in the force of the redness alone, and the whiteness does not act at all. "Atika Kadisha shines His whiteness." Meaning: this judgment is only because Binah is opened only in the source of Gevurah alone, as we shall explain at length in this Gate, in the coming chapters; and as he said, "in red color," which is the red without any action of the white at all, for Binah does not have so much effluence of whiteness. And he said that then, to sweeten this strong power of judgment, "Atika Kadisha shines," which is necessarily Keter, as this matter will be explained at length in the book Or Yakar. "His whiteness": meaning, as he said, "And the Ancient of Days sat; His garment was white as snow" (Daniel 7:9), for whiteness is related to Him in the secret of compassion.

And further, in the force of the aspect of His whiteness itself, which is the very aspect [of Keter], is the power of sweetening judgment. And therefore he said "His whiteness," meaning His [own] aspect, not the lower aspect; and by means of it all the sources are opened in Him in compassion, for there is no judgment there, as we explained above in chapter 3. And this "His whiteness" is the aspect of Binah that is in Keter, as we shall explain in the book Or Yakar, part 1; and therefore the power of sweetening judgment is in it. "And it blazes in Imma." Meaning: it shines in Imma, which is Binah with respect to her aspect called "mother," which has in her sources for all the roots: the root of Chesed, the root of compassion, and the root of judgment.

And further, the milk is related to the title "mother," for the mother is one who has milk; and the verse says "washed in milk," as he concludes. And therefore he said, "And it blazes in Imma, and she is filled with milk." When the effluence is poured forth from above, it is in the secret of subtlety; and therefore he said "and it blazes in Imma," the term "blaze" being like illumination and subtlety. But after it is poured forth in her, he said "she is filled with milk," which is whiteness, but it is more revealed and has thickened from light into milk. "And nurses all." Meaning: she pours forth into all the sources—into the source of Chesed and the source of compassion; and not as she was before, when she was opened only in judgment alone, as he explained: "the eyes blaze in red color" alone, and not the whiteness. And now, in the secret of compassion, "and she nurses all": the secret of the line of Chesed and the secret of the line of Rachamim. "And all the eyes are bathed in that milk." Meaning: for now the sucking and the effluence have changed from the custom. For until now, when Binah was pouring forth, she was pouring forth compassion to the line of Rachamim, and likewise judgment to the line of Din, and likewise Chesed to the line of Chesed; but now that the power of compassion has been aroused all the more, all must suck—even Gevurah, which is the line of Din—from the side of the line of Rachamim and the line of Chesed, in the secret of the milk. And this is what he said: "and all the eyes are bathed," meaning all the aspects of the eyes, both the whiteness and the redness, are washed and suck from "that milk of Imma," meaning the secret of compassion. And of the other aspects, which are the line of Rachamim and the line of Chesed, which did not suck good or ill, he said "and she nurses all"; and of the eyes, in the secret of the judgment that spread out in them, he said "are bathed," meaning they are washed of the judgment, so as to nullify it. "That flows and goes forth continually." Meaning: it is continually poured forth when she is called mother, for this is in the pouring-forth of the milk on the side of compassion and Chesed, which is always poured forth to those aspects—unless because of the iniquities, which inflame judgment and stop up the two sources, Chesed and compassion; for then she is not called mother, since she does not nurse milk. And now, when Atika Kadisha shines whiteness to sweeten the judgment, even all the eyes are washed of the judgment in that milk, and the left too becomes compassion. And this is what he said: "in the milk of Imma that flows continually and does not cease." Meaning: as long as she is called mother she has milk, for she always nurses the milk to the children. So there turn out now to be, in manifestation, three aspects. The first is the aspect common to every soul, in which she is called mother and nurses the children always and does not cease, in the secret of three lines: the line of Chesed, Chesed; the line of Rachamim, compassion—and the two of them are the secret of the milk; and the line of Din, judgment. And the second aspect is when she effects judgment alone and does not nurse the milk to the children, and is not called mother—that is to say, she is not called mother with respect to the milk; for it will already be found that she is called mother and yet indicates judgment, as we shall explain. And then, when she nurses Gevurah alone, the masters of judgment prevail and the eyes blaze. And when Atika Kadisha shines His whiteness, then the judgment is quieted; and this is the third aspect, in which the channel from Keter to her is opened, and all the channels are opened in compassion and in Chesed, and even Gevurah sucks compassion and is washed in the milk of the mother. Thus far the explanation of the passage. And according to what we have heard, we learn that to the other sefirot she pours forth continually, when she is in the aspect of the mother, from that milk which is the gladness; but to Gevurah and its powers she pours forth the gladness and joy at intervals, as in the matter of the third aspect that we explained above.

And further, we have learned that this innovation is by means of the pouring-forth of Keter into Binah, as we have explained. And by the way, it has been settled a little how she is compassion and nonetheless pours forth judgment; and we shall broaden the explanation of this matter in the coming chapters. And let us return to the matter of the passage (from the Song of Songs): "Just as [an arousal of joy] needs," etc. It was difficult for him: granted, according to the explanation of R. Shimon, who explained that the praise is to Malkhut—that is well, for she needs completion and the help of the lower ones, by means of whom she is unified on high with her husband, in the manner of "To You, YHVH, I lift up my soul" (Psalms 25:1), which is the giving-over of his soul, by means of which she is unified with her beloved; for the righteous are the female waters that she casts forth to receive the male waters, as we shall explain in this Gate. But Binah—what need has she of help and arousal from below, that they should sing to her? To this he answered: just as the matter is settled for us, and it is not strange in our mind, that Malkhut needs help from the lower ones—although the thing is strange in the extreme—so it is settled that Binah needs help from Malkhut. For the grades are in equality; and they are exalted all the more, for our relation to the Shekhinah is not equal to the relation of the Shekhinah to Binah. And therefore let it not be evil in the eyes of the discerning that Binah needs arousal. And the intent is that when Malkhut does not pour forth below, they will not give to her from above—like a woman's milk: as long as she nurses her child she has milk to nurse, and when the boy grows, the milk in her breasts diminishes. So is the matter with Binah: when she does not pour forth to the other sefirot, they will not pour forth to her abundant good as [they would] if she were pouring forth. And this is their intent in saying, "the Shekhinah among the lower ones is a need on high"; and likewise what is expounded in the Zohar in many places, "blessings dwell only in a place where there are male and female." And the reason is that every male pours forth and every female receives the effluence; and when there is a receiver, it is fitting that the blessings come upon the one who pours forth; but when there is no receiver—that is, male without female—it is not fitting that they give to the one who pours forth. And this is enough for us at this time.

And behold, there emerges for us from this passage good reason and knowledge that in Binah there is no judgment, but only that the judgments are aroused from her; and the intent is the effluence poured forth from her to Gevurah; and even to Gevurah she will at times pour forth compassion, and it will be whitened by her. And with this we shall understand the matter of the song of the Levites: for by means of their singing they would sweeten the judgment, and would open those channels from the light of Atika, which shines in Binah, and "the eyes were washed in milk." And this is "And the Levite shall perform—he [hu]" (Numbers 18:23); meaning, hu is Binah; and so it is explained in the Zohar, Vayetze (fol. 156b), and these are its words: "'And he lay with her that night—hu' (Genesis 30:16). Hu, certainly," etc. "'And the Levite shall perform—hu,' in order to draw blessings from it for all." Thus far its words. And the explanation of "for all": even into Gevurah it is necessary to pour forth blessings and compassion, in the secret of the song that opens that channel. And for this reason David was asking that the priests be Levites, as he said, "and Your devoted ones [chasidekha] shall sing for joy" (Psalms 132:9) (see Zohar, Pinchas, fol. 242a): to pour forth to Gevurah in the secret of the right, so that the light of Atika may shine in Imma all the more by means of the right. But on the side of idolatry, which is the left, it is the reverse, as in the matter of what Micah said (Judges 17:13): "And Micah said: Now I know that YHVH will do me good, since I have the Levite as a priest"; meaning, to strengthen the side of the Levite, which is Gevurah and judgment, in the secret of the husks. And one should not say the reverse—that "I have the Levite as a priest" [means] the left in the right—for that is not among the things that relate to idolatry and to the graven image. And behold, it is explicit that Binah is compassion and gladness, although judgments are aroused from her.

And further, we have a sound proof in the Zohar, Parashat Shemini (fol. 39), and these are its words: "'And Elohim created' (Genesis 1:27). Every place of judgment is called Elohim. And that supernal place, the place from which they go out—so it is called here. And even though it is compassion, judgments go out from it and hang on it." Thus far its words. And from this it appears explicitly that Binah is called Elohim, and not because it is judgment, but because judgment came out from it. And he was exact in his wording, in that he says "hang": because the judgments suck from it, and they are not in it, but hang from it; and therefore he said "hang." A further proof, in Parashat Emor (fol. 99a), and these are its words: "Come and see: this river, even though it is not judgment, judgments go out from its side and are strengthened by it." Thus far its words. And he was exact in saying "from its side": for the arousal is not literally from it, but from its side; that is, from its direction, from its aspect toward Gevurah, as in what we explained above. A further proof, in Parashat Va'etchanan (fol. 262b): "The fourth house—'And it shall be, if you will diligently hearken,' 'Take heed to yourselves,' 'and the anger of YHVH will be kindled'—is strong Gevurah and harsh judgment, and it goes out from the side of the supernal Imma. And we have learned: even though she is not judgment, from her side judgment goes out, the supernal Gevurah." Thus far its words. And behold, he said explicitly that she is not judgment at all, but judgment, which is Gevurah, was emanated from her, as is known. And this matter is found to be explained and proven by several faithful witnesses.

Although in the preceding chapter we went to great lengths in proofs that Binah is compassion, nonetheless we saw fit to copy this passage, since it is a proof of the aforesaid; and further, because from within it the matter is explained of how Binah is compassion and her arousal is judgment, although it is a strange matter; and likewise from within it wondrous matters are explained for this inquiry. And these are its words, in Parashat Acharei (fol. 65a): "Rabbi Elazar was sitting before Rabbi Shimon his father. He said to him: Have we not learned that Elohim is judgment in every place? Yod-Heh-Vav-Heh—there is a place where it is called Elohim, such as Adonai YHVH. Why is it called Elohim, when they are letters of compassion in every place? He said to him: So it is written in Scripture: 'Know therefore this day, and lay it to your heart, that YHVH is the Elohim' (Deuteronomy 4:39); and it is written, 'YHVH is the Elohim' (1 Kings 18:39). He said to him: This thing I know—that in a place where there is judgment there is compassion, and at times in a place where there is compassion there is judgment. He said to him: Come and see that so it is. YHVH is compassion in every place; and at the time when the wicked turn compassion into judgment, then YHVH is written and we read it Elohim. But come and see the secret of the matter. There are three grades, and each and every grade is by itself; and even though all is one, and they are bound into one, and this one is not separated from that. Come and see: all the plantings and all the lamps that blaze—all of them shine and blaze and are watered and are blessed from that river that flows and goes forth, for everything is included in it, and the whole of everything is in it. And this river is called mother to the garden, and above the garden, because Eden is partnered with her and is not separated from her. And therefore all the wellsprings go forth and flow and are watered to every side, and openings are opened in her. And therefore compassion is found from her, and compassion is opened in her. And because we call her mother, female, Gevurah and judgment go out from her. She is called compassion on her own, but from her side judgments are aroused. Therefore it is written [with] compassion and pointed with judgment: letters of compassion, and it flows on her side [into] judgment, in this manner: YHVH. This is one grade. The second grade: from the side of this first grade there goes forth and is aroused another grade, which is called Gevurah; and this is called Elohim in these very letters; and one beginning is from Zeir Anpin, and it is joined with it. And because this one is joined with that one, it is written, 'YHVH is the Elohim'—for YHVH is the Elohim—in these letters, and it is one. And this is the second grade. The third grade: Tzedek, the last crown, this is the King's court. And we have learned: Adonai—so it is written and so it is called; and Knesset Yisrael is called by this name; and this name is completed in this place. And these are the three grades that are called by names of judgment; and all is bound one to one, without separation, as we have established." Thus far its words.

And these are the difficulties to be raised in this passage. First: Rabbi Elazar asked this question—why the four-letter name, although it is compassion, is pointed with the vowel-points of Elohim, which indicate judgment. And since this is his intent and his question, what is the reason for his approach, in saying "Have we not learned," etc.? These are agreed premises; and it would have been fitting for him to be brief in his wording and say, "Why is the four-letter name [pointed] with the vowel-points of Elohim?" Second: what he said, "in every place"—what is "in every place"? Third: what he said, "such as Adonai YHVH"—did we not know until now that there is a four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim, that he needed to say "such as," etc.? Fourth: the objection goes to the root of the matter. What was Rabbi Elazar in doubt about? Who does not know, among all these, that the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim is a name related to Binah, which is not so with the other four-letter names, which are in Tiferet? If so, here is a great distinction, and the reason for the change of this name in its pointing. And if the essence of his question was to say, "Why is this name in Binah, and what is the reason?"—that is certainly a question, and this is what he ought to have asked. And if it seems [right] to explain that this is the intent of his question, why did he ask in a roundabout way? Let him go by the short way and ask the reason for this name's being related to Binah. Fifth: what did Rabbi Shimon answer him—"So it is written in Scripture," etc.? How did he answer him with what the verse says thus? For [the verse] would itself be a difficulty concerning our God, and a verse needs reasoning. And if his intent is to say the end of his words, which is one of the two answers that he gave him at the end, then how did R. Elazar say "This thing I know," etc., and Rashbi answer "so it is," when there is no answer there? And if we say that R. Elazar did not let him finish his word, this is certainly a great strain. Sixth: what R. Elazar said, "This thing I know," etc. If he knew that at times in a place where there is compassion there is judgment, then what was difficult for him? For on this account it is pointed with the vowel-points of Elohim, because judgment is mixed in there, as he himself explained. And if this is not an answer, what did R. Shimon tell him that was new, in what he said, "And at the time," etc.? For R. Elazar knew this, and nonetheless it did not satisfy him. And if we say that he told him something new—that they "turn," etc.—what does that matter to the answer, since it has already been stated to us that at times in a place of compassion there is judgment, which is the essence of the answer, and nonetheless it did not satisfy? And what does it matter to us whether it is because they turn [compassion into judgment] or in another manner? Seventh: what Rashbi said, "Come and see the secret of the matter," etc. It appears from these words that it is the secret of the answer, and there is no distinction between them, and it is all one answer; yet we see that there is a distinction between them "as the heavens are high above the earth" (Psalms 103:11), as is proven at a running reading of the passage. Eighth: what he said, "three grades," etc.—for it is length without benefit in answering the question; for with the first grade the question was settled, and what need is there to lengthen in making known the two others? And it is a strain to say that he mentioned it incidentally. Ninth: the length of his wording in the matter of "three grades, and each and every grade," etc., up to "Come and see"—for as it appears, it is length without benefit. And if the intent is to make known to us that we should not separate and divide the Emanation into parts—did this need to be said? Are these not premises that precede everything for every beginner in this wisdom? All the more so R. Elazar, who was a father in wisdom and in piety, that he should need this warning! For from his youth he was accustomed to the wisdom of the Kabbalah, as is proven in the Zohar in many places. Tenth: that he lengthened and called the sefirot "plantings" and "lamps"—why two names?

And further, they said "shine, blaze, are watered, are blessed"; and these are a doubling, four times over, and it is all one. And it is a strain to say that he doubled the matter in different words, all the more so when it is three- and fourfold. Eleventh: what he said, "for everything is included in it, and the whole of everything is in it"; for this is a doubling of a whole matter in different words, and this is a great strain. Twelfth: what he said, "And this river is called mother to the garden," etc.—who is the garden, and who is above the garden, and what does it have to do with this here, since no garden was mentioned here? Thirteenth: the length of his wording up to "the second grade," which is length of wording in a short matter; for all is included in short words: that it is compassion, and judgments are aroused from it from the side of Gevurah, and on this account the name is compounded of judgment and compassion—just as it is compounded of judgment with respect to the arousal of Gevurah, and of compassion with respect to itself. And it would have been possible to include this matter in short words, as is his way in Parashat Shemini and in Parashat Va'etchanan, whose wording we copied in the preceding chapter. Fourteenth: the objection goes to the root of the matter; for these are two opposites that the mind cannot bear. For how is it possible that it should be compassion and judgment be aroused from it? For fire does not produce coldness, and water does not produce warmth; and how is it possible that two opposites should be compounded? Fifteenth: what he said, "and one beginning is from Zeir Anpin." What is he saying? And who is the beginning of Zeir Anpin, which pertains neither to Binah nor to Gevurah? For Zeir Anpin is only either Tiferet or Malkhut, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles. If so, what is he saying, "and one beginning is from Zeir Anpin," etc.? What do Malkhut and Tiferet want here? And how does it settle with what he said, "YHVH is the Elohim"? Sixteenth: what he said, "Tzedek, the last crown, this is the King's court"; and these are three titles for Malkhut, without need; for it is enough for us that he say "Malkhut," and not double the words with words in which there is no need at all, neither for all of them nor for part of them. Seventeenth: what he said, "And we have learned," etc.: "so it is written"—here is one; "and so it is called"—here are two; "and Knesset Yisrael is called by this name"—here are three; "and this name is completed in this place," etc.—here are four things; and all of them are one, and the four of them are superfluous. Thus far our intellect has reached in raising difficulties in the wording of the passage, in order to understand it, to set it in order, and to support it.

It is fitting to state first that, from Rashbi and R. Elazar, peace be upon them, the answer of his fellow was neither hidden nor concealed from either of them; and neither interrupted his fellow in words until each of them had completed the main intent of his answer; and nonetheless their words are right and straight. And the main intent of R. Elazar in his question is to rule out two answers that fall within his question; and he meant to show that neither one suffices for his question, nor the two of them together. And the two answers are these. One is to say that, because judgment is included with compassion and compassion with judgment, it is therefore no difficulty that the name of compassion should have some judgment with it, all according to the prevalence; that is, when judgment prevails with the compassion, at times it is related to the name of compassion, and this is at known times. The second is that it is fitting that judgment be hinted at in the name of compassion, and that they not be separated, just as the actions are not separated at all; for judgment and compassion agree together in every action, as was explained above in chapter 6; and since judgment is included in the actions of compassion, it is fitting that one name be related to both of them. And these are the two answers, such that by each of them it would be fitting for the four-letter name to come with the vowel-points of Elohim. And there is a distinction between them: for the first answer is a sound reason, except that it is difficult [in that it implies] that at times compassion ought to be called by a name indicating the inclusion of judgment with it, all according to the prevalence and according to the blending; the second is a sound reason, except [that it implies] that compassion ought always to be called by a name indicating the inclusion of judgment with it. And R. Elazar intended to rule out these two answers in the wording of his question, in saying, "Have we not learned that Elohim is judgment in every place": meaning, since it has already been established for us that there is a name for judgment by itself—although there is no simple judgment with which compassion is not mixed—and it is the name Elohim, which is the name of judgment without compassion at all, then it is fitting that the four-letter name should always come indicating compassion without any admixture of judgment at all. And this is [his answer] to the "always": for just as the name Elohim is a title for judgment without the joining of compassion, so it is fitting with the four-letter name that it always indicate compassion without admixture of judgment. And so the second answer is rejected by what he said: one cannot say that the name of compassion ought not to be called without admixture of judgment because compassion is included with judgment; for just as judgment is called by the name Elohim without the joining of compassion, although it is not found by itself, so the four-letter name ought to be called by a name that is simple for compassion, without admixture of judgment, although judgment be included with it. And to the answer that is particular—saying that at times, according to the prevalence and the blending, it is called by the name of judgment, and [judgment] is mentioned within the name of compassion because the judgment prevailed and was blended until it rose into the name—to this he said, "Elohim is judgment in every place": meaning, the name Elohim is judgment in every place; for even if compassion prevails a little, nonetheless it does not change, but in all places Elohim is written equally, indicating judgment and force. And according to this, the four-letter name too ought not to change, but ought always to be called by the name of simple compassion; as you know that the four-letter name, spelled out in full, amounts to Mah [45], which is Chokhmah—ko'ach mah [the power of Mah]—which indicates compassion, as is known and will be further explained. And he said, "there is a place where it is called Elohim, such as," etc.: in his question he intended also another question; for the four-letter name is never found with the vowel-points of Elohim except with the name Adonai; and one needs to know the reason why—for what relation does this have to that?

And behold, the first, second and third difficulties have been resolved. [And to] the fourth difficulty that we raised—that the objection goes to the root of the matter, etc.—we say that R. Elazar already knew that Binah is called so because of the compounding of judgment and compassion; but the main thing in his question was that this matter should be related to a single name that would settle it, and not to the four-letter name, for this name is not fitting for that, for the reason that we have said; rather, a single name should be compounded of letters indicating judgment and compassion, and be related to Binah. And to this question of his Rashbi, peace be upon him, answered with a reason of substance, and said, "So it is," etc.: meaning, the verse comes to inform us and to bring us out of this intent, in saying, "Know therefore this day, and lay it," etc. Meaning: although you find that the four-letter name is simple compassion in its letters and in its matter, nonetheless you should know that "YHVH is the Elohim": in it is the power of strong judgment. And do not despair of retribution; for even in the attribute of compassion, at times judgment is compounded, and it turns into it. And this is the explanation of "Know therefore this day," etc. And Rabbi Elazar answered and said, "This thing I know": meaning, it was not because this verse was hidden from him that he asked his question. However, this verse is no proof at all. For just as the verse informed us of this premise—that at times judgment is mixed into the four-letter name, which is compassion—so necessarily at times compassion is mixed with judgment; and just as, in the place where compassion is mixed with judgment, no vowel-point or matter is mentioned in the name Elohim that would indicate it, so in the four-letter name it is not fitting that judgment be mentioned. And this is what he meant in saying "that in a place where there is judgment there is compassion": meaning, in the place of judgment too there is compassion, and nonetheless it is not mentioned in the name at all; so "in a place where there is compassion," although there is judgment, it is not fitting that that judgment be mentioned. And he was further exact in saying "and at times in a place where there is compassion," etc.: for in the place of compassion there is judgment at times, and rarely; but in a place where there is judgment, compassion is always mixed in there, for "He does not stir up all His fury" (Psalms 78:38), and the measure of good is greater than the measure of retribution. And now: if, in the place where compassion is constantly mixed with judgment—which ought to have been mentioned, in accordance with its constancy—nonetheless it is not mentioned and does not rise into the name, then in the place where judgment is [present] rarely and at known times, how much more is it not fitting that it be mentioned in the name! And to this Rashbi answered that, on the contrary, [the answer comes] from the very place from which you came: for what is the constant admixture of compassion is all included in the name Elohim; but here, where it is a thing that arises anew from time to time, that prevailing judgment ought to be called by name. And this is what he said: "Come and see that so it is." Meaning: as you said, and from the place from which you came—for the four-letter name is compassion in every place; and therefore, when judgment is aroused upon it because of "the wicked who turn"—that is, the turning of the compassion itself into judgment—it is therefore then fitting that the judgment itself be mentioned in the four-letter name. And although the four-letter name is written, "we read it Elohim": the intent is to show that although we read it Elohim, nonetheless its root is compassion. And indeed we read it with the name of judgment as a mere reading; for it is borrowed for the reading alone, for us, not with respect to itself—for with respect to itself it is compassion: "the four-letter name is written," but we read it as a mere reading. And therefore it is not such a strain. And with this the fifth and sixth difficulties are resolved. "But come and see the secret of the matter," etc. Know that now he comes to say how the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim is in Binah, and is called so because they make judgment prevail over it, in that they literally turn compassion into judgment; and this is the essence of the answer, and it is all one answer. And likewise he comes to resolve what he asked: why the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim always comes in union with the name Adonai. And to resolve this he was compelled to say, "There are three grades," etc. For the third grade is Malkhut, and Malkhut is called Adonai, a term of judgment, from the side of Binah (perhaps it should read "Gevurah," and so it appears below and in chapter 9), which is called Elohim; and all is one, unified; and they are three grades, and they are one. For by reason of the union in which they are unified, the name Adonai is related to Malkhut from the side of Binah [Gevurah], which is called Elohim. And when Malkhut is called by the name Adonai, then Binah is called by the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim. And Elohim and the name Adonai both indicate judgment, and all is one at a particular time. And the union of Malkhut with Binah in the aspect of judgment is Gevurah, which is called Elohim. So it turns out now that they are three grades, and they are unified with the true union, and they are three. And this is what he said: "There are three grades"; meaning, Binah and Gevurah and Malkhut. And so that the inquirer should not wonder that Gevurah is called Elohim only in union with Binah, and likewise Malkhut Adonai only in union with Gevurah—from which a strain would follow: that the name Elohim ought to be found only in union with the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim, and likewise Adonai, and it would be necessary that the three of them always come together, and this is not so—he saved us from this error, and said, "and each and every grade is by itself": meaning, it is not necessary that the three of them be together, but each one by itself. And although the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim is always unified with the name Adonai, it is for the reason that we shall explain.

And behold, with this the seventh, eighth and ninth difficulties are resolved. "Come and see: all the plantings." We have already explained in the Gate of the Order of the Emanation that Binah—although it is the root of judgment and its source, as we shall explain—nonetheless Chesed and compassion and judgment spread out from her, and from her the three lines were emanated, in the secret of Chesed, judgment and compassion: three patriarchs, Gedulah, Gevurah, Tiferet; and sons, Netzach, Hod, Yesod.

And behold, the branches and the sefirot, which are the seven days of the Structure, are discerned in two aspects: the aspect of judgment for all of them, and the aspect of compassion for all of them. And with respect to the aspect of compassion they are called "plantings," which grow on the waters of compassion; to all of them the blessing is poured forth. And with respect to the aspect of judgment they are called burning lamps of fire. And this is why he called the sefirot here "plantings" with respect to compassion, and "lamps" with respect to judgment. And because he needed to prove that the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim is in Binah—meaning that judgment and compassion went out from her, as we shall explain, for this is the reason for this preface and this length—therefore he took these two aspects in which the sefirot are discerned. And [it is] further because each of the two aspects is discerned in two other aspects, and they are little judgment and abundant judgment, little compassion and abundant compassion. And the explanation: although all the sefirot may incline toward the side of compassion, there are aspects to that inclination. Either the prevalence of compassion is such that judgment has not risen in it into the name, and nonetheless the prevalence is not so great, for the things are not yet in completeness, although it is compassion; and this we title by the name "little compassion." And the second, that the power of compassion prevails, and the light is revealed, and the effluence increases, until "the mountains drip sweet wine" (Joel 4:18), etc.; and this we title by the name "abundant compassion." And when it is neither of the two, but all the sefirot incline toward the side of judgment, and judgment increases—but not, God forbid, a prevalence of judgment to the point of destruction, but judgment plainly—this we title by the name "little judgment." And when the power of judgment prevails, and indignation increases, and judgment comes to pass, as at the time of the Flood and of the destruction of the Temple, when the thing was, God forbid, near to annihilation—this we title "abundant judgment." And since these four [measures of] judgment are poured forth into the sefirot in the aspects of judgment and of compassion, he said, "all of them shine and blaze"—meaning the lamps, which are the aspects of the sefirot with respect to judgment: "shine" with respect to little judgment, and "blaze" with respect to abundant judgment, which is the fire of the flaming-up of the fire of Gevurah and its judgment. And this is what he said, "shine and blaze," with respect to these two aspects. And with respect to compassion he said, "and are watered and are blessed": "and are watered," with respect to the watering that the plantings need, which is compassion, though not intrinsically; and with respect to abundant compassion he said "and are blessed" [mitbarkhan], which is like a pool [berekhah] of water. And with this the tenth difficulty is resolved. "From that river that flows and goes forth": meaning, these four aspects that we have explained, which are little judgment and abundant judgment, and little compassion and abundant compassion—all is poured forth from Binah, which is called "the river that flows and goes forth," as is explained in many places. And he called Binah by the name "river" because this name is related to Binah with respect to the watering, as is known.

"For everything is included in it," etc. To understand this matter we must state first that holiness and emanation are not in the way of other matters. For holiness always increases. And when the grades were emanated from Binah, which is the place of the first planting, to the place of the transplanting, not on that account was the planted manifestation nullified altogether; on the contrary, the first manifestation remained, subtler and brighter than the second. And the first manifestation is a root and a source and a track by way of which the second, lower manifestation receives the effluence. How so? The choice manifestation that remains within Binah is subtle with the utmost subtlety and near to the Emanator, the root of roots; and therefore, because of its nearness to its source, it is a track and a source for the very self of the sefirot that are emanated below. It turns out, according to this, that the Chesed planted within Binah is a source for the Chesed emanated in its [own] place. And let not the discerning one imagine that by this he has reached the bottom of our view on the manifestations; for the matter needs the Gate of Manifestations, in which this premise will be explained at length. And besides this manifestation that the sefirot have in Binah, they have there yet another manifestation, in the way of this premise, although it is not so concealed and excellent as the first. And it is this: after the sefirot were emanated below in their place, then, when the Will, blessed be He, ascends from Him, the sefirot ascend and are unified with the place from which they were emanated, and there they receive abundant effluence and blessing. And when they return to their place, the manifestation of their ascent remains there, after they were emanated below; and it is subtle and choice, but not like the first manifestation. And the reason is that the first manifestation is subtle with the utmost subtlety, because it is found from the manifestation of the sefirot before their emanation and their revelation and their thickening at all; but the second manifestation is a manifestation found from the sefirot after the emanation and the revelation, and their manifestation is not as subtle as the first.

And further, the first is a manifestation found from the sefirot from above to below, at the time of their emanation; and the second is found from below to above, after the emanation. And there is a great difference: for this one pours forth and that one receives the effluence, as we shall explain in the Gate "From Below to Above."

And behold, these two manifestations are the sources of the sefirot. The first, subtle manifestation is a choice manifestation, through which the choice aspect is poured forth, which is abundant effluence and blessing; and through the second manifestation little effluence, little compassion, is poured forth. However, little judgment and abundant judgment are on the side of Gevurah alone, as we explained above in chapter 6, and we shall explain [further] from this.

And behold, he intended these two manifestations here in saying, "for everything is included in it, and the whole of everything is in it." Meaning: of the first, choice manifestation he said "for everything is [included] in it"; meaning, the whole circuit is included in it, in the secret of their subtle manifestation before their revelation and their emanation. And of the secret of the second manifestation, which includes the revealed sefirot, he said "and the whole of everything is in it"; meaning, the whole of the sefirot after their emanation are all in it, above, in Binah. And the reason for all the length in this premise is to establish the intent concerning the matter of judgment in Binah, around which the essence of the inquiry turns, as we shall explain. And behold, the eleventh difficulty is resolved. "And this river is called mother to the garden," etc. The matter of the supernal father and mother, who are Chokhmah and Binah, is already known, as we shall explain below in chapter 17.

And behold, "mother" is not related to Binah except in union with the father, who is Chokhmah. For by means of Chokhmah, which pours forth, Binah is called a receiving female; and if there is no Chokhmah, male, father, there is no Binah, mother, female. And so they explained in the Tikkunim, and proved the matter from the verse, "Yea, if [im] you call for understanding [binah]" (Proverbs 2:3), whose explanation is: do not read im but em [mother]. And the verse said that the aspect called Binah is the aspect called mother. And she is called Binah only in her union with her husband, by means of Da'at; and her permutation is בן יה (ben Yah); and as is explained by us in the explanation of the passage in its place. And let us return to our matter: Binah is called mother from the side of her union with Chokhmah. And now it is already known that Binah is called "mother to the garden," that is, Malkhut; and likewise she is called mother to the other plantings of the garden, which are the sefirot that are above the garden. And this is "mother to the garden, and above the garden."
