And the reason that he said "mother to the garden" and did not say "mother to the seven sefirot," as would be fitting: the intent is to explain the principal union of Binah with Malkhut, in order to resolve the matter of the name Adonai YHVH, as we shall explain. Or "and this is called mother to the garden" means: "garden" is the name for the whole of the plantings, which are the sefirot that are watered from her; and she is called mother to them, and she sits above the garden; for then she is called mother, when she crouches over her children to water them and to nurse them, as we explained in chapter 6. And this is "and above the garden." True, it is a terse expression. And the reason that he called them a garden is that they are called "plantings," which relates to "are watered and are blessed," which he said above. "Because Eden is partnered," etc. Meaning: the reason that she is called mother is that Eden, which is Chokhmah, is unified with her to pour forth to them, and does not depart from her; therefore she is called mother, as we explained above. "And therefore all the wellsprings go forth," etc. The intent is to resolve how she is necessarily compassion and [yet] judgments are aroused, etc. And this is what he said, "And therefore": meaning, because she is included in the manifestation of the sefirot, as we have explained, and likewise all of them are poured forth from her as she is called mother—and the principal thing is the union of Chokhmah with her—by means of this she is necessarily compassion. For the whole that is within her is mostly Chesed and compassion, and they receive Chesed and compassion from Eden by means of the river; and since it is so, she is necessarily compassion. For her reception of compassion is by means of the extremities that are in her in a concealed manifestation, as we have explained, and they are simple compassion; and she receives compassion and pours forth compassion. And necessarily, although her nature is judgment, with all this her root is compassion, because of the three aforementioned causes. The first is because of the reception that the concealed, subtle extremities within Binah receive, which are the very essence of compassion. And the second is because of the pouring-forth of Chokhmah into her, so that those sources may receive. And the third is because of the pouring-forth that she pours forth to the revealed extremities, which are emanated in their place. And of these three causes he said, "all the wellsprings go forth and flow and are watered to every side," etc. Meaning: the sources are filled and receive, and they are poured into from every side from Chokhmah, in the secret of compassion. And this explanation is compelled: [it does not mean] that the wellsprings go forth and flow—that is, go out from her and water every side. For if so, he ought to have said "and water [ashkiyan] to every side," etc.; but he said only "and are watered" [ishtakiyan], in the reflexive, which is "are watered" from Chokhmah. And let not his saying "go forth and flow" be difficult; for its explanation is: they go forth from Chokhmah into Binah, into the very sources. Or we may say that the term ishtakiyan is like ashkiyan, and it refers to the pouring-forth that is poured from it to the sefirot below by means of the sources and the roots concealed within her; and this is "the wellsprings go forth and flow" in its plain sense; and "wellsprings" are the sources and the concealed manifestations, as we have explained. And the first is, in our view, the principal one. "And openings are opened in her": meaning, they open her and fill her with the effluence of compassion, as a male who fills the female; and likewise the concealed sources, by the pouring-forth of Chokhmah that comes upon them, open Binah. And this is the one aspect, which is the effluence of Chokhmah that is in her. And of the other, which is the pouring-forth of compassion, he said, "compassion is found from her"; meaning, compassion is found from her and is poured forth from her side to the lower extremities, that is, in the place of their emanation. And of the other—that in her own self she is compassion, because the extremities and the sources concealed in her are compassion—he said, "and compassion is opened in her"; meaning, in herself, in her own self, she is the power of compassion, and compassion is opened in her.

And behold, by these three reasons it is proven that she is compassion: whether from the side of her receiving, or from the side of her own self, or from the side of her pouring-forth. "And because we call her mother," etc. Meaning: because she is female, as is known, and every female is judgment, in the secret of the inverted tree, which is turned from below to above and turns its face to receive, as will be explained in the Gate "From Below to Above." And Binah is female relative to Chokhmah, for the reason that she receives beings [havayot] from it, as we shall explain. Therefore judgment must go out from her. It turns out, according to this, that her being called compassion altogether does not settle with her, because judgment and Gevurah go out from her; and judgment does not settle with her, because she is the outlet of compassion, and she is compassion, and her receiving is compassion. And this is what he said: "She is called compassion on her own"; meaning, that she should be called by the name of compassion alone does not settle at all, "because from her side judgments are aroused." And therefore this name was related to her, whose principal letters are compassion, to hint that her principal [nature] is compassion; and we pronounce its letters with the name Elohim, as a mere reading, to hint that judgments too are aroused from her. And this is what he said: "letters of compassion," which is the principal thing, "and pointed [with] judgment," because "judgment flows from her side." And all is explained. And what he said, "we call her mother," etc.—we have already examined his intent above, in the preceding chapter. And here is one grade. And with this the question of R. Elazar concerning the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim is resolved. But the reason for its being always unified with the name Adonai he comes to resolve at the end of the passage, as we shall explain. And now the twelfth, thirteenth and fourteenth difficulties are resolved. "The second grade: from the side of this first," etc. Meaning: from the side of Binah, which is the first grade of judgment, there goes out a second grade, and it is Gevurah, which is called Elohim in letters and in pointing, as he goes on to explain. And he was exact in saying "from the side of this first grade," and did not say "from the first grade" literally; because the root of Binah is not judgment, God forbid, as we have explained, but her root is compassion, and "from her side judgments are aroused." Therefore he said "from the side," whose meaning is "from her direction," not intrinsically in her. And this rule will be of use in many places. "And the beginning of Zeir Anpin," etc. Meaning: Gevurah is the beginning of the emanation of Malkhut, as is known; for Malkhut is on the side of Gevurah, as is explained above in the preceding gates and in the gates to come. And he needed this in order to explain that the third judgment, which is Malkhut, is unified with Binah by means of Gevurah, in the secret of the judgments. And now the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim will settle beside the name Adonai, to hint that, for the reason that the name Adonai, which is Malkhut, and its cause, which is its beginning toward judgment—which is "its beginning," namely Gevurah, the name Elohim—goes out from Binah, therefore Binah is called the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim. "And it is joined with it": meaning, he returns to what he left off from, namely Binah. And because of the union of Gevurah, the name Elohim, with the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim, and its arousal from Binah, the verse said, "for YHVH is the Elohim." Meaning: YHVH, which is the four-letter name, is unified with the name Elohim, in the letters of Elohim, that is, Gevurah. And he said YHVH, with the four-letter name in its plain sense, and its explanation is that the four-letter name, which is in Binah intrinsically, "is the Elohim": it is the arousal of the name Elohim. And what is mentioned in one place, in general, in the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim is explained in particular in two names, YHVH Elohim, each one by itself. And therefore what is explained in the Zohar in other places—that YHVH Elohim is in Binah—is not difficult; for this is general and that is particular. And so the matter is explained in the verse "for YHVH is the Elohim," which is the verse mentioned above. And now, with this thing, it is explained how the wicked turn the attribute of compassion into the attribute of judgment. For when Chokhmah is raised up and the sources of compassion are stopped up, Binah turns out to arouse Gevurah alone, by the power of the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim. And the parable of this: when we picture in our intellect the light of a candle against the light of the sun—for certainly "a lamp at noon is of no use" (Chullin 60b), and the candle does not perform its action at all, although its light is certainly not diminished from what it was; but because of the great brightness of the sun its actions make no impression. And so is the matter with Binah: when she pours forth to all the lines their effluence, behold, she is compassion, because most of the sources are compassion; and Gevurah, before the other sources, is like a lamp at noon. And not only that, but at times it too is clothed [in compassion], in that its judgment is subdued by the abundance of compassion, as we explained in chapter 6. But when the wicked cause the sources to be stopped up, and Binah is opened only in the source of Gevurah alone, and judgment comes to pass—behold, the wicked have turned Binah, which was the attribute of compassion, into judgment, in that she pours forth judgment and is opened in the sources of judgment. And with this it is explained that the two answers are one; and from the beginning of the words of Rashbi to their end, all is one answer, and it does not change from matter to matter. And the fifteenth difficulty is resolved. "The third grade," etc. We have already explained above that he needed this in order to explain the matter of the union of the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim with the name Adonai. And he called it here Tzedek, because Malkhut is called Tzedek from the side of Gevurah, as we shall explain in the Glossary of Titles. And because the principal judgment is in the secret of her aspect called "sea," which draws near to the depth of the sea in her last aspect, he said "the last crown"; meaning, the last aspect is called Tzedek, and it is the court, the place of judgment and of Gevurah, for in this aspect she is called "court." And he called it "court" because the name Adonai is a court, meaning the court of Tiferet; as is known that the name Adonai is a house and palace for the four-letter name, and we shall explain it in the Gate of Names, at the name Adonai. If so, since the name Adonai is called "court," it appears that the name Adonai is judgment, which is called Tzedek, etc., from the side of Gevurah, which is unified with Binah, as we have explained.

And behold, the sixteenth difficulty is resolved. "And we have learned: Adonai—so it is written," etc. Meaning: the name Adonai is not like the four-letter name, which is written YHVH and read Adonai; for because of its concealment it is not read as it is written, but it is read by its palace, by its titles; and the title and palace of the four-letter name is Adonai, as we have explained, and it will be explained in the aforementioned Gate. But the name Adonai is not so; rather, it is written Adonai and read Adonai. And this is what he said: "Adonai—so it is written and so it is called": its writing and its pronunciation are equal. And this indicates its revealedness. "And Knesset Yisrael is called by this name." Meaning: Malkhut is called by this name, and in the aspect in which she is called Knesset Yisrael. And Malkhut is called Knesset Yisrael in her last aspect, in the aspect of the judgment that is in her; for by the power of the judgment with which she judges the world she receives and does not pour forth at all. And this indicates the force of her judgment: that she receives, and nonetheless does not wish to pour forth, but gathers in [makhneset] and does not give out; and it will be explained in the Glossary of Titles. And the intent in this is to prove that in the aspect called Tzedek she is also called Adonai, and it is the third court; and so he proved from the Tosefta, in that he said "and we have learned." And this is what he said: "and this name is completed in this place"; because places are already found from which it appears that the name Adonai is compassion (see Zohar, Balak, fol. 185b).

However, its principal completion is only in the aspect of judgment, as is known from the matter of the letters דן (dan, "judges") that are mentioned within it; and likewise in that it is the reversed light, as is well known, for the Yod is below, in the secret of הוהי, as we shall explain in the Gate "From Below to Above." Behold, its principal completion is in the secret of the aspect of judgment. "And these are the three grades": meaning, they are three in union; for the name Adonai is unified with the four-letter name with the vowel-points of Elohim by means of the name Elohim. And this is what he said, "and all is bound one to one," etc., as we explained above.

And behold, the seventeenth difficulty is resolved, and the explanation of the passage is completed, with Heaven's help. And from the whole of his words there has emerged for us the explanation of a great matter: the manifestation of Binah, how she is complete compassion and the judgments are aroused from her, as we have explained; and likewise the matter of the turning of the attribute of compassion into the attribute of judgment, and of the attribute of judgment into the attribute of compassion. And blessed is He who graciously grants to man knowledge [and] understanding [binah].

Although our conclusion in the preceding chapters was that even Binah is compassion—needless to say Chokhmah, and all the more so Keter—let not the inquirer think that, in our saying that they are compassion, our intent is that they are equal compassion. Rather, the compassion of Keter is compassion simple in the utmost, and the reason is the sufficiency and the capacity that is in its hand, because it is the source of the blessings. And Chokhmah is compassion, but not like the compassion of Keter; and likewise Binah, not like the compassion of Chokhmah. For they rise in grade, one above another; but the name "judgment" is not titled to any one of the three. And the lessening of compassion in one relative to its fellow is because of the capacity and the sufficiency that each one of them has over its fellow, as is known. And concerning the source of judgment many were confused, asking: if it is true that there is no judgment at all in Keter, then how can there be judgment from there downward? For whence did judgment come out, and whence its cause and its emanation? For in Keter, which is father to all the sefirot, there is no judgment at all; if so, whence did the force of judgment come out? And they almost wished to say that in Keter too there is some judgment; and they hung their eyes on a thing that it is forbidden to think, all the more so to mention. And this was the portion of some of the Kabbalists of our generation, who are among the spoilers of the vineyard of YHVH of Hosts. And we have no portion with such as these, God forbid; for not because of a perplexity or perplexities that fall into our tradition shall we deny the plain sense of the plain passages and of most of the views. It is far, far more fitting to say that the way of wisdom is concealed and exalted. And there are some of the earlier commentators who resolved [it] in another way, and among them is Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla, in the book Sha'arei Orah (Gate 5, fol. 45), and these are his words: "Know that in all the holy names and the titles, from Keter downward, you have no simple attribute that is not mixed with its fellow. How so? The Chesed of Abraham is not complete Chesed, for the attribute of judgment of Isaac is mixed with it. And you have no attribute of compassion that has not some judgment in it, and you have no attribute of judgment that has not some compassion in it. And if you should reply and say, 'If so, why do you call it the attribute of compassion, since there is judgment in it? Or why should we designate it the attribute of judgment, since there is compassion in it?'—know that the attribute whose root is compassion, and most of which is clothed in compassion, although there is some judgment [in it], we call the attribute of compassion; and every attribute whose root is judgment, and most of which is clothed in judgment, although there is some compassion in it, we call the attribute of judgment. But there is no name, and no attribute, and no title, from Ehyeh downward, that is all complete judgment or all complete compassion. For if you say so, you will be found cutting among the saplings and separating the union. For if you say that the attribute of compassion is complete compassion, it will never join with the attribute of judgment, Gevurah; they will be found like two opposites that never draw near to one another. And if they do not join, then the union is separated into parts: the attribute of compassion by itself, and the attribute of judgment by itself. And of this it is said, 'a whisperer separates the Champion' (Proverbs 16:28). But the secret of the bond of the sefirot, and the names, and the titles, and all the attributes one with another, is as I shall tell you. Know that the attribute of the supernal Keter, which is all compassion, is joined first with the side of Chokhmah that faces upward, which is also compassion; and from the side of [Binah] [the second side of Chokhmah], which faces downward and is called the back, the attribute of judgment is born. And from the side of the attribute of judgment of Chokhmah, which faces toward Binah, that side, which is called judgment, comes round to be called compassion in relation to the array of Binah. For the farther they are from Keter, the more the attribute of judgment is born among them. And if so, the back of Chokhmah is called judgment in relation to Keter, and is called compassion in relation to Binah. And from these two sefirot, called Chokhmah and Binah, all the other names and titles are emanated. You learn, then, that every right is from the side of Chokhmah, and every left is from the side of Binah. And although the right is from the side of Chokhmah, Chokhmah is not complete compassion; for, as we have said, the back of Chokhmah is called judgment over against Keter—all the more so the right that is drawn from Chokhmah, which has in it compassion and judgment. But this is the rule: all the sefirot emanated from the side of Chokhmah are all called the attribute of compassion, and all the sefirot emanated from Binah are all judgment. And therefore, in the array of these beside those, these are called compassion and those judgment—not because those of the right side are complete compassion, but because most of them and their root are compassion, though there is some judgment in them; and not because those of the left side are complete judgment, but because most of them and their root are judgment, though there is some compassion in them. And this is the bond of the sefirot and the chariots: for were it not for the mixing of the attributes, they would never draw near and be bound one to another." Thus far his words.

And when we examine his words with the utmost exactness, and the bottom of his view—in that he said that "the farther they are from Keter, the more the attribute of judgment is born in them"—then there is no doubt that Chesed is farther from Keter than Binah is; and if so, why is Chesed at the right, in the secret of compassion, and Binah at the left, in the secret of judgment? And likewise: just as Binah sucks from the back of Chokhmah, which is judgment, so Chesed too sucks from the back of Chokhmah; and there is no doubt that the face of the back of Chokhmah that shines into Binah is more excellent than the face that looks toward Chesed, because Binah is second to Chokhmah and Chesed third to it—to the point that the first three are reckoned as one, as we shall explain. And if so, why is Binah at the left, judgment, and Chesed at the right, compassion? It ought to have been the reverse.

And further: since, in the first three, the back of Chokhmah is judgment over against Keter and is compassion in relation to Binah, and likewise the face of Binah is judgment over against Chokhmah—for this is his intent—then likewise the back of Binah should be compassion toward the face of Chesed, and the face of Chesed judgment in relation to Binah. For as is the relation of Binah to Chokhmah, so is the relation of Chesed to Binah. And besides this, it is well known that Netzach is farther from the source of compassion than Gevurah is; or at the least they should be equal: for Gevurah receives from Chokhmah at the third grade, and Netzach receives from Chokhmah at the third grade; so Gevurah is found to be [third] to Chokhmah by means of Binah or Chesed, and Netzach too [third] to Chokhmah by means of Chesed. And according to this it would be fitting, at the least, that there be a prevalence of judgment in Netzach as in Gevurah; and you cannot say this thing in any way, for it is known that Gevurah is the harsh attribute of judgment, and Netzach is compassion, in the secret of Chesed. And in this way the question falls upon all the sefirot according to their grade, grade after grade: for the more the grades spread out, the more judgment ought to increase, according to his words; and this is not so, as is well known.

And further: in Binah and in Gevurah and in Hod, why should they not be judged by the judgment of the first three, so that the back of Gevurah would be compassion in relation to Hod, since Hod sucks from the back of Gevurah? And why is Gevurah harsh judgment, and Hod not so much? And if it is true that his words are right—that the face of Chokhmah in relation to Binah is the back in relation to Keter—this will be only with respect to subtlety and spirituality, but not with respect to judgment and compassion. For judgment does not depend on subtlety or on spreading out, as he thought. For the angel Michael, who is a branch of Chesed below, in the secret of the angels, is without doubt more Chesed than Gevurah, which is the harsh attribute of judgment—although this one, beside that, is like a mustard seed to the great sea, and more. For there is no relation between them: this one is subtle with the utmost subtlety, cleaving to the Emanator, one of the emanated; and that one is small, low, low, and "came down wondrously" (Lamentations 1:9). And in these ways with all the angels and the powers. And this thing is clear, and to lengthen on it is almost a vain exercise. And indeed it is in our power to nullify this question about judgment from its root, by saying that this question should not fall, just as it does not fall concerning the matter of Gevurah [itself]: how from the limitless was the limited emanated, and from what has no end how did what has an end come out, and from what is not body how did body come out, and from nothing how did something come out? For all these are of the kind of this question; and it is near to say that they have no answer [other than to say] that there is no reason in the Will, and so it arose in His Will to draw out the things for the governance of the world. And so is the matter with judgment: for "He spoke, and it was" (Psalms 33:9). But nonetheless, since we choose the truth in what is true, our wish is to restore the things to their proper measure, "and the palace shall stand in its proper place" (Jeremiah 30:18). And the matter is known: Keter is the utmost subtlety among the emanated, and with all this it is the root of Chesed and compassion and judgment. However, the judgment in it is not literally judgment—that is, that it effects judgment there, God forbid—although its root is there; rather, it is concealed, in the way that we explained above in this Gate, in chapter 3. And likewise it includes Chesed and is called supernal Chesed; and of the power of compassion it is the foundation and the root, as is known, for it is the father of the middle line, the line of Rachamim. And we have already spoken at length of this in the preceding gates, and we shall explain it in this Gate and in the Gate of Tzachtzachot. And from this root two powers spread out, which are the power of Chesed from the side of Chokhmah and the power of judgment from the side of Binah—not that Chesed and judgment are literally there, but they are there in subtlety, in the way of the subtlety of the four elements, which are air, water, fire, earth, and whose source is in four supernal attributes, which are Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Malkhut. Not that in these attributes there is fire or water or air or earth; rather, the source of these elements is there, in these attributes. And so is the matter with Chesed, judgment and compassion: they are poured forth from Keter, Chokhmah, Binah, and they are in them in subtlety, and are revealed intrinsically in Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet—Chesed, the power of Chesed; and Gevurah, the power of strong judgment; and Tiferet, the power of compassion, intrinsically. And from these, three branches branch out that serve them, and they are Netzach, Hod and Yesod, over against the three upper ones. And the matter is this: just as Keter, Chokhmah and Binah were concealed in their source, in the Ein Sof, blessed be He, including the whole Emanation, unified and concealed, subtle with the utmost subtlety, as we shall explain in the Gate of Tzachtzachot, and nonetheless after their emanation their power and their matter are revealed—so is the relation of the three attributes in [their] actions, which are Chesed, judgment and compassion: they are concealed in Keter, their first source, and neither Chesed nor judgment nor compassion is judged in it; but just as is said concerning the roots in the Ein Sof, so is the matter of the actions in the supernal Keter. For as is the relation of their emanation, in the manifestation of the very self of the sefirot above in the Ein Sof, so is the relation of the aspect of their action, which are Chesed, judgment and compassion, in the supernal Keter. For the actions are drawn from the attributes; so the attributes are causes of the actions, and likewise the Ein Sof is cause of Keter. And as is the equality of the attributes in the Ein Sof, so is the equality of the actions in Keter. For the attributes were concealed in their source and unified with the utmost union, and were not in the literal manifestation of the sefirot; but after their revelation in Keter, three roots were emanated and revealed, which are Keter, Chokhmah, Binah—not a revelation of [their] self, but some revelation, revealed relative to the first source; and still the actions are concealed, so that there is no judging in them, until they come to the place of their revelation, which is Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet. And in order to bring the inquirer to the content of these words of ours, he must grasp what we shall write on this in the Gate of Tzachtzachot, concerning the matter of primordial light, clear light, refined light: for although they are three, they are one, unified. And now the question "whence did judgment come out?" does not fall; for the source of the sefirot and the source of judgment and compassion and Chesed are all one thing. For they are three roots—the root of Chesed, and the root of judgment, and the root of compassion—and they are primordial light, clear light, refined light, concealed in one root and revealed in Keter, Chokhmah, Binah; and the actions are concealed, and are fully revealed in Gedulah, Gevurah, Tiferet (see Asis Rimonim).

And after we set right, in the preceding chapter, the matter of judgment and its source, it remains for us to explain the matter of the bond of the sefirot and their union; for it is the inquiry that compelled Rabbi Joseph to the matter mentioned in the preceding chapter. And we have in this a fine way, on the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, as we shall copy his wording here. And the matter is that all the sefirot include ten, as we spoke of at length in chapter 2; and with this thing the matter of their union and their bond will be explained. And the matter is that Keter is unified with Chokhmah from the side of the Keter that is in Chokhmah, and likewise it is unified with the other sefirot from the side of the Keter that is in them; and it turns out, according to this, that each and every sefirah has many bonds with the sefirot. The example of this: Gevurah with Chesed from the side of the Gevurah that is in Chesed, and Chesed with Gevurah from the side of the Chesed that is in Gevurah—besides their being able to be unified and bound from the side of the other nine parts of the other sefirot. The example of this: the Keter that is in Chesed with the Keter that is in Gevurah. And so for all the other parts, concealed in themselves within the parts themselves; that is, the parts of the sefirot that are in each and every sefirah are themselves unified with one another, in the way of the sefirot themselves. For there is no part in the world that does not include ten; for so we are obliged to believe, for if not so, it is separation and cutting, God forbid. And this very matter Rashbi explained in the Zohar, in Parashat Va'era (fol. 23b), and these are his words: "Rabbi Shimon said: Come and see: four are the first; they are the secret of faith, and they are the fathers of all the worlds, and they are the secret of the holy supernal chariot. And they are four elements—fire, air and water and earth. These are the supernal secret, and these are the fathers of all the worlds, fathers of everything. And from them go out gold and silver and copper and iron, and beneath these other metals that resemble them, in the manner of these. Come and see: fire, air and water and earth—these are the first, and the roots of above and below, and the upper and the lower stand upon them. And these are four to the four sides of the world, and they stand in these four: north and south, east and west—these are the four sides of the world, and they stand in these four. Fire to the side of north, air to the side of east, water to the side of south, etc., earth to the side of west. And these four are bound in these four, and all are one. And these make four metals, which are gold and silver and copper and iron. Here they are twelve, and all are one. Come and see: fire is the left, to the side of north; for fire—the force of heat is in it, and its dryness is strong; and north is its reverse; and they are blended one with the other, and it is one. Water is to the right, and it is to the side of south. And the Holy One, blessed be He, to join them as one, made the blend of this like the blend of that. North is cold and moist, fire hot and dry: He exchanged them to the side of south. South is hot and dry, water cold and moist; and the Holy One, blessed be He, blends them as one: for the waters go out from the south and enter into the north, and from the north the waters flow; fire goes out from the north and enters into the force of the south, and from the south the force of heat goes out to the world. Because the Holy One, blessed be He, lends this to that, and each and every one lends to its fellow from its own, as is fitting for it. In this manner air and east: because each one lends to its fellow, and this is included in that, so as to be joined as one. Come and see: fire from this side, water from that side, and they are a dispute. Air enters between them and holds the two sides. This is what is written: 'and the spirit [ruach] of Elohim hovered over the face of the waters' (Genesis 1:2); for fire stands above on this side, and water stands on the face of the earth; air enters between them and holds the two sides and separates the dispute. Earth: water stands upon it, and air and fire, and it receives from all of them by the power of these three that stand upon it. Come and see: air and east. East is hot and moist; air is hot and moist; and therefore it holds the two sides. For fire is hot and dry, [and water cold and moist]; air is hot and moist: the side that is hot holds to the fire, the side that is moist holds to the water; and therefore it makes agreement between them and separates the dispute of fire and water. Earth is cold and dry; and therefore it receives all of them upon itself, and all of them do their work in it, and it receives from all of them, to bring forth by their power nourishment for the world. Because in the west the earth is held, which is cold and dry, [and the side that is cold holds] to the north, which is cold and moist—for cold holds to cold; therefore north is held to west on this side. South, which is hot and dry, by that dryness of its own holds the dryness of the west on the other side; and the west is held on two sides. And likewise south is held to east, for the heat of the south is held in it by the heat of the east. And east is held to north, for its moisture is held to the moisture of the north. Now it is found: south-east, east-north, north-west, west-south; and all are included one in another, to be linked one in one." Thus far his words.

And from within it there appears explicitly the union and the bond of Gedulah, Gevurah and Tiferet and Malkhut, which are water, fire and air and earth: Gedulah is unified with Gevurah and Gevurah with Gedulah by means of their equal parts; and likewise Gedulah with Tiferet, and Tiferet with Gevurah, and the three of them with Malkhut, by means of their parts that are equal, each with its brother; and this is the cause of their union. And likewise from this we shall learn concerning the other sefirot and the manner of their union and their bond, as we explained above. However, what he said [in another version], that air is cold and dry, is difficult: for by way of what is seen in experience, air is hot and moist; it is equal to fire in its heat and to water in its moisture; and so all the investigators agreed. And so Rashbi, of blessed memory, wrote in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 69, fol. 104b), and these are his words: "A point in the middle, shuruk, which blows with the wind upon the waters, which holds both of them; and it is hot and moist." Thus far his words. It appears from it explicitly that the view of Rashbi is that it is hot and moist, and that it is equal between the two of them—meaning fire and water, which are two opposites, as we have explained.

And further, in another place (Tikkun 21, fol. 62), R. Shimon holds that air is hot and moist. And it is possible that in this passage too the principal [reading] is "air is hot and moist," but a scribal error fell into the books. And the passage needs some explanation, and this is its explanation. "And they are the fathers of all the worlds": meaning, from them is linked the rest of the chain of the emanated and the created and the formed and the made; for all of them are divided into these four parts, as in the matter of "its seat of purple [argaman]" (Song of Songs 3:10), which corresponds to Gedulah, Gevurah, Tiferet, Malkhut, which are Abraham—Michael, Isaac—Gabriel, Jacob—Uriel or Nuriel, David—Raphael. And likewise the matter of the division of fire and water and air and earth. And likewise the twelve constellations are divided into these four divisions. And likewise in the chariot: lion, ox, eagle, man. And these are the four great rivers, as it says, "and from there it parted and became four heads" (Genesis 2:10); and likewise for the other parts of reality. And likewise in the matter of the attributes themselves: all of them are divided into these four divisions, in different aspects—as if to say Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Malkhut: here are four. And of these he said, "and the secret of the holy supernal chariot."

And further, the reason of this matter will be explained: because they are Chesed, judgment and compassion, and the whole of everything. And if so, this matter will further require a second way of dividing them; and it is that Chokhmah, Binah, Chesed, Gevurah are literally these four mentioned. And Chokhmah is man, because it is the whole of everything, and from it is the source of everything; and just as Malkhut is the whole of everything because she receives from everything, so Chokhmah is the whole of everything because it emanates everything, as it says, "In wisdom You have made them all" (Psalms 104:24). And likewise Binah is eagle, and of it is said, "the great eagle, great of wings" (Ezekiel 17:3); and Chesed lion, and Gevurah ox: here are four faces. And further, four second faces: Tiferet man, Netzach lion, Hod ox, and Yesod eagle.

And further, a third face: Malkhut, the pattern of the palace (another version: "of everything"); and in this way Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (in the Introduction, fol. 3b, and in Tikkun 1, fol. 16b). It turns out that "the secret of the holy supernal chariot" is literally the chariot of the Emanation, as we have explained. And he was exact in this, in saying "supernal holy"; and it is not included in his saying "of all the worlds," which are the worlds that are below the Emanation. And now he explained who these four are, and said, "and they are fire and air and water and earth." And the matter is that the lower form is a seal of the pattern of the upper ones, like one who seals, with engraved seals, a fine form on four plates: one of gold, the second of silver, the third of copper, the fourth of lead. For the first form is in all the places, and they were sealed with one seal and made at once; except that, according to the descent of the sealed seal from the engraved seal, so its form thickens; and likewise, according to the thickness of the materials that receive the seal, so is the descent of the sealed form. And this is the reason that these four elements are spoiled and thick and coarse, coming to be and passing away, like the form sealed in lead, whose form is easily spoiled. But the four elements that belong to Michael and Gabriel and Raphael and Uriel have a lovely form and a pure matter, which received that form; and their form is not spoiled, because of its nearness to its source, to the upper seal that seals. And this is the plate of copper.

And further, the Throne has four lovely pillars of silver, above the four aforementioned living creatures, and they are pure as silver, nearer to their source, without their form being spoiled; and likewise the gold above them. And in this way for the whole order of the worlds and the chariots. And always, whether above or below, they are certainly water, fire and air and earth; except that these are sealed at one grade and those at a second, etc., until their descent to the lowliness of corporeality. And this is what he said: "and they are four elements, fire, air, water, earth," which we said above—not that they are literally fire, air, water, earth, but a subtle being [havayah], not like this one. And this is what he said: "these are the supernal secret," in the secret of the four elements that are in the Emanation, which are water—Chesed; fire—judgment; air—compassion; earth—the whole of the three of them. "And these are fathers," etc.: for they are a seal with which everything from them downward was sealed. "And from them go out," etc.: the matter is that east and west and north and south are unified in the secret of the water and the fire and the air and the earth; and they are four females and four males. And the reason is that Chesed and Gevurah and Tiferet and Malkhut pour forth into the lower aspect that is in Malkhut, in which the four of them are included together, as Rashbi explained on the Song of Songs, on the verse "And behold, one wheel upon the earth" (Ezekiel 1:15), etc. And the four sides turn out to be four females to the fire and the air and the water and the earth. And the offspring that goes out from the union of four with four is four kinds of metals, which are gold, silver and copper and iron; and they are emanated from these four aspects. And this is what he said: "And from them go out gold," etc.—for they are literally offspring to them—as he goes on to explain: "Here they are twelve, and all are one." For they are four males unified with four females, and four go out from them; and all is one matter and one manifestation.

And behold, since by the way of natural coming-to-be it is necessary that the male and the female not be equal—and if they are not opposites in their nature they do not beget—so the four males in the four females are opposites in their nature, so that the blending of judgment and compassion may be blended, and the Emanation that comes to be will be toward judgment and compassion. And this is what he said: "Come and see: fire is the left"—which is literally in Gevurah; and it indicates the nature of Gevurah, which by the abundance of its judgment dries up the effluence and parches it, so that it does not pour forth at all. And this is what he said: "for fire—the force of heat is in it, and its dryness is strong," which indicates the drying-up of the effluence, God forbid. "And north"—which is the lower Gevurah, which comes from the upper Gevurah, being female to the male—"is its reverse": for the judgment of Malkhut is not to dry up the effluence, but to hold it back and withhold it, and there is no union; and it is indicated by the matter of the cold, which congeals the waters and withholds them.

And behold, when the judgment of Gevurah partners with her, it warms Malkhut with its judgments and arouses the coupling and the effluence; and there is the source of the gold, which is the wine that gladdens. And this is what he will say: "and they are blended one with the other, and it is one." And likewise in the literally lower things, to sustain the power of the creation and of the creatures, so that they not be nullified through excessive dryness or excessive cold prevailing over them; for the excessive prevalence of one element is the cause of sicknesses and of the nullification of the elements, as is known; and the cause of all is their supernal root, as we have explained. And because the heat and the dryness that are in the south—although it is hot and dry—are not as strong as the heat and the dryness of fire, as he concludes, therefore he said, "for fire—the force of heat is in it, and its dryness is strong": meaning, the power of strong dryness and heat, as we have explained, which is not so with the south. "Water to the right," etc.: from the side of Chesed; and they are cold and moist, indicating the prevalence of the effluence and of compassion. And south is hot and dry—not like the heat and dryness that are in fire, as we have explained, but hot and dry in the measure of the lower Gevurah; and it indicates the drying of the waters from upon the earth, so that there is no effluence at all. And behold, the female is the reverse of the male, as we explained above. "And the Holy One, blessed be He, to join them," etc.: for it would have been fitting that the proper order be north, which is cold and moist, indicating the waters, on the side of Chesed, which is water cold and moist; and south, which is hot and dry, on the side of fire, which is hot and dry—not in reverse, as they are now. But "the Holy One, blessed be He, to join them as one, made the blend of this like the blend of that"; that is, that the side of the females be the reverse of the side of the males, so that the coming-to-be may be blended and the aforementioned matters come to be from within them. And the example of this: the north side is cold and moist from the side of the waters of Chesed that are over against it, so that our saying that north is the side of the Chesed that is in Gevurah is true; and the south is hot and dry from the side of the fire that is over against it, so that our saying that south is the Gevurah that is in Chesed is true. And behold, north and south are the side of the females, and their exchange indicates the power of blending and of arbitration. And indeed the matter of cold and moist, or hot and dry, and the like, will be explained in the Gate of Arbiters.

And behold, according to the proper order of the matter, the side of Chesed pours forth into the side of the female that is over against Gevurah, and the side of Gevurah pours forth into the side of the female that is over against Chesed; and this is the form of the matter, to make it plain to the ear. And this is what he said: "the waters go out from the south and enter into the north"; for from the south, which is Chesed, water, is the source of the waters, and they are poured forth only by means of Malkhut, that is, "and enter into the north," and from there they are drawn to the lower ones. And likewise the judgment of Gevurah: "fire goes out from the north," that is, from Gevurah itself, "and enters into the force of the south," that is, into Malkhut herself, from the side of Chesed and Gevurah, and is drawn to the lower ones. And this is what he said: "and from the south the force of heat goes out to the world," etc. "In this manner air and east," etc.: the intent is that air and east unify them. That is: because the side of the east is hot and moist, it unifies north and south—for it is hot in the south and moist in the north—and behold, south and north are unified by means of both of them. And likewise air is hot and moist; it unifies the water and the fire, for water is moist and fire hot, and air is equal to water in its moisture and to fire in its heat. And yet air and east are not literally equal: for the hot side of the air is the moist side of the east, and the hot side of the east is the moist side of the air. And the reason is that the water is to the south, and from its side, to the side of the right, the air is moist; and the fire is to the north, and from its side, to the side of the left, the air is hot. Behold, the air is moist from the side of the right and hot from the side of the left. And not so the east, which is moist from the side of the left, where the north is, and hot from the side of the right, where the south is. If so, it turns out that just as north and fire are opposites, and south and water are opposites, so east and air are literally opposites: for the hot side of the east is the moist side of the air, and the hot side of the air is the moist side of the east; and behold, hot is the opposite of moist, and moist the opposite of hot. And this is what he said: "In this manner air and east: because each one lends to its fellow." Meaning, how so? The hot in the air pours forth into the moist side of the east and warms it, and from there heat is drawn into the world; and likewise the moist side of the air pours forth into the hot side of the east and moistens it, and from there moisture is drawn into the world, as we explained concerning north and south. And this is what he says: "In this manner," etc. And because this matter was hidden from the copyists, they corrupted the books below and copied "air cold and dry," the opposite of the east, which is hot and moist. And it is a corruption; rather, air is hot and moist, as we have explained, and it is the truth, as Rashbi explains in the Tikkunim and in other places. And the rest of the words of the passage in this premise are clear, and will be explained in the book Or Yakar. Further, this matter of bond and union is found explained in Sefer ha-Bahir (cited in the Tosafot to the Zohar, fol. 12, at the end of the book of Bereshit), and these are its words: "And why is it called shamayim [heaven]? Rather, it is round like a head; and it teaches that water is on its right and fire on its left, and it is in the middle: שא מים—from fire and from water; and it brings peace between them. The fire comes and finds on its side the attribute of fire; the water comes and finds on its side the attribute of water. And this is 'He makes peace in His heights' (Job 25:2)." Thus far its words.

And the explanation of "round like a head": that it is round like the heavens. And the reason that he said "like a head" and did not say "like the heavens" is that Tiferet is called head, for the head tips the balance between the arms; and just as the head is above the arms, so Tiferet is at times above Gedulah and Gevurah. And he proved the matter of the roundness from the head, which is round and resembles it. And the explanation of "round": the intent is that just as a circle has no head and no end, and its foundation is the place of the center point, a point subtle in the utmost, so Tiferet has no head and no end, and its foundation is the first point, and it is the point of the Emanation, the first three. Further, Tiferet is the world of the circumference, in the secret of the six extremities; and therefore it is called round, and the heavens are round, to hint at the circumference. And the rest of the words of the passage are clear of themselves. And likewise our intent is explained without doubt: that he said that the heavens are bound to Gedulah and Gevurah from the side of water with water and fire with fire; and likewise from this side Gedulah and Gevurah are bound to it. And what is fitting to lengthen on in this matter we explained in the Gate of Channels, chapter 5.
And behold, the bond and the union of the sefirot have been explained without our needing the words of Rabbi Joseph, the author of Sefer ha-Orah.

The intent in this chapter is to explain a passage that at first sight appears the reverse of all that we explained above, where we said that judgment is from the first three downward, and the first three are not included. And [in Chagigah] (fol. 5b) the reverse is implied, and these are the words of the Gemara: "'But if you will not hear it, my soul shall weep in hidden places' (Jeremiah 13:17), etc. Rav Shmuel bar Inya said in the name of Rav: The Holy One, blessed be He, has a place where He weeps, and its name is Mistarim [Hidden Places]. And what is 'because of pride' [mipnei gevah]? Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak said: Because of the pride of Israel, which was taken from them and given to the nations of the world. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: Because of the pride of the Kingdom of Heaven, which was taken. But is there weeping before the Holy One, blessed be He? Did not Rav Papa say: There is no sorrow before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, 'Glory and majesty are before Him, strength and joy are in His place' (1 Chronicles 16:27)? It is no difficulty: this is in the inner chambers, that is in the outer chambers. And in the outer chambers not? But it is written, 'And on that day YHVH Tzeva'ot called to weeping and to mourning and to baldness and to girding with sackcloth' (Isaiah 22:12)! The destruction of the Temple is different, for even the angels of peace wept, as it is said, 'Behold, the Erelim cried outside; the angels of peace weep bitterly' (Isaiah 33:7)." Thus far. It is implied from within it that in the inner chambers there is weeping and sorrow and judgment, from his saying "this is in the inner chambers, that is in the outer chambers." And Rashi explained: "In the inner chambers there is, as it is written, 'in hidden places,'" etc. It is certainly implied, from his saying "in hidden places shall weep," that the place where He weeps is the Mistarim. And so it is certainly implied, from our seeing that he objected, "And in the outer chambers not? But it is written," etc.—for it appears that the answerer answered him that in the outer chambers there is no sorrow, since he objects, "And in the outer chambers not?" etc. And so that the reading not be corrupted, Rashi explained: "'And in the outer chambers not'—so we read: 'And in the outer chambers there is not? But it is written, "And He called,"' etc.; for every 'calling' is making a voice heard outside." Thus far his words.

And he proved from the two verses that the principal explanation is that the inner chambers are the place in which the weeping is fixed, whether for the destruction or after the destruction, at every time: from what he said, "The Holy One, blessed be He, has a place where He weeps, and its name is Mistarim," and this is the inner chambers; and from what he also said, "And in the outer chambers there is not? But it is written, 'And He called'"—and every calling is making a voice heard outside. If so, the main objection is to the outer chambers, of which he said that there is no weeping there. And this is difficult for all that we explained above in the preceding chapters, for he said that in the inner chambers, that is, the first three, there is no judgment, that is, weeping and sorrow. And Rabbi Todros ha-Levi, in the book Otzar ha-Kavod, wrote, and these are his words: "Rabbi Shmuel said, etc. There are books in which is written 'and in the outer chambers not,' and it is an error; for it is impossible so, according to the give-and-take of the passage, and according to the proof brought from the angels of peace; for these Erelim are outer, as it is written, 'cried outside,' that is, the outer chambers.

"And now I will explain to you the secret of their words. What he said—'the pride of Israel,' 'the pride of the Kingdom of Heaven'—all is one; for the pride of Israel is none but the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, 'and who is the sword of your pride' (Deuteronomy 33:29). But Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explained explicitly that in the destruction of the House, as it were, the pride of the Kingdom of Heaven was diminished—as in the matter that they said, that the legs of the Throne were diminished, or that the wings of the living creatures were diminished, and the household on high was diminished. And the place that the Holy One, blessed be He, has, whose name is Mistarim—they are the inner chambers; they are the inner crowns, of which it is said, 'rays from His hand are His, and there is the hiding of His strength' (Habakkuk 3:4). And the angels of peace receive from there in truth, and they too wept for the destruction of Jerusalem and of the Temple below, for this depends on that, as we have hinted in several places. And the outer chambers are the central pillars on which the world stands, and in them the Netzach, the pride and the Hod of the Holy One, blessed be He, spread out; and the Righteous One of the world is Yesod; and they are 'two golden spouts' (Zechariah 4:12), for so we have hinted to them; and this is enough. And some say: the inner chambers are the first five, and the outer chambers the last five; and it is all one intent." Thus far the words of Rabbi Todros ha-Levi, of blessed memory. And his words are astonishing: for he emended the books, and said that it is impossible so "according to the give-and-take of the passage, and according to the proof brought," etc.; and we do not get to the bottom of his view. For, on the contrary, the give-and-take does not imply so, but rather [accords with] the reading of the books that he emended, as we proved above, and as Rashi explained. And we can only say that perhaps he had another version of this passage. And with all this, the matter is as I wrote, the reverse of what the Rav explained: rather, certainly the constant weeping is in Mistarim, the inner chambers; except that the destruction of the Temple is different, for even the angels of peace in the outer chambers wept. For this is the sense of the passage, and this is the principal reading in most of the books that are found with us. And on the rest of his explanation of the passage we do not wish to lengthen, since our intent is to explain it in its proper measure. Further, Rabbi Joseph Gikatilla followed this view, in the book Sha'arei Tzedek, which is attributed to him in most books; and these are his words, at the sefirah of Binah. He said that Binah is called the Upper Chamber [aliyah], and said: "If a righteous man merits to ascend to the attribute of the Upper Chamber, he tears up every decree of judgment in the world. And the reason is that whoever cleaves to the attribute of the Upper Chamber—no harm, and no evil occurrence, and no lack cleaves to him in that place; for it is the place complete in every kind of completeness, and there are constant gladness and joy. And this is what they said in every place; and they call it the inner chambers. And what they said in Chagigah—'it is no difficulty: this is in the inner chambers, that is in the outer chambers'—know that the inner chambers are what is called from Binah upward, which is the secret of the Upper Chamber; the outer chambers, Tiferet and Malkhut. And because around Tiferet are seventy princes, who are the oppressors of Israel when they sin, and around Malkhut all the thrones of the foreign kingdoms—and she is 'like a rose among the thorns,' etc.—there are in that place the tumult and the troubles and the lacks, and the kinds of harm and the sorrows. But from Binah upward there is nothing there but joy and gladness; there is no adversary and no evil occurrence, for all is in fullness." Thus far his words, for our matter. And in truth he went in the way of Rabbi Todros; and that is not the reading of the Gemara, and according to this the passage does not settle. And besides all this, in the Zohar it is explained explicitly as Rashi, of blessed memory, explained in the Gemara; and these are its words, in Parashat Noach (fol. 61b): "Rabbi Elazar was going to Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakunya, his father-in-law. When he saw him, he prepared a seat for him [tofsisa de-kumra be-matun de-kulfa], and they sat. His father-in-law said to him: Perhaps you have heard from your father this that is written: 'YHVH has done what He purposed; He has fulfilled His word [bitza imrato] that He commanded from days of old' (Lamentations 2:17)? He said to him: The Companions have established it: 'bitza imrato'—that He tore His purple robe. 'That He commanded from days of old': for that purple robe He deposited from those first, supernal days; and on the day that the Temple was destroyed He tore it, because this purple robe is His glory and His tikkun, and He tore it. He said to him: 'YHVH has done what He purposed'—does a king plan beforehand to do harm to his children before they come to sin? Rabbi Elazar said to him: [It is like] a king who had a precious vessel, and every day he was afraid for it lest it break, and he would look at it, and it was precious in his eyes. In time his son came and angered the king; the king took that precious vessel and broke it. This is what is written: 'YHVH has done what He purposed.' Come and see: from the day the Temple was built, the Holy One, blessed be He, would look at it, and it was very dear to Him; and He was afraid for Israel lest they sin and the Temple be destroyed. And so every time that He would come to the Temple He would put on that purple robe. After they caused sins and agitated the King, the Temple was destroyed and He tore that purple robe. This is what is written: 'YHVH has done what He purposed; He has fulfilled His word,' etc. This 'His word' [imrato] at first sat 'on the top of the bough' [rosh amir] (Isaiah 17:6), and behold, it was crowned [it'atru] as a diadem [atarah] for the head, and a lovely tree before Him; and it is 'from days of old' certainly. And then there was sorrow before Him in the outer chambers, certainly; 'and behold, the Erelim cried outside' (Isaiah 33:7); 'and on that day the Lord YHVH Tzeva'ot called,'" etc. Thus far its words.

Behold, he agreed that at the destruction of the Temple weeping and sorrow arose anew in the outer chambers—so it appears that the constancy is in the inner chambers, as Rashi explained. And this thing needs no further proof. And before we come to the explanation of the passage, we wish to explain this matter and bring it out to the light. And the matter is that although judgment and its action are in Gevurah, nonetheless its dependence is on Binah; and according to what is poured forth from above, so they act below, for it is not in their power to add or to subtract. And these are the words of the Zohar, in Parashat Noach (fol. 70a): "'And YHVH smelled the pleasing odor' (Genesis 8:21); and it is written, 'a fire-offering, a pleasing odor' (Leviticus 1:9). 'Fire-offering' [isheh]—so I have heard: smoke and fire are joined as one, for there is no smoke without fire, as it is written, 'And Mount Sinai was all in smoke, because YHVH descended upon it in fire' (Exodus 19:18). Come and see: fire goes out from within, and it is subtle, and it takes hold of another thing outside that is not so subtle; and they are held one with the other, and then smoke rises. What is the reason? Because the fire takes hold of a thing that is coarse. And your sign is the nose, from which smoke goes out from within the fire. And therefore it is written, 'They shall put incense before You [be-appekha, in Your nose]' (Deuteronomy 33:10): because the fire returns to its place, and the nose is gathered in by that odor, inward, inward, until all is unified and returns to its place, and all is brought near within the Thought, and it becomes one desire [re'uta]. And then [it is] a pleasing odor [re'ach nicho'ach], for agitation rests and rest is made. For the smoke is gathered in, and enters, and is pressed into the fire, and the fire is held in the smoke, and both of them enter within, until agitation rests. And when all is held one with the other and agitation rests, then it is rest and one bond, and it is called rest: the rest of all, the rest of the spirit, the joy of all as one, the light of the lamps, the light of the face. And therefore it is written, 'And YHVH smelled the pleasing odor'—like one who smells and gathers everything inward to its place. Rabbi Yeisa came and kissed him," etc. Thus far its words.

And from within this passage a great light goes out for us on this inquiry, and we shall explain it in brief. He said, "smoke and fire are joined as one": meaning, fire is the effluence of Gevurah that goes out from Binah; and from there goes out the flame, the blaze that takes hold of a somewhat coarser, revealed matter, which are like the wood, as will be explained. And the smoke is the powers of Gevurah that spread outward to act in Gevurah. And in truth fire and smoke are joined as one: for just as smoke cannot act without fire—for when it is separated from the fire its power is nullified, as in "As smoke is driven away, so drive them away" (Psalms 68:3)—so too the action of fire is only by means of the smoke, which are the emissaries of the fire, the emissaries of judgment; and therefore they are joined as one. And the proof is from reality itself: "for there is no smoke without fire"; so the powers of judgment cannot act unless judgment is aroused from above. And he proved the matter from what is written, "And Mount Sinai was all in smoke," etc. And the explanation of the verse: Mount Sinai was all full of the powers of judgment, in the strengthening of Gevurah; and he gave the reason, "because YHVH descended upon it in fire"—meaning, the Torah was given by means of Gevurah, and therefore the power of Gevurah necessarily prevailed. "Come and see: fire goes out from within, and it is subtle": meaning, the fire goes out from inside, from within Binah, in the root and source of Gevurah that is within Binah, as we have explained; and the effluence is the fire, the flame; and it is subtle because it is near to the source; and that fire does not act, and the smoke does not prevail by means of it, until it is poured forth to Gevurah. And this is "and it takes hold of another thing outside that is not so subtle," that is, Gevurah, which is the power of judgment in actuality. "And then smoke rises": that is, the powers of judgment that spread outward. "What is the reason?": meaning, what is the reason that they did not spread out and did not prevail when the judgment was poured from the source, but their power had to be by means of Gevurah? And he said, "Because [the fire] takes hold," etc.: meaning, when the judgment is in subtlety it is above, near to its source, and has no action; but after it is poured forth to the place of its action, then it acts with all its powers in Gevurah. "And your sign is the nose," etc.: all this is to explain the verse "And He smelled," with which he opened. And he said that the matter is like the hot breath that comes by way of the nose. And when a person smells an odor, that odor rises upward to the brain, for in it is the sense of smell; and that breath turns out to return to its source—and not only to its source, but above its source: for its source is Binah, and above its source is the Thought, Chokhmah—to sweeten the judgment in the light of Atika, which is explained in the preceding chapters. And this is what he said: "the nose is gathered in by that odor"; that is, by means of the odor the breath and the smoke return inward. And this is what he said, "and returns to its place," which is Binah; and afterward "all is brought near within the Thought." And he did not say "and returns within the Thought," because it does not literally return to Chokhmah, but to Binah; but it draws near to Chokhmah, that is, the shining of Chokhmah in Binah, until the judgment is made fragrant even on the side of Gevurah, as we explained above (see Ra'aya Mehemna, Pinchas, fol. 224a; and below, in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles, at the entries "smoke," "odor" and "incense"). "And then a pleasing odor," etc.: meaning, an odor that makes rest; for by means of the odor—that is, the return of the judgment to its source and its drawing near to Chokhmah—by this the agitation rests. "Then it is rest and one bond," etc.: that is, all of them suck from the side of compassion and Chesed, as we have explained. And this is what he said, "the rest of all": even Gevurah itself is clothed in compassion, needless to say Chesed and Tiferet. "The joy of all as one": he explained to us that there are two kinds of judgment. The one is agitation and judgment; the second is the wine of Binah, which gladdens and does not intoxicate like the first. And now, in the return of the judgment to its source, when it is made fragrant, then that judgment becomes gladness, and is poured forth even into Chesed and Tiferet; and this is what he said, "the joy of all," which is in the aspect of the judgment that gladdens. So: "the rest of all"—that is, even Gevurah is clothed in compassion; "the joy of all"—for even Chesed is clothed in the judgment that gladdens. "The light of the lamps, the light of the face," as in the matter of "to make the face shine with oil" (Psalms 104:15).

And behold, from within this passage it appears explicitly that the root of judgment is from above, and below there is only what is poured forth from above—like the parable of the wood: for if there were no flame, there would be no smoke that brings down tears, which is from the eyes, which are what blaze in judgment. And likewise it is explained that the flame does not raise smoke except by means of the wood. It turns out, according to this, that the root of the sorrow and the judgment is in the inner chambers, which is Binah; for in the outer chambers, which are the other attributes, there is no sorrow, for it is not in the hand of Gevurah to add to the judgment, to act, except according to the measure poured forth to it from above, from Binah. And in truth there is no judgment above in Binah, since the flame does not act at all except by its taking hold in the wood of Gevurah, as he explained. And this matter is further explained there (fol. 70b), and these are its words: "Rabbi Chizkiyah said: 'I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake' (Genesis 8:21)—what is it? Rabbi Yeisa said: This I have heard from R. Shimon, who said: Whenever the fire above increases in strength, the smoke, which is the judgment below, strengthens the agitation and destroys everything; for when the fire goes out it has no cessation until the judgment is completed. And when the judgment above does not increase in strength, the judgment below executes judgment and ceases, and the judgment is not completed to destroy." Thus far its words.

And behold, he said that when [Binah] does not add its effluence from above, the lower Gevurah and its powers cease; for there is no smoke except from the power of fire, and [it acts only] when they add this judgment from above. And it turns out, according to this, that judgment is the reverse of compassion: for it is the way of compassion and of the good effluence to increase, as we shall explain in the Gate of Manifestations, in the first chapter; which is not so with judgment, which, if it is not poured forth from above, will not be effected and will not increase below. And this is "in the outer chambers there is no sorrow": he means that there is no judgment in them, since they have no power to add to it and to increase it except according to what is given from above. And with this thing we shall understand what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma, fol. 76): "the measure of good is greater than the measure of retribution"; for the measure of good increases continually, and the measure of retribution decreases. And this is of the greatness of our Creator, and of His delight in compassion and in the sustaining of the world. And after we have settled the matter of the passage, it is fitting that we come to its explanation as is fitting. And before we come to the explanation of its wording, we shall examine in it some points of exactness. First: they said, "What is 'in hidden places'? Rav Shmuel said: The Holy One, blessed be He, has a place where He weeps, and its name is Mistarim." And why did he explain that Mistarim is its name—which indicates by this that it is not literally in a hidden place, but is called Mistarim? It would have been more fitting for him to explain: the Holy One, blessed be He, has a place where He weeps, and it is in a hidden place, and therefore it says "in hidden places"; and this is literally the inner chambers, of which the Gemara explains. Second: what was difficult for him in the verse, that he turns to explain it? For the verse is expounded according to its plain sense—that in hidden places, literally, the inner chambers, He will weep if they do not hear. And if so, what was he asking, in saying "What is 'in hidden places'?", that he turns to explain it? Third: what was difficult for him from what Rav Papa said? These are verses! And why did he not set the verses against each other—for [one] says "in hidden places shall weep," which implies that there is weeping, and another verse says "strength and joy are in His place"—so that the verses contradict each other? Fourth: what did Rav Papa come to teach us? For it is the plain sense of the verse, in which is written "strength and joy are in His place." Fifth: they said, "And in the outer chambers there is not?" What is this? For until now he wished to say that there is no sorrow at all; and now that he answered him, "this is in the inner chambers, where there is, and in the outer chambers there is not," he objects that even in the outer chambers there is—astonishing! Sixth: they said, "The destruction of the Temple is different, for even the angels of peace," etc. What is "even"? It implies: not only the Holy One, blessed be He, but even the angels of peace. He ought to have said the reverse—even the Holy One, blessed be He, wept—which is the novelty. And now we shall come to the explanation of the passage, so that everything may be set right. "What is 'in hidden places'?": because the sense of the verse implies that the weeping and the judgment are in hidden places; and the first three are called Mistarim, for so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (in Tikkun 10, fol. 24a) on the verse "The hidden things belong to YHVH our God" (Deuteronomy 29:28): that the hidden things are the letters Yod-Heh, that is, the first three, Yah; and the revealed things, that is, Vav-Heh, which are Tiferet and Malkhut, with the whole of the rest of the Emanation. And if so, how did he say "in hidden places shall my soul weep," indicating that judgment is poured forth from the first three? And this is a great strain—that we should say that judgment is poured forth even by means of Keter; for in truth there is no judgment there at all, as is explained above in the preceding chapters. And therefore he changed the sense of the verse and said, "The Holy One, blessed be He, has a place where He weeps, and its name is Mistarim": meaning, it is one place only, that is, one sefirah, not three, as the plain sense of the verse implies.

And the matter of Mistarim: not because the weeping is in all three hidden places; rather, "its name is Mistarim"—that is, in it two others are included; and this is Binah, and in it Keter and Chokhmah are included; therefore it is called Mistarim; and in it is the weeping, as we have explained—not because there is weeping in all the hidden places, God forbid. And the explanation of "has a place," etc.: he means that Tiferet, which is what is titled here "the Holy One, blessed be He," has a place from which judgment is poured forth to it; and this is "where He weeps," "and its name is Mistarim," as we have explained. "Because of the pride of Israel": the intent is, because of the effluence and the light that was poured forth to Israel by means of the Shekhinah; and now, by iniquities, it was taken from them and given to the nations of the world. And this matter is like the matter of "They made me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I have not kept" (Song of Songs 1:6) (see Zohar, Tazria, fol. 45b). For when we are in exile among the nations, and the Shekhinah is with us and among us—certainly to guard us—then she pours forth to us abundant good in the impure lands; and so this effluence turns out to be poured forth to them, and we eat of its residue. And the reality of this matter: for example, in Egypt, when Israel were exiled among them, the food of Israel was given to the prince of Egypt so that Israel would be fed—as in the matter of a father who feeds his son by means of an agent: necessarily the food of the king's son is given to that agent. And so, when we are exiled under harsh masters, the Shekhinah our mother pours forth her effluence to us by means of that prince; so the prince turns out to feed and sustain the members of his household with our food, and we eat of their residue and their leftovers. And this is what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avodah Zarah, fol. 8a): "Israel outside the Land are worshippers of idolatry in purity." For their prayer is to pour forth to the Shekhinah, and the Shekhinah pours forth upon them.

And behold, the Shekhinah, when she pours forth, pours forth to them only by means of the prince under whose rule they are; so they turn out, God forbid, to bring an image into the Sanctuary in complete purity. And this is David's complaint, in saying, "For they have driven me out this day from cleaving to the inheritance of YHVH, saying, Go, serve other gods" (1 Samuel 26:19), as [our Sages, of blessed memory,] explained (Ketubot 110b). And therefore our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah 13b) that in every place to which Israel were exiled, that nation was exalted—because it is the one that sits first in the kingdom.

And the matter that [our Sages], of blessed memory, said—that we eat literally of their residue—is visible to the eye. For the blessing rests on the foods, on the rain of the land and on the order of the years that are drawn for blessing; and behold, Israel buy their sustenance from them for full silver. So the root of the blessing turns out to be theirs alone, and Israel do not have their sustenance in ease. And this is visible to eyes of flesh, all the more so to the eye of the intellect. And this is what is intended by the wording "the pride of Israel, which was taken from them and given to the nations of the world"—literally, as we have explained. And Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, who said "because of the pride of the Kingdom of Heaven," went deeper, and said: not only this, but also from above—from the mother who sustains, who is called the Kingdom of Heaven when she is unified and "leans upon her beloved" (Song of Songs 8:5), whose explanation is: the Kingdom that is unified with Heaven, that is, Tiferet. And he said that from her too the effluence departed; for because of the wickedness of the children the mother's food is removed, and she is driven from the King's palace, God forbid. "But is there weeping before Him? Did not [Rav Papa] say," etc.: he did not set the verses against each other, because they do not contradict; for we explain "strength and joy are in His place" to mean that most of the time, or always, there is joy; but when some cause occurs, then it is possible that there be weeping and judgment; and therefore the verses do not contradict. And the main objection is from what Rav Papa explained, "There is no sorrow before the Holy One, blessed be He," which appears to intend ruling out judgment altogether. Therefore it is difficult for what he said, "The Holy One, blessed be He, has a place," etc.

And behold, this objector—whether he is the anonymous Talmud or another—did not distinguish between "before" and "from before," for "before" is in Malkhut. Rather, we had in mind that all is one; and he objected from the words of Rav Papa, who said, "There is no sorrow before Him." And the explanation of "before," according to what we now have in mind, is in Binah; and "before" means "prior," that is, prior to the Holy One, blessed be He—that is, prior to Tiferet—which is Binah. Or we may say that he objected that, since "before" is the Shekhinah, then [it would be a case of] "the native on the earth and the convert in the highest heavens": and likewise, if in Malkhut there is no judgment and sorrow, all the more so in Binah, which is above, it is not fitting that there be, God forbid, any judgment at all. And this is the principal [explanation] in our view. And he answered him: on the contrary, in the inner chambers there is, and in the outer chambers there is not—according to what we explained above, that the intent is that the root of judgment is from Binah; for in Malkhut it is not increased, but according to the measure that is poured forth, so it acts; and on the contrary, the more it is poured forth by way of the grades, the more it decreases. This is according to the second explanation. And according to the first explanation, he answered him that the matter of "before" means in the outer chambers, that is, in Malkhut; but in the inner chambers there is, as we have explained.
