"And from these [the others] separate": meaning, although at first glance it would appear that the aspect of Malkhut is an aspect set apart by itself, that is no proof; for she is included in these, and from these three she branches out, and not that she is an aspect by herself, as it appears. Thus far.

And behold, from this passage it is explained that the whole Emanation is included in these three aspects, which are Chesed, Din, Rachamim — that is, the line of the right, the line of the left, the middle line. Rabbi Elazar explained this matter further in Parashat Shemot (fol. 14), and these are his words: "Behold, we have learned that with ten utterances the world was created; and when you look, they are three, and the world was created with them: 'with wisdom, and with understanding, and with knowledge' (Exodus 31:3)." Thus far its words, as relevant to our matter.

And behold, these three are three grades, which are Chesed, Din and Rachamim. However, they are roots, and in them are concealed the branches, which are three and three, as we explained. And one must be precise: why are they not included in Keter, Chokhmah and Binah, which are the roots of the three lines, as is explained in the Gate of the Order of the Emanation? And Da'at — what is it doing here? And the reason is that in Keter neither judgment nor compassion applies. For compassion includes Din and Chesed, being the line of the mean; and Keter is the secret of Chesed and Rachamim that has no admixture of Din at all; and therefore our saying of it that it is the line of Rachamim would not be correct in truth. And Da'at is the aspect of Tiferet before its expansion, with respect to its aspect in Keter between Chokhmah and Binah, in the secret of arbitration, as will be explained in the coming Gate. And therefore, when we wish to include the second aspect, which is the aspect of Rachamim, we cannot include it in Keter itself, for it would not be correct, for the reason that we explained. However, we can include it in Da'at, which is the aspect of Tiferet and the aspect of Keter — that is, Tiferet, which rises up to Keter; and in its rising there, in their upper manifestation, it turns out that it is the root and totality of Rachamim, with some judgment included with it. But Keter itself is a concealed root; in it the three aspects are included in concealment, like the hiddenness and concealment of the emanated branches in the Emanator. And therefore, because of this, judgment is not correct of it, as we explained above in chapter 3. And now, according to this, the sefirot turn out to be included and regarded in three aspects, by their breadth and by their length, although they have neither length nor breadth, thus:

Behold, three by three. Keter, Chokhmah, Binah: the intelligible world; Gedulah, Gevurah, Tiferet: the perceptible world; Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malkhut: the natural world. Behold, their aspect divided by breadth. And by length they are: Chokhmah, Gedulah, Netzach — behold, the world of Chesed; Binah, Gevurah, Hod — behold, the world of Din; Da'at, Tiferet, Yesod — they are the world of Rachamim. And above them is Keter, including all three aspects, just as it includes the first three; and although it includes Din — for it includes Binah, which is the root of Din — this matter does not entail Din in it at all, as we explained in chapter 3. And below all of them is Malkhut, including three aspects, for she is the one who includes all the sefirot, as is known. It turns out according to this that Chokhmah and Binah and Da'at, which is in the place of Keter, are the secret of the actions in potential; and Gedulah and Gevurah and Tiferet, the secret of the actions in actuality; Netzach, Hod, Yesod are the messengers who perform the actions. It turns out according to this that Keter is a soul to Tiferet, in the secret of Da'at; and Chokhmah a soul to Gedulah; and Binah a soul to Gevurah; and Chesed a soul to Netzach; and Gevurah a soul to Hod; and Tiferet a soul to Yesod; and Yesod, which receives from the three of them, a soul to Malkhut, who includes all of them.

The principle that emerges from the previous chapter is that Keter and Chokhmah and Binah pour forth into Chesed, Tiferet, Gevurah, and Chesed, Tiferet, Gevurah pour forth into Netzach, Hod, Yesod. However, Yesod receives all of them and pours forth to Malkhut; and apart from Malkhut they have no governance in the world. For all is given into her hand, and they have no permission to pour forth to the lower ones except by her means. And so Rashbi explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 4, fol. 19a), and these are his words: "And there is no sefirah among all the sefirot that has permission to empty out blessings and to pour forth to the lower ones except through Bat Sheva, because she is the bond of all the sefirot. For if the sefirot were emptying out apart from her, there would be separation; and therefore there is no permission to empty out blessings and to pour forth to any place apart from her, toward the lower ones. And therefore it is said of her, 'Let not the wise man glory,' etc., 'but in this,' etc. (Jeremiah 9:22–23)." Thus far his words.

And it is clear for our matter. And the truth is that the pouring forth of the sefirot into Malkhut is by means of Yesod, as we explained in the Gate of Channels, chapter 3; and, God forbid, when Yesod withdraws, the effluence and the good withdraw. And if the questioner asks: how is it possible to suppose that the effluence of Yesod withdrew from Malkhut and the world would endure? This is no difficulty, for this question has already been asked in the Zohar, Parashat Terumah (fol. 166b), and these are its words: "This light the Holy One, blessed be He, sowed in the Garden of His delights, and made it rows and rows, by means of this Righteous One; and he is the gardener of the Garden. And he took this light and sowed it, a seed of truth, and made it rows and rows in the Garden of Eden; and it begot and sprouted and made fruits, and from them the world is sustained. This is what is written: 'Light is sown for the righteous,' etc. (Psalms 97:11). And it is written, 'and as a garden causes its seeds to sprout' (Isaiah 61:11). What are its seeds? These are the seeds of the primordial light, which is sown constantly: now it begets and makes fruits, and now it is sown as at first; before the world eats this fruit, it begets this seed and gives fruit, and does not subside. And therefore all the worlds are sustained by the provision of that gardener who is called Righteous One, who does not subside and never ceases — except at the time when Israel are in exile. And if you say: at the time of the exile it is written, 'The waters fail from the sea, and the river is drained dry' (Job 14:11) — how does it make offspring? Rather, it is written 'sown': it is sown constantly. And from the day that river ceased, the gardener did not enter that Garden; and that light, which is sown constantly, makes fruits, and from them, of itself, it is sown as at first, and does not subside, constantly — like a garden that makes offspring, and from that seed that fell in it, in its place, of itself it makes offspring as at first. And if you say that those offspring and fruits are as they were at the time that the gardener was there — it is not so; but this sowing is never withheld. In this manner, 'and the Torah is light' (Proverbs 6:23): the Torah [that was given from the side of that primordial light] is thus sown constantly in the world, and makes offspring and fruits, and never subsides; and from that fruit of it the world is sustained." Thus far its words.

And the intent of this passage is to prove that Yesod is what pours forth into Malkhut; and he is the man who tills this ground, and there is none who breaches the fence and trespasses his border to sow or to till besides him. And this is the point around which the wheel of this passage turns. For above this matter he said that Tiferet is called "light" from the side of its sucking from Chesed, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles, under the entry "light"; and he said that this light, which is the effluence that is poured forth, is poured forth by means of the Righteous One, the foundation of the world. And he explained that the one who pours forth is Tiferet, the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the master of the seed; and the tenant farmer who tills the ground is Yesod; and the garden in which the seed is sown is Malkhut. And he called her by the name "garden" on account of the wording of the verse, which says, "Light is sown" (Psalms 97:11), and the expression "sowing" applies to a garden; and on account of the verse that is written, "and as a garden causes its seeds to sprout" (Isaiah 61:11), for from there is his proof, as will be explained.

And further, because there are fifty-three [gan] portions in the Torah; and this is the secret of the verse "and the Torah is light" (Proverbs 6:23), for it is about this that [the passage] stands there. And when she receives from Tiferet, which is the Torah, then she is called gan [garden], to allude to its fifty-three portions. "And made it rows," etc.: the intent is to resolve the verse, which said "its seeds," in the plural; and so that, from the expression "its seeds," which implies many, we not come to say that many sow in her, and she sprouts and grows all the seeds, each after its kind — for this he spoke first, to save us from the error. And it is true that in the seed of the Righteous One there are many kinds of effluence, each one to the storehouse fit for it: storehouses of life and storehouses of wealth, storehouses of wisdom and storehouses of Torah and storehouses of understanding; and this is "and made it rows," which are the storehouses. "And he took this light," etc.: it was difficult for him: if so, it would follow according to this that the seed that goes out from the Righteous One is not as the Righteous One receives it from above, but is changed in the self of the Righteous One. For otherwise, how would the word "sown for the righteous" be correct? For if the effluence is poured into her as it is poured from above, what benefit is drawn from this to the Righteous One, that the name "sown for the righteous" should be related to him? To this he said, "and he took this light," etc.; and the explanation is: he takes the light and pours it forth, and sows it as light, just as it is poured from above; and it is not in his hand to hold it back or to change it — just as there is no power in the organ of intercourse to change the seed from its nature, which belongs to it by means of the two that empty it out. And this is what it says, "and he sowed it, a seed of truth": meaning, a seed of truth [emet], that is, Tiferet; and even after the sowing it is a seed of truth, related to Tiferet. And as to what was difficult for him — what benefit is drawn from this to the Righteous One, or what is his action, that the saying "sown for the righteous" should be correct — to this he answered, "and made it rows and rows": meaning, the light and the effluence come mixed, without being separated each after its kind, and Yesod is the one who divides it to the storehouses, each one according to its nature, decreed from its root — in the way of the tenant farmer, or the man who tills the ground, who "puts the wheat in rows, and the barley in its place, and the spelt at its border" (Isaiah 28:25).

And further, besides this, he begets it and makes it sprout; and this is what it says, "and it begot and sprouted," etc. And the reason for this doubling is to allude to two things: the one, for the matter of the effluence that is poured forth for the sustenance of the world and its provision and the other matters of the world; and the second, for the matter of the souls. And this is his intent: "and it begot" souls, "and sprouted" fruits and seeds; for both of them are the sustenance of the world. "This is what is written: 'Light is sown,'" etc.: he settled the matter from two verses. From the first verse, which is "Light is sown for the righteous," he proved that the one who sows this seed is the Righteous One, as it said, "Light is sown for the righteous." And from the second verse he settled and proved that the one who receives the effluence is the chosen garden; and this is "and as a garden," etc., as we explained. "What are its seeds? These are the seeds," etc.: it was difficult for him: if so, it turns out that the garden, after its sowing, will afterward necessarily change the seed from how it was; and in the end the expression "light is sown" would not be precise, for after it is sown it is not light. For this he said, "What are its seeds? These are the seeds of the primordial light": meaning, just as the primordial light was — by which is intended the effluence poured from Chesed into Tiferet, to pour forth to the bride — so, after it is sown in Malkhut, and after its sprouting, the name "light" is still upon it. And this he intended in saying, "the primordial light, which is sown constantly": the intent is that it never changes from how it was in its place. "Now it begets and makes fruits," etc.: it was difficult for him: if so, why did the verse say "its seeds she causes to sprout," a name implying "its seeds," that they are hers, so that it is in her hand to change them? For otherwise it ought to have said "she causes seed to sprout"; what is "its seeds"? For this he answered that what is now renewed in Malkhut is that it makes offspring and fruits, which it did not before. And this is what it says, "now," etc.: meaning, after it is sown, "it begets and makes fruits." "And now it is sown as at first": meaning, even now, at the time that it makes the fruit, it is light, as before its coming to Malkhut, the place of its sowing. And he took the expression "sown" to be precise in the expression "light is sown for the righteous," which proves that even after its sowing it is called light, as we explained, and that it never changes from how it was in its place: light. "Before the world eats this fruit," etc.: it was difficult for him: what necessity is there for the manifestation of this matter, that it be light as before its coming? And why not say that it changes, in the way of all sowings, which change to a manifestation other than their sowing — for they rot and change into the manifestation of sprouting, which is grass, and from it that seed is born? For this he answered that it is not fitting to say so of the manifestation of the effluence poured to Malkhut. For if we said so, it would follow that the effluence is somewhat limited at the time that it sows, and if so, it changes to a manifestation other than the manifestation of its coming, and afterward sprouts; and if so, between this and that the world would be destroyed. Rather, certainly we are compelled to say that as it is in its source, so it is poured to Malkhut; and as it is at the time of its pouring forth, so it is at the time of its growing and making fruits; and there is never any delay, for all this is as an instant. And this is what it says: "before the world eats this fruit, it begets this seed and gives fruit, and does not subside." "And therefore all the worlds are sustained by the provision of that gardener," etc.: the intent is to explain what has already preceded for us, that the Righteous One is called "the river that flows and goes out and never ceases"; for the thing cannot be held back in any way in the world, for the world would be destroyed, as it is after the destruction, as he goes on to explain. "And if you say," etc.: meaning, according to your words, that there is no manifestation for the world except by means of the drawing of the effluence without delay — if so, at the time of the exile, when no effluence is poured forth, as is proven from the verses, how does the world endure, and from where are those fruits from which the world is sustained?

And further: since the effluence has withdrawn from Yesod, if so, how does Yesod make offspring and fruits? So his question turns out to be in two respects: first, concerning Malkhut — how is there a manifestation for the world, for it is written, "The waters fail from the sea"? And the second, concerning Yesod — how does it pour forth, for it is written, "and the river is drained dry"? And he answered to this that from the day the Temple was destroyed, effluence has never been poured forth by means of Yesod, that is, the gardener; "and he did not enter the Garden," meaning, he did not unite with Malkhut, because they are not found together, as it is written, "The righteous one is lost" (Isaiah 57:1), as is explained in the Zohar. And to the question, by what is the world provided for — it is by means of the effluence already poured forth, which was sown from the time before the destruction. And the matter is that the way of holiness is to increase and not to diminish, as we shall explain in the Gate of Manifestations, chapter 1. And if so, the effluence itself is never withheld; rather, a manifestation other than it comes to be from it, to sustain and to provide for the world. And this is the parable of the sown garden, [in which afterward, from the seeds that fall,] of themselves, it is sown and grows there out of the seed sown before. "And if you say that those offspring," etc.: it was difficult for him: if so, what advantage is there for a person in all his toil in union, since the effluence grows of itself, and other sustenance comes to be from it, from which the world is sustained? If so, the union with Yesod neither raises up nor brings down, since the garden is sown of itself. To this he answered: and do you think that the seed sown of itself, and the manifestation that comes to be, are equal to the manifestation of the literal watering — so that it would appear that there is no advantage in the gardener's being within the garden, and in the river that waters it? God forbid; the thing is not so. For now manifestation comes to be from manifestation, and manifestation from manifestation, and they are not the light itself; for the light itself always remains there, to bring into being a manifestation other than itself, which is the seed that is sown. But when the Righteous One is within his Garden, and waters it and sows it, since the light is drawn and does not cease, the world is sustained from the self of the light itself, not from its manifestations; and, on the contrary, the manifestations increase and the blessings increase in the world. And this is what it says, "but this sowing is never withheld," etc.: the intent is that it is true that the sowing is never withheld, but not that it is of the value and equal to the time when the Righteous One is within his Garden, as we explained. "In this manner, 'and the Torah is light'": he returns to explain the verse with which he opened, that is, "For the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light" (Proverbs 6:23); and the intent is that the Torah is like the sown light, which always makes fruits and never ceases. Thus far the explanation of the passage. And the principle that emerges for us is that the sustenance and the effluence poured to Malkhut are by means of Yesod, and not by means of another sefirah besides it. And even at the time of the exile, when the Righteous One is not in his lodging, nevertheless the world is sustained from what he poured forth before. And among the things one must know: since at the time of the exile the world is sustained from effluence that was poured into Malkhut before, if so, what will intention in prayer and union give, and what will it add? And all the more now, in this bitter exile, of which it is said, "The righteous one is lost," and likewise, "The waters fail from the sea" — if so, what do prayer and supplication and union accomplish, since the righteousness of the Righteous One pours forth neither little nor much, as is proven from the previous passage?

And this matter they explained in the Zohar, Parashat Shemini (fol. 40), and these are its words: "And whoever knows how to unite the holy name — although blessings are not found in the world — he supports and props up Knesset Yisrael in the exile." And behold, explicitly: although the blessings are not found, nevertheless there is in the matter support and prop.

And the matter of support is that Malkhut, who is "the falling booth of David" in the exile, has no rising until He looks down and sees, and that hour arrives in which the verse that is written will be fulfilled: "On that day I will raise up the booth of David that is falling" (Amos 9:11). And he was precise in the word "falling" [nofelet], a participle in the pattern of po'elet, nokemet. And the intent is that she is forever falling; for that effluence — as long as the time of the destruction continues and there is no renewal in it — is like the parable of the seed of the garden that is sown of itself, which, if they do not renew it, will be spoiled, God forbid. And therefore "there is no day whose curse is not greater than that of its fellow," because the power of the female has weakened, God forbid; and this is "falling." And because of this she needs supporters, so that she not fall altogether.

And the matter of the support is by means of some pouring forth [which will be found from above, "from the juice of pomegranates" (Song of Songs 8:2)], as through the cracks of a needle, to renew support in the world. And all those who make the prop and the support, their reward is doubled and redoubled; and of them it is said, "Rejoice for joy with her, all you who mourn over her" (Isaiah 66:10). And the matter is that they be united — even if the union of their aspect is not as it was before the exile — until the Temple is built and the verse that is written is fulfilled: "And YHVH shall be King over all the earth; on that day YHVH shall be One and His name One" (Zechariah 14:9).
And with this this Gate is concluded; and praise to God, the true Helper. And we journey on to the Gate of Arbiters.
The Ninth Gate: The Gate of Arbiters.
The intent in this Gate is to explain the number of the arbiters between Chesed and Din: how many they are, and how the manifestation of the arbitration is.
Chapter One:

The intent in this chapter is to make known the matter of arbitration. And the matter is this: when the Holy One, blessed be He, emanated His holy Emanation, He emanated two opposite attributes, which are Chesed and Gevurah, from which reward and punishment are drawn. And since it sometimes happens that the world needs punishment, but not so much, and likewise it sometimes needs reward, but not so much, therefore the Emanator emanated the middle line between the two extremes; and it is what is called the arbiter line. How so? Chesed is an attribute that inclines to reward and to the good, and to pour forth upon the wicked and the good, as its name, which is chesed [kindness]. And so it is explained in the Zohar, that Chesed is to pour forth upon the wicked and the good. And these are its words in Parashat Terumah (fol. 168b): "'And in His goodness,' and not 'from His goodness.' 'And in His goodness' — this is the supernal right. And 'from His goodness' — this is another grade, which comes from the side of the right, and it is a grade below it. Because by that good the world was built, and by it it is fed. Why is it called 'good,' and why is it called 'Chesed'? It is 'good' when all is included within it and it has not spread out to descend below; it is 'Chesed' when it descends below and does good to all creatures, to the righteous and to the wicked, and does not care — even though it is one grade. And from where do we know? For it is written, 'Surely goodness and kindness shall follow me' (Psalms 23:6). If goodness, why kindness? And if kindness, why goodness? For one would suffice. Rather, 'good' includes all within it and has not spread out below; 'Chesed' descends and spreads out below and feeds all, the righteous and the wicked alike. And here, since he said 'and in His goodness we live,' he went on to say, 'who feeds the whole world in His goodness, in kindness.'" Thus far its words.

And there are things to be precise about in it. First: his saying, "And 'from His goodness' — this is another grade, which comes from the side of the right, and it is a grade below." Once he has said that it is "another grade, which comes," etc., why did he go on to say "a grade below"? For it is understood of itself: since it is drawn from the right, it is certainly below the right. Second: his saying, "because by that good [the world] was built," etc., which is the reverse of what he explains at the end of his words; and the beginning contradicts the end. At the beginning he said that by the good the world is fed, and at the end he said that "good" is before the drawing-forth, when it does not feed at all; and he contradicts himself. Third: further, his saying, "even though it is one grade" — what is "even though"? Do not all the sefirot have aspects, each aspect with a title of its own, as is explained in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles? If so, what is "even though"? Fourth: his saying, "and from where do we know," etc. — why that? Let us say that they are two attributes, and that is why he asks of the attribute of good and of the attribute of Chesed; and there is no proof from the verse for what he intends. Fifth: according to the explanation that "good" is "when all is included," etc., which is a holding back of the effluence, so that it is not drawn forth — if so, why should David ask for "goodness," which is before it has spread out, since he has Chesed? Let him say "kindness" and be silent about "goodness." Sixth: as to the Grace after Meals, according to what he explained concerning "who feeds the whole world," etc. — if so, why should we say "goodness," so that we must afterward say "kindness"? Let us say "kindness" from the outset and be silent about "goodness"; better that we say the cure and not come to the wound at all. And to settle this passage we say that the sage who is the author of this passage found it difficult, in the Grace after Meals, that we say "in His goodness," so that we are compelled afterward to say "in grace, in kindness" to set it right; and it would have been better to say "in kindness" from the outset. And to answer this matter he first asked another question: the reason for what is said in Tractate Berakhot (fol. 50): "One who says 'from His goodness we live' is ignorant; 'and in His goodness we live' is wise." And he explained and said, "'And in His goodness' is the supernal right," meaning Chesed; and "from His goodness" is Yesod, which is drawn from Chesed, meaning Yesod, which receives from Chesed. And this is "from His goodness," whose explanation is "part of His goodness": the intent is the thing that is drawn from the good. And "in His goodness" means His goodness literally, that is, His Chesed. And this is what he says: "'from His goodness' — this is another grade, which comes from the side of the right," that is, from the side of Yesod, which is drawn from Chesed. And so that we not say that the explanation of "from His goodness" is "from the effluence of His goodness," that is, the effluence of the good, which is Chesed — for this he said, "and it is a grade below": meaning, it is literally another grade and another attribute, drawn from Chesed and sucking from it, not the effluence of Chesed itself. "Because by that good," etc.: it was difficult for him: since he has explained that "from His goodness" is another grade below, which is Yesod or another, then, since it is an attribute drawn from Chesed, why is one who says "from His goodness" ignorant? For "from His goodness" is an attribute that receives effluence from the supernal good. To this he gave a reason and said, "because by that good" — meaning, by the good of the upper world, which is Chesed, was the building of the world, as is known; and therefore the sustenance of the world and its effluence come from the place of its building. And therefore one who says "from His goodness" is ignorant; rather, the correct thing is "in His goodness," which is Chesed, for it built the world, and it sustains it and provides for it. "Why is it called 'good,' and why is it called 'Chesed'?": since both are in one aspect, according to what I explained, that by means of the good was the building of the world, that is, literally Chesed, as it is written, "The world is built by kindness" (Psalms 89:3) — if so, it turns out that they are equal aspects; and if so, why did their names change, since they are equal aspects according to your view? And to this he said, "It is 'good' when all is included within it and it has not spread out to descend below." The intent is that Chesed includes the whole Structure. And so the Zohar explained (in Parashat Balak, fol. 191), on the verse "And YHVH went before them by day [yomam]" (Exodus 13:21), that Chesed is called yomam, meaning a day that includes all the days; and we explained it in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles, under the entry yomam. And the intent is that Chesed includes all the extremities, in the secret of "For I said, the world [olam]" — which is the whole circumference [that is called olam] — "is built by kindness": meaning, by Chesed it was built, and became thick, and was revealed. And therefore, while it is in Chesed before its revealing, [as] an aspect being revealed, that aspect is called "good" [tov], which is from the expression "when he dresses [be-heitivo] the lamps" (Exodus 30:7); the intent is a light by which all of them shone with a great light, and before they were [dressed] they did not shine. And this is their building: their revealing and their tikkun into a manifestation that is revealed. And this is what he said: "when all is included within it and it has not spread out to descend below; it is 'Chesed,'" etc. That is, after the things there became thick and shone so as to be revealed, and spread out, then Chesed pours forth its effluence, and its nature is [to pour] upon the wicked and the good; and this is what is called Chesed, "and does not care." "Even though it is one grade": meaning, although all is one aspect — for the very one that was good is what became Chesed, since from the place where they were built their sustenance is drawn — nevertheless, with respect to these two matters, it is called by these two names. And so is the matter with the effluence: for in the good it shines and is revealed, and afterward it is called Chesed, because from there it is poured forth upon the wicked and the good, as we explained above. And now by this it is settled why we need to say in the Grace after Meals "goodness" and afterward "kindness," and likewise with David. For from the work of Creation we learn that the revealing must first be "good," and afterward be "Chesed"; if so, when we ask for sustenance, we need the good first, so that it become thick and be revealed, and afterward that it be drawn forth, that is, Chesed, which is [given] according to law and not according to law. And he proved the matter from David, peace be upon him, who said, "Surely goodness and kindness shall follow me," etc. And he asked: if David's need was for Chesed, that is, to pour forth according to law and not according to law, why did he ask of the attribute of good? Now, if he had Chesed, did he need goodness? And if he did not want the attribute of Chesed, so that it not be poured forth upon the enemies, but [wanted] the attribute of good — as it occurred to us that "good" is an intermediate attribute that pours forth upon the good — then why did he say "kindness," since Chesed is even for the wicked? Rather, what must you say? That "good" is the place in which the effluence shines, or [in which] the beings [become] a revealed being; and Chesed is their pouring forth after their revealing. And therefore he was compelled to say "goodness and kindness": goodness in order to bring the effluence into being, and kindness in order to pour it forth. If so, we too say so in the Grace after Meals: we need to mention these two matters, first "in His goodness," that is, the place where the effluence comes into being and is made good, and afterward "in kindness," that is, its drawing forth upon the wicked and the good. And so we learn from this passage that the attribute of Chesed is to pour forth upon the wicked and the good, as is proven from the plain sense of the words. And one cannot say that the aspect of good is what pours forth upon the righteous alone, and Chesed upon the wicked and the good, for several reasons. First, he said, "it is 'good' when all is included within it and it has not spread out to descend below"; and if it were true that the attribute of good pours forth upon the good, why did he say that it is called "good" when all is included, etc., "and it has not spread out"? Behold, it spreads out to pour forth upon the good! Further, his saying, "when it descends below and does good," etc., shows that when it does kindness with all, then it spreads out, and the spreading out was needed for the good as it was needed for the wicked. Rather, it must be as we have said: when it is called "good" it does not pour forth at all, for it is a holding back of the effluence, to receive a revealed being; and it is Chesed when it pours forth, for then its nature is to pour it forth upon the wicked and the good. It turns out that the attribute of Chesed, as its name, pours forth its effluence upon the wicked and the good.

Just as in the attribute of Chesed there is the virtue of the opening of the hand — not distinguishing between righteous and wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve Him, as regards the effluence and sustenance — so in the attribute of Gevurah there is the virtue of the closing of the hand: pouring forth only by the attribute of hard judgment, upon one who stood the test and was tested by it. As in the matter of Isaac, who stretched out his neck upon the altar for the service of his Master when he was in the full strength of his might, thirty-seven years old; and then it is in its hand to reward. And it is exacting with the righteous to a hair's breadth, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Kamma, fol. 50) on the verse "and round about Him it storms [nis'arah] mightily" (Psalms 50:3). And when a man sins, the outburst goes out from before it and destroys him in an instant. And since neither of these two extremes is the intent of the creation of the world, and the master of an extreme is not complete, as we shall explain, it was necessary that there be an arbiter between the two extremes; and that is the line of Rachamim. For from the side of Chesed they incline to the right, to the scale-pan of merit, and from the side of Gevurah they turn to the left, to the scale-pan of liability; and the line of Rachamim tips the balance between them. And since a third view does not arbitrate — rather, the inclination of the arbiter must be near to one of the two extremes — and since the line of Rachamim, being in the middle, includes both, it would tend to the mean, and this arbitration would be no arbitration; therefore it must be drawn from Keter Elyon, so that by the power of the compassion of the supernal whiteness it inclines to the side of Chesed. And this is what is called "inclining toward Chesed." And since Chesed "sits first in the kingdom" (see Esther 1:14), it was necessary to open with merit first. And this is the reason that our sages, of blessed memory, said, "one opens with merit first"; and if the Sanhedrin opened with guilt first, they would not judge him at all. And so our sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Sanhedrin, fol. 2): "'the congregation shall judge … and the congregation shall deliver' (Numbers 35:24–25) — we need a congregation that judges and a congregation that delivers"; for we need an allusion to the two powers of Din and Chesed. And since water and fire do not mix together except by means of an intermediary, because of their great distance, air was needed, which is the middle arbiter line, which includes the two extremes; and therefore it is called shamayim [heaven], whose intent is esh [fire] and mayim [water]. And one may ask: it would have been fitting to say "water-fire," for water is first, as we explained; if so, it ought to have been mayimesh. And one may say: since the intent of the arbitration is to incline toward Chesed, as we explained, for this reason he said first sh-mayim: the fire set toward the water. And this is the intent of the mishnah (Avot, chapter 5): "Every dispute that is for the sake of Heaven [shamayim] will in the end endure" — that is, Chesed and Gevurah, which are in dispute and delight in the middle arbitration, which is shamayim, as we explained. And therefore in the end it is united and endures, for it is within holiness and the pure Emanation. But a dispute that is not for the sake of Heaven, where they do not delight in arbitration but only dispute out of contentiousness, cleaves to the fire of Gehinnom, which is the husk that does not accept arbitration; and they are the side of the left, who always turn to the left, to the pan of liability, and do not want the arbitration of Chesed. And therefore separation is said of it, as in "And God separated between the light" — which is holiness — "and the darkness" (Genesis 1:4) — which is the darkness of Gehinnom, as in "and the wicked shall be silent in darkness" (1 Samuel 2:9). And it is separated from holiness because it distanced itself from the Din that accepts arbitration. So it was in the matter of Korach and his congregation, whose root was Levites, from the side of Gevurah; and Aaron the priest was the man of Chesed; and Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was the arbiter line, which is his attribute. And Korach's congregation did not want arbitration; therefore separation is said of them, as in "Separate yourselves from among this evil congregation" (Numbers 16:21). And therefore Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said, "But if YHVH creates a new thing," etc. (Numbers 16:30): since they had become equal to the evil husk, which is "evil congregation" — there is no congregation of fewer than ten, and it was evil — therefore he brought them into Gehinnom, kind to kind. But a dispute that is for the sake of Heaven is like the dispute of Hillel and Shammai. For Hillel was the Nasi, a man of Chesed, and Shammai the Av Beit Din, a master of Gevurah; and they are recognized by their attributes, for Hillel never grew irritated in his days, so as not to blemish his attribute, and Shammai was given to agitation, for his attribute caused it. And the root of their dispute was for the sake of Heaven, to accept arbitration; and therefore their dispute endured. And in this way will be understood what our sages, of blessed memory, said (Eruvin, fol. 13): "Why did Beit Hillel merit to have the halakhah fixed according to them? Because of their humility." And the intent is that they cleaved to the side of Chesed, in humility and lowliness and in being easygoing; and therefore the halakhah, which is the Shekhinah, is according to them, for her inclination is to the side of Chesed, as in what our sages, of blessed memory, said (Megillah, fol. 13): "Esther was greenish, but a thread of Chesed was drawn over her." And in this way will be understood what our sages, of blessed memory, said (there in Eruvin): "These and these are the words of the living God," etc. Meaning, "the living God" [Elohim Chayyim] is Binah, from which the whole Structure is poured forth. And he said that both those who declare impure, unfit and liable — who incline to the side of Gevurah, to stringency, to show that the husks have permission there, and therefore "liable, unfit, impure" — and those who declare pure, fit and innocent — who incline to the side of Chesed, to leniency, to show that the husks have no permission and dominion there, and therefore "innocent, fit and pure" — all is from Binah, from which is the pouring forth of the two extremes. And when the hand and the effluence that increases from one of the two lines prevails, then the halakhah is according to it, to forbid and to permit, etc. And therefore, both the one who declares pure and the one who declares impure, each one's words are correct. And therefore sometimes, too, the halakhah will be according to Beit Shammai, though with difficulty, for the greater inclination is to the side of Chesed. And to alert us to this matter our sages, of blessed memory, said, "Beit Hillel are lenient, Beit Shammai stringent" — this one to Chesed and that one to Gevurah, according to their attributes — except in a certain number of cases, as is known. And the reason for the reversal sometimes is in the way of "Here I am, my son" (Genesis 22:7): that sometimes Chesed is toward the side of Gevurah and Gevurah toward the side of Chesed, for fire is included in water and water included in fire, as we explained in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 16; and this is the reason for the Binding of Isaac, as is explained in the Zohar, in the portion of the Binding. And with this will be understood the reason for their reversal in some of the Trees [ilanot], Abraham to the left and Isaac to the right, especially in the parchment [Yeri'ah, a particular chart of the Tree].

After we have occupied ourselves in the previous chapters with the matter of arbitration, we shall now come, in these chapters, to the number of the arbiters. And what is agreed in the mouth of all the commentators is that the arbiters are two. The one is Tiferet, which tips the balance between Gedulah and Gevurah; and they are the three Patriarchs: Abraham, the man of Chesed; Isaac, the master of Gevurah; and Jacob, "a perfect [tam] man, dwelling in tents" (Genesis 25:27). And the explanation of tam: the intent is "complete." For it is not fitting that one be called complete in essence who is compelled to one action and does not change from it — like Gevurah, which is the power of judgment, and likewise Chesed, the power of kindnesses, which are the two extremes; and the extremes are not completeness. And so it is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Terumah (fol. 167), and these are its words: "'And God saw the light, that it was good' (Genesis 1:4): this is the pillar that stands in the middle, and stands and holds on this side and on that side. And when there was the completeness of the three sides, 'that it was good' is written of it, which was not [written] of those others, because there was no completeness until the third light, which completed all the sides. And once this third came, then it separated the dispute of the right and the left." Thus far its words.

And above this he explained that "Let there be light" is Chesed, and "and there was light" is Gevurah; and this is va-yehi, an expression of sorrow. And now he said that "And God saw the light, that it was good" is Tiferet. And he lengthened his language in saying, "this is the pillar that stands in the middle," etc. The reason is that Tiferet has two manifestations. The first is its simple manifestation, which is the self of Tiferet, the secret of the third line, the line of Rachamim, without its holding on to either of the extremes at all. And the second manifestation is its composition from three lines, three colors, and its arbitration among them, because it inclines toward one of them and reconciles them. And because deficiency already applies to the first manifestation as well — for it is a third view, being the line of Rachamim, a line by itself, without inclining toward either of the extremes, and this is no arbitration, for a third arbitration does not arbitrate — therefore it too is not called complete. But the second manifestation is called complete, for in it is the power of all three views; and for this he said, "this is the pillar that stands in the middle." And besides its being in the middle, "it stands and holds on this side and on that side," which is its being included of the three lines; and then it is complete. And this is what he said: "and when there was the completeness of the three sides," which is the completion of the three lines, which are Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet. And he was precise in what is expounded, in saying "the completeness of the three sides": for if the intent were Tiferet as intermediate between the two, he ought to have said "the completeness of the two," which are Gedulah and Gevurah. Rather, certainly it is as we explained: that it itself, in its first manifestation, needed peace in order to be an arbiter. And to stand on the clarification of this matter one must look into the Gate "Ten and Not Nine," chapter 2. And what we say, that the extremes are not in completeness — the intent is not deficiency, for there is no deficiency in the Emanation, God forbid, for there everything is in truth complete; and the intent in this is to put it gently to the ear. And the master of opposites is called complete in truth; and this applies only to Tiferet in its second manifestation, where it is called tam, complete. And this is what is said, "a perfect man, dwelling in tents": the intent is two tents, which are Gedulah and Gevurah. And to indicate the matter of this arbitration the author of Sefer Yetzirah said, in chapter 3, and these are his words: "Three mothers, Alef-Mem-Shin: their foundation is the pan of merit and the pan of liability, and the tongue of law tips the balance between them." Thus far his words.

And the intent is that the author of Sefer Yetzirah divided the letters into three parts with respect to creation. And the first part is Alef-Mem-Shin; and he called them "mothers" [immot] because they are mothers to all that is emanated and created and formed and made. And the meaning of our saying "mothers" is totality: in them everything is included, and from them everything goes out, as we shall explain. And there are those who explained the word Alef-Mem-Shin as the initials of emet [truth], mishpat [justice], shalom [peace]. And this is not correct, for these three words are titles of Tiferet, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles, and that is not the intent here, as we explained. And he said "guilt and merit and arbiter." There are those who explained that they are Gedulah, Gevurah, Tiferet; and this is the more correct and settled. And they are Alef-Mem-Shin: avir [air], mayim [water], esh [fire]: air is Tiferet, water Chesed, fire Gevurah. And it is already explained that in this world the element of fire is above and the element of water below, and the element of air is between the two, tipping the balance: equal to fire by its heat and to water by its moisture, for air is hot and moist. And the reason that water is below and fire above — the reverse of the Emanation, where Gedulah, the element of water, is above, and Gevurah, the element of fire, below — the reason is that earth is over against the fourth leg, which is Malkhut; and she is the upper element of earth, and of her it is explained, "Esther was greenish, and a thread of Chesed was drawn over her." And therefore He placed the element of water next to the element of earth, and impressed in it the imprint [teva] of heaviness, so that it would join to the earth. Another correct reason: the principal upper governance with the created is by means of Chesed, and so our sages, of blessed memory, explained; and the earth is the dwelling of the lowly lower ones; therefore He distanced them from judgment as far as possible, for everything that is nearer to the earth is more compassion than its fellow. And therefore upon the element of earth is the element of water, which is over against Chesed; and upon the element of water the element of air, which is over against Tiferet, which is compassion; and above all, fire, which is judgment, distant from the created by a third degree. And now one must ask: since Alef-Mem-Shin means air, water, fire, why is the element of earth not mentioned in the whole of Sefer Yetzirah, being the fourth element of creation, as we explained? And this thing will be understood from what the philosophers explained: that the element of earth, although it is a fourth element, is the totality of the first three elements, which are water, fire, air, and from them the fourth element came into being. And they gave a demonstration of this: if a person boils a vessel of water on the fire in such a way that its boiling never quiets or rests — and if the water lessens he adds more to it — until some time passes over it, there will come to be within the water an earthy matter like stone.

And behold, when a person considers in his mind the element of fire in its great power — for the compound fire among us is not one part of many of the elemental fire — with the great air blowing in the element of fire, and the water boiling in it, then the creation and coming-to-be of this earth will not be far from him. And since its coming-to-be is like a composition, as we explained, therefore Sefer Yetzirah mentions only the principal elements, which are air, water, fire. And likewise in the matter of the Emanation: it is all included in these three parts, which are air, the line of Rachamim; water, the line of Chesed; fire, the line of Din; and the action of Malkhut is an action composed of the three of them. And this is with respect to action, not with respect to the Emanation; for our intent here is not like the words of R. Yehudah Chayyat, God forbid — may the Compassionate One save us from his view. Rather, our intent is to her actions, which are from the side of her receiving from these three lines; and we already went at length on this in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 25, with the help of the Name. And this is what is meant here in our saying "mothers": that they are mothers to all the parts of existence. "Their foundation is the pan of merit," etc.: it is already known that the letters, in their spirituality, are an emanation emanated from the upper roots, and they are vessels and palaces for the honored roots, which are the sefirot, as we shall explain in the coming Gates. And therefore he said "their foundation": meaning, the foundation and root of these letters, which are Alef-Mem-Shin, is the pan of merit, etc. And "the pan of merit and the pan of liability" are Gedulah and Gevurah, with their upper sources, which are Chokhmah and Binah, as we shall explain. And "the tongue of law" is the middle line, the arbiter. And kaf [pan] is derived from "the pan of a balance"; and the intent is that Gedulah, which is the right, is the pan that weighs toward the pan of merit, and Gevurah, which is the left, is the pan that weighs toward the pan of liability. And "the tongue of law" is the tongue of the balance, whose place of inclination is toward the side of the arbitration. And in saying "the tongue of law" he intended that Tiferet is called "tongue" from the side of Binah, as we explained in the Gate "Ten and Not Nine," chapter 1; and he intended Tiferet and the manifestation of the concealed Da'at in Binah and from Binah upward, as we explained in the Gate of Whether the Ein Sof is the Keter, chapter 8; and they are two arbiters. And "law" [chok] is Yesod, the third arbiter, as we shall explain the matter of three arbiters in the coming chapters; and the three of them tip the balance between the pans of merit and the pans of liability. And we have already proved above, in the Gate "Ten and Not Nine," chapter 2, the matter of this arbiter from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him. And what is fitting that we know is that the completeness of the arbitration does not belong to Tiferet except by means of Malkhut. And the matter is this: Chesed is the element of water, and Gevurah the element of fire. And water and fire are opposites to one another in two respects: first, that water is cold and fire hot — behold one opposition; further, water is moist and fire dry — behold a second opposition. And therefore we needed two arbiters, for it is impossible with one. For air is hot and moist, and is equal to fire by its heat and to water by its moisture: fire comes and finds on its side the heat of the air; water comes and finds on its side the moisture of the air. It turns out that air reconciles them and tips the balance in these two respects. And still their dispute stands from the side of cold and dryness, until the element of earth, which is over against Malkhut, tips the balance between them. For earth is cold and dry: water comes and finds on its side the coldness; fire comes and finds on its side the dryness. And so earth turns out to be equal to both of them, and tips the balance. For it is impossible for one element to be composed of two literal opposites — of cold and heat, and moist and dry — which are two opposites in one subject. And in two subjects, which are fire and water, they are not equalized; all the more so they will not be equalized in one subject. Therefore they are equalized by there being in one subject two aspects that are not so opposite, like the cold and the dryness in earth and the heat and the moisture in air. And therefore the arbitration between Gedulah and Gevurah, which are fire and water, is only by means of Tiferet and Malkhut, which are air and earth.

And the matter of cold and moist in Chesed, and hot and dry in Gevurah, means that the actions in Chesed over against Gevurah are two, and likewise in Gevurah over against Chesed. The one is the arousal of Chesed to annul and extinguish the power of the fire, that is to say, to annul the judgment; and this is attributed to the word "cold," and the intent is that it cools the foreign heat poured forth from Gevurah, so that a person can live. And the second action of Chesed is to pour forth literal Chesed, so that the world be conducted in kindness. And this is a new manifestation, which is not the previous action, the action of coldness. That one is the matter of indignation, in which it is indignant at the angels of judgment [text: kings of judgment], so that they not act, and quiets the power of judgment and cools the fire of Gehinnom; afterward it must pour forth the effluence of Chesed, which is to conduct the world by its attribute; and this is attributed to the name "moisture," which is the pouring forth of literal water that moistens the thirsty. And likewise Gevurah has two actions opposite to Chesed. The first is a power of arousal to annul and to dry up the power of the moisture, and to be indignant at the angels of Chesed and at Chesed, so that the world not be conducted by it; and this is attributed to the word "dry," and the intent is that it dries up the moisture of the waters poured forth from Chesed. And the second action of Gevurah is to pour forth and arouse literal judgment in the world, so that the world be conducted by the attribute of judgment and by its mighty acts and its powers. And this is a new manifestation, which is not the previous action: for the action of drying is indignation, in which it is indignant at the angels of Chesed so that they not act, and quiets their power and dries up their moisture; afterward it must pour forth the effluence of Gevurah, which is to conduct the world in judgment; and this is attributed to the name "heat," which warms and burns.

And behold, the nature of Tiferet is hot and moist, because these are two aspects that are not so opposite, being the pouring forth of judgment and compassion together. For it is impossible for it to be hot and cold, for the cold is to annul the power of the heat — that is, the pouring forth of Chesed to annul the pouring forth of judgment, as we explained; and likewise it is impossible for it to be dry and moist, for dryness is the power of Gevurah to annul the effluence of Chesed, which is moisture. Therefore the Emanator impressed in it the power of heat and moisture, which is the pouring forth of judgment and compassion. And to say that it would be cold and dry is impossible, for coldness and dryness are to annul the power of heat and moisture, and it is what blends the two governances and pourings forth together. And if Chesed and Gevurah were further to pour forth the power of dryness and coldness, then the blending of Tiferet's pouring forth would not avail, for its actions would be annulled: by the cold poured forth from Chesed the action of the heat in it would be annulled, and by the dryness poured forth from Gevurah the power of the action of the moisture in it would be annulled. Therefore Malkhut came, and the Emanator impressed in her that she blend the cold and the dryness, so that the actions of Tiferet not be annulled. So we learn that the matter of the arbitration of Gedulah and Gevurah is by means of Tiferet and Malkhut. And we shall go on at length further in the matter of this arbitration in the Gate of Particulars of Names, chapter 16. And the inquirer needs understanding and contemplation in these matters, with good insight.

After we have occupied ourselves in the previous chapter with the one arbiter, which is Tiferet, between Gedulah and Gevurah, we come to explain the matter of the other arbiter, which is Yesod, which tips the balance between Netzach and Hod. And so all the commentators agreed, and called it the second arbiter. And the matter is that Netzach is the branch of Chesed and Hod the branch of Gevurah, and as is the action of the roots, so is the action of the branches. And therefore, just as the matter of arbitration was needed between the two roots, as expounded in the previous chapter, so the matter of arbitration was needed between the branches. And this arbiter between the two branches is also a branch of the upper arbiter root, for Yesod is the branch of Tiferet, as is explained in the previous Gates. And so they called it "the extension of the Vav"; and the matter of its arbitration is explained in the Zohar in many places. And these are its words in Parashat Vayikra (fol. 12b): "Rabbi Yehudah said to him: 'Thanksgiving' [todah] is known; 'his peace-offerings' [shelamav] — what is it? Two. He said to him: Two Vavs,  V V, that is shelamav: the peace of all." Thus far its words.

And the intent is: "thanksgiving" is known to be in Malkhut; but "his peace-offerings" was difficult for me, for he ought to have said "upon the sacrifice of thanksgiving of his peace-offering [shelamo]," that is, Tiferet, which is called "peace" [shalom], with which the thanksgiving is united. And he explained that shelamav are two Vavs, for both of them are called "peace": Tiferet, peace between Gedulah and Gevurah, and Yesod, peace between Netzach and Hod, as we explained. And there are many passages in the Zohar on this which indicate this matter. And according to this it turns out that Netzach is the element of water, and Hod the element of fire, and Yesod the element of air, and Malkhut beneath them the element of earth. And so Rashbi explained in Bereshit Rabbah (chapter 11), and these are his words: "Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai taught: The Sabbath said before the Holy One, blessed be He: To each You have given a mate [ben zug], and to me You have given no mate. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to it: Knesset Yisrael shall be your mate. And when Israel stood before Mount Sinai, He said to them: Remember that thing that I said to the Sabbath, 'Knesset Yisrael shall be your mate [bat zug].'" Thus far his words.

And R. Menachem Recanati explained, and these are his words: "'Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy' (Exodus 20:8): the Sabbath alludes to the Foundation of the world, which is the foundation of the souls. And before the diminution of the moon, when the two kings used one crown, the Sabbath had no mate to receive from it, as the other beings have, until the moon was diminished; and then the upper Knesset Yisrael was given to it as a mate. 'They are joined one to another' (Job 41:9); 'like a man joined with his companion' (1 Kings 7:36) — as a man clinging to his companion." Thus far his words.

And behold, according to what appears from his wording, he wished to explain that Yesod asked for a sefirah beneath it into which it would pour forth. And it is difficult: what was Yesod's intent in this? For that sefirah that would be beneath it would also ask who would be its mate. And the existence of the world is impossible unless there is one sefirah that receives from all, poured into and not pouring forth. And what was its intent? If the Emanator emanated another sefirah beneath it, that other would also ask for its mate, and another, another; if so, the thing has no end. And if the intent is to say that it would be ninth and the other tenth, then one must ask what its intent was: "What makes you think that your blood is redder?" Will not the tenth also say, "To each You gave a mate, and from me You withheld a mate"? Further, it asked for a ben zug, which appears to be asking for a male, and did not say bat zug, which is a female. Further, according to his explanation, the matter of this request was for a female mate, and they answered it "Knesset Yisrael," which is Malkhut — and this was before the accusation. Is He "awesome in His dealings" (Psalms 66:5) with His emanated ones, that before the moon had accused she was given as a mate to Yesod, for when she would accuse? I am astonished! Further, the accusation of Yesod would be greater than the accusation of the moon; and this is forced, for the moon was stricken, and this one was healed. Further, after the thing is set right, when it is so, who will be its mate?

Therefore it seems [right] to explain that Yesod did not ask for a mate to pour forth upon; for such is the way of the sefirot, to pour forth, and what is it to them whether they pour forth into another sefirah or into the grade beneath them? Rather, its question was: "To each" — that is, Tiferet — "You have given a mate," so that by means of both of them there would be the arbitration; "and to" Yesod "You have given no mate" for the arbitration, but it alone would tip the balance. And they answered it, "Knesset Yisrael shall be your mate." And there is no doubt that this matter was before the accusation; and nevertheless they answered it, "Knesset Yisrael shall be your mate," because Malkhut serves above and below for the arbitration. For by means of Malkhut and Yesod there is peace between Netzach and Hod: before her descent she would serve above and below, with Tiferet between Gedulah and Gevurah, and with Yesod between Netzach and Hod — and this although she is certainly above them; and all the more so now, after the accusation. And this matter is necessitated by what is explained in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Pinchas, fol. 247), in the matter of "it is impossible for two kings to use one crown": that Netzach and Hod were sucking from Malkhut, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Diminution of the Moon. And therefore the arbitration was by means of Malkhut joining with Tiferet and with Yesod, and the arbitration is completed by her means. It turns out that the arbitration of Tiferet is no arbitration except by means of Malkhut, and the arbitration of Yesod is no arbitration except by means of Malkhut. And therefore we were commanded concerning "Remember the Sabbath day," whose intent is to unite Malkhut with Tiferet and with Yesod, so that their arbitration be complete. And this is what appears to us in the explanation of this passage. And now, after the accusation, too, the arbitration is by her means. For even whenever she rises to the bosom of her husband, nevertheless her manifestation remains below; and so they explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 1, fol. 16b). And likewise, whenever she comes below, her manifestation is above, in the secret of "Set me as a seal" (Song of Songs 8:6), as is explained there. And there is a great difference between the arbitration of Tiferet and the arbitration of Yesod: for the arbitration of Tiferet is to the right, inclining toward Chesed, and the arbitration of Yesod is toward the left. And the reason is that Tiferet, since it sucks from the supernal whiteness, inclines toward Chesed. But Yesod, when effluence is poured upon it from Tiferet, it does not suffice to incline it to the side of compassion; rather, its inclination is toward judgment, by the intent of its Emanator — so that the whole inclination not be to the right by means of Tiferet, but that there be some counterweight to it: Yesod, which inclines to the side of judgment. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim, and we explained it in the Gate "Ten and Not Nine," chapter 2.

After we have explained in the previous chapters the matter of arbitration for the two arrays, which are the lower and the middle, it is fitting that we look closely at the third, upper array, which is the first three: whether arbitration applies to them, or who would be the arbiter. And as to whether an arbiter applies to them, we could already say that there is no arbiter between them and they do not need one, because they are simple compassion; and even Binah is not judgment in essence, but by reason of the pouring forth to Gevurah, as we explained in the Gate of Essence and Governance. And nevertheless there is some support from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that they need arbitration, as we shall explain, because they are roots for the revealed actions. And there are those who thought that Chokhmah is complete judgment, and Keter compassion, and Binah not so much, and that she tips the balance between Chokhmah and Keter. And they said that Keter is white points, the utmost whiteness, according to the number of keter [620]; and Chokhmah thirty-two red points, the utmost redness; and Binah fifty points inclining to redness and to whiteness.

And behold, they intended explicitly that Binah tips the balance between Chokhmah and Keter. And they wished to find support in her name: that she is called Binah from the expression bein [between], as in "the man in between" (1 Samuel 17:4), because she tips the balance between the two attributes, Keter and Chokhmah. And we already wrote this opinion in the Gate of Essence and Governance, chapter 5. And likewise among the holders of this opinion are those who draw Keter on the right and Chokhmah on the left and Binah in the middle, as we wrote in the Gate of the Order of Their Standing, chapter 1 — although R. Shem Tov wished to reverse the matter according to his way, as we explained there. And there is some support for this view in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Pinchas, fol. 247), and these are its words: "'And I am in the midst of the exile' (Ezekiel 1:1): this is the Shekhinah; in her the Holy One, blessed be He, is one, the Vav in addition: va-ani [and I]. He is the river, the Righteous One, Life of the Worlds. 'And a river goes out from Eden to water the garden' (Genesis 2:10): what is Eden? This is Binah. The river that goes out from her — this is Vav, ben Yah [the son of  Y H], the grade of the Faithful Shepherd. And the Faithful Shepherd goes out from the supernal Imma and spreads into six sefirot as far as the Righteous One, and from him he waters the garden, which is the Shekhinah. What is Kevar [Chebar]? Kaf, Keter; Bet, Binah; Resh, reshit [beginning], Chokhmah: Keter on the right, Chokhmah on the left, Binah in the middle; rekhev [chariot] above, to the Cause of Causes. All ten sefirot are included in the river, which spreads out as far as the Righteous One, who is kol [all], including all; and on his account they established it: 'a great and mighty tree,' etc.; and on it all depends." Thus far its words.

And the explanation of this passage according to them is: Keter on the right, in the secret of Chesed and whiteness; Chokhmah on the left, in the secret of judgment and redness; and Binah in the middle, in the secret of compassion, tipping the balance between the right and the left. But it is not fitting to believe that this passage teaches us about the matter of judgment and compassion and arbitration. For we proved in the Gate of Essence and Governance that Keter is simple compassion, and likewise Chokhmah is compassion but not like the compassion of Keter, and Binah compassion but not like the compassion of Chokhmah; and likewise we proved in the Gate of the Order of Their Standing that Chokhmah is on the right, in the secret of the line of Chesed, and Binah on the left, in the secret of the line of Din, because "from her judgments are aroused," etc.; and all this by the power of the passages of the Zohar. And since this is so, how is it possible that we should say that she tips the balance between Keter and Chokhmah, both of which are more compassion than she, when she does not incline toward one of them but is an aspect by itself, less compassion than both — besides other reasons that we have explained? And from this passage there is no proof for this matter at all, as we shall explain. And this is its explanation. "And I am in the midst of the exile — this is the Shekhinah": meaning, Malkhut, which is called "I" [ani], as is known and will be explained in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles, with the help of the Name. "In her the Holy One, blessed be He, is one, the Vav in addition: va-ani": meaning, the Vav of va-ani alludes to Tiferet, united with Malkhut. And the intent is that both of them were with them in the exile, to guard them; for this matter was needed, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Zohar (Lech Lecha, fol. 85, and at the beginning of Parashat Shemot), that this prophecy was a need of the hour. "He is the river, the Righteous One, Life of the Worlds": meaning, the river mentioned in the verse is the Righteous One, Life of the Worlds, which is Yesod. And he intended to title it by the name "Life of the Worlds" because his intent is to say that it waters the garden; and this is its title "Life of the Worlds," whose explanation is that it gives effluence and vitality to all the worlds. And the intent of the verse is that he saw Malkhut united with Tiferet upon Yesod, according to her way before the diminution and at the time of the union. "And a river goes out from Eden: what is Eden," etc.: his intent in all this length is because his intent is to explain "river" as the Righteous One, as we explained. And this is forced, for the principal [sense of the] word "river" is in Tiferet.

And further, the expression "goes out from Eden" does not settle. For granted, Tiferet literally goes out from Eden, which is the first three; but Yesod does not literally go out from Eden, for it receives from Eden by means of Tiferet. And perhaps because of this we would be forced to say that Eden is Tiferet and the river that goes out from it is the Righteous One; and then the expression "goes out from Eden" would be correct, for according to this way it literally goes out from Eden, which is Tiferet. For this he said first, "what is Eden? This is Binah": the intent is that the title "Eden" is not correct everywhere, but at the least in Binah or from Binah upward, as we shall explain in the Gate of the Glossary of Titles. And he said "this is Binah," and not another title, to show that the word Binah indicates this permutation, which is ben Yah [B N  Y H], as he goes on to explain: that it is the river, Tiferet, that truly goes out from Eden. And he said, "this is Vav, the grade of the Faithful Shepherd," to allude to the manifestation of the concealed Da'at, which is the grade of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, as we explained in the Gate "Ten and Not Nine," chapter 2. And it is the manifestation of Vav, which includes all six extremities and spreads out within them and waters them in a concealed and hidden way. And he intended Da'at, so that it would be possible for the river to be in Tiferet and possible also in the Righteous One; for in the secret of Da'at it begins from Tiferet and spreads out and goes as far as the Righteous One, for so it includes six sefirot, according to the number of Vav. And this is what he said, "goes out from the supernal Imma," which is the precision of the expression "goes out from Eden"; "and spreads into six sefirot as far as the Righteous One" — that is, the Righteous One itself is the river, since it is the extension of the river. "And from him he waters the garden, which is the Shekhinah": meaning, if we say that the whole essence of the river is Tiferet, the expression "to water the garden" will not be precise, because it does not water by itself, but by means of Yesod; and if so, the expression "to water the garden" will not settle. And to say that the Shekhinah is above with Tiferet, in the secret of her place before the diminution, is impossible; for the verse said "to water the garden," and she is called "garden" in the secret of her aspect in the tenth grade. And this is what he was precise about in his wording, saying, "and from him he waters the garden": that is, "from him," by means of the Righteous One, for he is the true waterer. And he was precise in saying "the garden, which is the Shekhinah," for she is called Shekhinah when she dwells and resides among the lower ones; and in that aspect she is called "garden," which is a lower aspect, receiving upon itself all the plantings, in the aspect that is below Yesod. And therefore it was necessary that Yesod be the one who waters the garden; and the matter of the river is as we explained. "What is Kevar," etc.: to understand this matter it is fitting to know that Chokhmah and Binah are  Y H, as is known. And sometimes they are  Y H, whose explanation is that the male, which is Yod, rules over the female, which is Heh; and sometimes they are  H Y, for sometimes the female rules over the male. And Keter is always over both of them, whether it be this way or that.

And the matter of our saying that Heh rules over Yod, or Yod over Heh: the intent is that in Binah there is the aspect of Chokhmah, and in Chokhmah the aspect of Binah, in the secret of "Set me as a seal" (Song of Songs 8:6); for after both of them are united, they are sealed in one another and pictured in one another. And since Chokhmah is the male and the aspect of Binah is subordinate to it, therefore from its side Yod prevails over Heh, and it is male; and this is why Chokhmah is called  Y H. And since Binah is female relative to Chokhmah — for so they are called Abba and Imma — the aspect of Chokhmah is subordinate to her; therefore from her side Heh prevails over Yod, and she is female; and this is the  H Y  of Elohim. It turns out according to this that Keter is always more compassion than both of them and does not change, but Chokhmah and Binah exchange according to their aspect. And Rashbi explained that from the side of Yesod Heh prevails over Yod; that is to say, in Yesod these two sefirot appear with Binah above Chokhmah. And perhaps the reason is that since Yesod inclines toward judgment, as we explained in the previous chapter, therefore from its side it shows, in the matter of prophecy, the power of judgment, which is the prevailing of female over male, which is judgment — as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained: "every havayah in which Heh rules over Yod," etc., "is female and judgment." And from the side of Tiferet, whose inclination is toward compassion, it shows, in the matter of prophecy, the power of compassion, which is the prevailing of Yod over Heh. And so Rashbi taught us in the Ra'aya Mehemna (Vayikra, fol. 17), and these are his words: "The Righteous One includes six grades; and therefore they instituted to interpret a dream by it with three 'peaces' and three 'redemptions,' which are six, the number of Vav. And he is the ladder of Jacob's dream, which includes six sefirot. 'Set up on the earth' (Genesis 28:12): the lower Shekhinah, and this is the lower Heh. 'And its top': this is Yod; in it he is the seventh, the Righteous One. 'Reaching to heaven': this is the supernal Imma, and this is the upper Heh. For from the side of the dream Heh rules over Yod, which is the top of the ladder:  H Y  of Elohim. And therefore, 'and behold, the angels of Elohim ascending,' etc., and not the angels of YHVH." Thus far his words.

And although this passage needs a broad explanation, nevertheless from it we have learned that from the side of the Righteous One, which is the ladder, which is Vav, with the Yod, which is its top, it becomes Zayin. And this is what he says, "in it he is the seventh, the Righteous One": meaning, after it is with the Yod, the top of the Vav, it becomes Zayin, which is the diadem on the head of the Righteous One; and it is the Sabbath of rest. And this top of his reaches to heaven, which is Binah. It turns out that the Heh of Binah is over the Yod. And he said "from the side of the dream," for Jacob's vision was in a dream. And from the side of the Righteous One, Malkhut is called "a vision in a dream," as Rashbi explained (in Tikkun 18, fol. 30), and these are his words: "In the closing of the eyes she is called 'a vision in a dream'; and the secret of the matter is 'I sleep, but my heart wakes' (Song of Songs 5:2). And in the opening of the eyes she is 'a vision in waking,' etc. From the side of the central pillar the Shekhinah is 'a vision in waking,' and Moses on its side, of whom it is written, 'mouth to mouth I speak with him' (Numbers 12:8). From the side of the Righteous One, who is the light stored away for the righteous in the future to come (another version: for the World to Come), she is called 'a vision in a dream.'" Thus far his words.

And behold, from this passage it is explained that, apart from the prophecy of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, all the prophecy of the other prophets is from the side of "a vision in a dream," that is, from the side of the Righteous One. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (in the Introduction, fol. 6) that the prophecy of Ezekiel, in his ten visions, was a vision in the closing of the eyes. And the principle that emerges from all this is that Malkhut is "a vision in a dream," and the closing of the eyes is from the side of Yesod, from whose side it was necessary that the Yod be under the Heh. And since the prophecy of Ezekiel was in the closing of the eyes, as we explained, therefore it appeared to him that Binah is above Chokhmah. And by this will be explained the length of the wording of the passage, which said, "all ten sefirot are included in the river, which spreads out as far as the Righteous One": the intent is that since the totality of the river is in the Righteous One, there is no wonder that the river is called  K B R  [Kevar], whose explanation is Keter, Binah, Chokhmah, in the reverse of the order of the attributes; and it is not called  K R B, whose explanation is Keter, Chokhmah, Binah, in the order of the attributes — for the reason that the essence of the river is drawn to the Righteous One. And this is a proof that the river is the Righteous One and not Tiferet: for if the river were Tiferet, it would have been fitting that the attributes be in their order, that is,  K R B. Rather, certainly the river is the Righteous One, which is the principal extension of the river, and from its side the order is  K B R, which is Heh over Yod, as we explained. And with this it turns out that there is no proof at all from this passage for the views that Binah tips the balance between Keter and Chokhmah. (See Pelach ha-Rimmon, Gate 6, chapter 2, and you will understand; it is enough for the understanding. And see Asis Rimmonim.)
